paragraphs: Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.

The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.
He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1% each year.

Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.
Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.
It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.
In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.

Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.

Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.
The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.

Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."
The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.

After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.
Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.
Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.
With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.
Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres.
Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.

It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.

And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.
The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.
Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

articles.title: 'I wasn't thinking straight' says five jobs civil servant
articles.standfirst: Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently juggling multiple public sector jobs.
paragraphs: Kashim Chowdhury wears dark sunglasses, a hat, hoody and gloves as he arrives at court. His face is largely obscured.
A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple public sector jobs has told the court he "wasn't thinking straight" when he allegedly misled future bosses about his employment status.
Kashim Chowdhury said he was "in a panic" when he applied for a job at the Department of Health (DHSC), failing to declare he was already working at the Department for the Environment (Defra).
The prosecution said he already had three full-time jobs at the time, including roles at the London Borough of Tower Hamlets and East London NHS Trust.
The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

Chowdhury said he was "in a panic'' because he feared losing his Defra job and was uncertain about his future. He told the jury he was "not paying attention, I was not thinking straight',' when filling out the application.
The prosecution said Chowdhury held five jobs on full-time salaries at the height of the alleged deceit.
In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Defra, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office.

The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.
Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work-from-home culture which began during the Covid-19 pandemic to hide his multiple jobs and took sick leave from some employers to manage the workload.
But Chowdhury told the court he had not wanted the jobs at the DHSC, Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office.

He told the jury: ''I sent out a flurry of these applications. The offers for these jobs came all at once. I had discussions with my line managers saying that I did not want these jobs and explained my circumstances. These were all short term and probationary and my priority was to look after my mother.''
He added that around May and June 2022, his mother's health "deteriorated".
He said: "That overwhelmed me at the time. It just destroyed me."
Chowdhury described the jobs as his "lifeline at the time".
"They gave me a link to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time."

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".
The trial continues.

articles.title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
articles.standfirst: The bank says it is using more AI leading to a 5% reduction in its workforce.
paragraphs: Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.
The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.
The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.
Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.
Although not all of the cuts are due to AI, their scale will prompt further concern over the impact of the new technology.
Company spending on AI is increasing along with claims new tools can replace some of the basic tasks currently done by staff such as administrative and programming work.
HSBC, Standard Chartered and Danske Bank have also flagged AI-related job cuts this year.
"It is a hot button topic," said AJ Bell investment analyst, Russ Mould.

However, banks had not yet made big moves towards the widespread introduction of AI and they would be considering the implications for security and customer service before implementing AI technology to make financial savings, he said.
"Any company at any time needs to keep on top of its cost base," he said.
"It will be intriguing to see what other banks say in their results in the coming weeks.
Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union that represents banking sector workers said the company was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce".

"Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," she said.
Barclays is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme  focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.
AJ Bell's Russ Mould said despite "reaching for the AI lever" Barclays had failed to match expectations with its financial results.
Barclays also revealed it made £2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.
Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business.
"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future.
"We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake.
"Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."
Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.
Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".
"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.
Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further £1.1bn of savings in 2027.
How has AI changed your job or the type of work your do?

articles.title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?
articles.standfirst: How fair are AI recruitment tools that help decide our future, and what happens when we click "apply"?
paragraphs: Sheeraz Gulsher says there are "huge worries" about AI
I have lost track of the number of people who have told me they have applied for hundreds of jobs, only to be met with rejection after rejection.
Often, they said it felt like a human had not even looked at their applications.

There are lots of different types of recruitment tools. Some match candidates to jobs, others grade and screen CVs. Employers use them to save time sifting through applications, but there are growing concerns that these tools could be biased.
I want to find out how fair AI recruitment tools being used to help decide our futures really are - and what happens when we click "apply".
There are concerns about the increasing use of AI in recruitment
A London-based non-profit organisation, People Like Us, is raising awareness of people's legal right to challenge automated decisions when they disagree with the outcome.
A survey conducted by Censuswide among 2,000 UK workers who had applied for at least one job in the past 24 months found that 75% were unaware of their right to challenge an automated rejection.

Sheeraz Gulsher, CEO of People Like Us, is leading the campaign called Reject the Rejections, which calls on employers to improve transparency and accountability in the use of AI and automated recruitment systems.
He describes the current situation as an "AI war", with candidates "resorting to AI to bolster their applications" while "employers are dealing with huge amounts of applications".

Gulsher said: "We can't say for certain that every company is operating its automated or AI systems without bias. That's why we're calling for companies to audit these systems, publish the results and have them independently assessed.

"In our research, we found guidance from the Information Commissioner's Office stating that people subject to certain automated decisions have the right to request a human review. We're trying to remind people of that right, as many simply aren't aware of it."

The research also found 70% of ethnically diverse jobseekers had altered or concealed information on their CVs, including their country of origin, religion or name, out of fear that recruitment software or AI tools would reject their applications. This compares with 57% of white candidates.
Vivi says she needs feedback as a jobseeker
Business consultant Vivi, who lives in Lewisham, was made redundant earlier this year. She says she has applied for so many jobs that she's given up and started her own company.

"There's one instance where applications closed on Friday and I got a reply on a Saturday morning basically saying that I should work on my skills and come back in six months. But it was so obvious that nobody had assessed my skills."
If she had known she could ask for a human to review her application, she might have done things differently.
"I would definitely go back and ask for a human to look at my application and if it is a 'no', that's fine, but feedback helps me as a jobseeker."
Hema was made redundant in June
Hema, 49, from Surrey, is an HR and talent professional who has worked internationally across multiple sectors.
She was made redundant in June and has since tracked more than 100 job applications and recruitment opportunities.
"A lot of them have been automatically rejected within 24 to 36 hours."
She added: "I've always landed a job in 10 applications, so to be nearing 100 is completely out of this world."
While she is "hesitant" about asking for a human review in case she jeopardises her application, she believes "a human recruiter can see the fuller picture".
"If you've got an in-house recruitment team, they know the culture, they can see the type of language that you're using in your CV, in your cover letter, during a phone screen."
Of the 425 recruiters CV-Library spoke to, about 90 said they used AI in the CV screening stage.
Alec Stanwell, director of marketing, believes there is a "perception gap".

"Candidates almost universally believe that employers are using AI to screen their CVs, filter them and to screen them as they go through the process and that is happening but nowhere near as much as candidates think it is.
"That perception gap is a problem because candidates are now writing their CVs, and applications, through the lens of 'an AI bot is going to be reviewing this rather than a human'.
He adds this is a problem because recruiters are seeing all CVs look the same because "they're all written by AI, or polished by AI".
He says this creates a "perfect storm" because AI is then more likely to be used to filter through a large volume of applications.
"We're going to end up with computers hiring computers, but we're actually in the world of hiring people."
In the four years to December 2022, Stanford researchers analysed four million job applications processed by an AI hiring tool.
Some candidates were rejected from multiple roles more often than would have been expected if they had been assessed by each employer independently.
The analysis also indicated black and Asian applicants were recommended for jobs at lower rates.
But the evidence is limited. They only looked at one AI hiring tool, and other factors such as education and immigration status could have also played a role.
The hiring tool assessed did not respond to our requests for comment.
The people I have interviewed are not talking about any company in particular, but concerns over AI used in recruitment are also playing out in the courts.
One company, Workday, is facing legal claims in the US, alleging that its tools discriminated against job applicants.
The case is ongoing, but Workday denies the claims and says its tools do not make hiring decisions.
More generally, it says its tools "support rather than replace human judgement".
Barb Hyman's company grades candidates on text-based chat interviews
What makes this even more difficult is that AI hiring tools work in different ways, with some not even screening CVs in the first place.
I spoke to one company that grades candidates on text-based chat interviews.

Barb Hyman, founder of Sapia AI, said: "We don't know anything about you from a demographic perspective and we don't know whether or not you were hired or not hired for a previous role. So I think you've really got to look at the nature of the AI and how it's built. Not all AI is the same.

"At least in the enterprise space, every company we speak to is very conscious of the EU AI Act, even if they don't see themselves as having to comply with that yet. And that requires a level of accountability."
She added: "No company ever built a high-performing culture by monitoring its people, and you won't build a fair hiring process by policing candidates either.
"Start by earning candidates' trust: tell them what you're measuring, how they'll be scored, and give them feedback. Fraud gets smaller when people trust the process."
Alec Samways says his company has seen "huge uptick" in applications, which "all look the same"

Alec Samways, CEO of London-based Splendid Communications, says they usually get three to four hundred applications for three places on their annual intern programme but last year they saw triple the numbers.
"We saw a huge uptick in applications, but strangely, they all look the same. Our suspicion was candidates all of a sudden were using AI to make the applications themselves."
Samways used two different AI tools to help the company understand how much of the content was produced by AI but they "produced such a variety of responses".
"We found we couldn't trust them and we had to literally sift through those, applications in a human way in the end.
"It's just clear that at this point we're not prepared to trust AI for this kind of decision-making."
An ICO spokesperson said AI and automation could "make recruitment quicker and more efficient" but "must not come at the expense of people's rights".
They said: "Employers should be upfront about when automated decision-making is being used, how it works and how it could affect someone's application.
"Bias can appear at different stages of building and using AI products, and we expect all organisations to take steps to identify and mitigate it."

A government spokesperson said that "while AI can help employers manage large volumes of applications and reduce administrative burdens, it is vital that recruitment processes remain fair, transparent and accessible".
They added: "Existing legal protections, including equality and data protection law, already apply to AI systems, and we will act where additional protections are needed."
There seems to be a real fear of the unknown because we are often unsure what happens on the other end once we click "apply".
But given it seems AI is here to stay, how can we ensure it's fair?

articles.title: Jackdaw is a distraction from Aberdeen’s much bigger problem
articles.standfirst:
This article was originally published on our Substack. After years of back and forth and months of mounting speculation, this week the Government gave the green light to the Jackdaw gas field. But one small hydrocarbon project dominating headlines risks missing the much bigger – and more important – question over where tomorrow’s good jobs … Continued
The post Jackdaw is a distraction from Aberdeen’s much bigger problem appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: After years of back and forth and months of mounting speculation, this week the Government gave the green light to the Jackdaw gas field. But one small hydrocarbon project dominating headlines risks missing the much bigger – and more important – question over where tomorrow’s good jobs in Aberdeen will come from.

When we visited Aberdeen earlier this year, we saw what the city has to offer and the incredible depth of expertise and infrastructure it has built over decades, but to put this to best use, we need to start focusing more on the city’s future and less on its past.

Aberdeen remains at the centre of the UK’s oil and gas industry, and when the industry has boomed so has the city. In the early 2010s, total disposable incomes in Aberdeen exceeded the UK average by a fifth, and the earnings of people working in the city by almost half (47 per cent).

The flip side to this is that when the industry has suffered so too has the city. When oil prices halved between 2014 and 2016, the city sank into decline, and Aberdeen’s earnings premium over the rest of the UK has since fallen by three-quarters, while payrolled employment is down 8 per cent since 2015.

Now, Aberdeen faces a new problem: after extracting close to 48 billion barrels of oil equivalent, reserves are running dry. UK oil and gas production is down 76 per cent on its 1999 peak and is set to fall by another 40 per cent by 2030 (and by over 90 per cent by 2050). While Jackdaw will increase output, its contribution will only be marginal: the new field will generate fewer than 30 permanent roles.
For Aberdeen and its specialised workforce there is now no other option than to look elsewhere for jobs that can fill the gap the oil and gas industry is already leaving behind.
Green jobs can help but aren’t arriving fast enough or are arriving in the wrong order

Aberdeen is a natural fit for offshore wind thanks to its subsea engineering capability, offshore logistics, deep harbour, and long experience with operating in harsh North Sea conditions. But despite Scotland’s largest offshore wind farm, Seagreen, sitting nearby, the city hasn’t seen the green jobs boom it was hoping for.

Much of this is down to timing, as wind capacity has arrived before the grid upgrades that would enable the electricity generated to be used by households across Britain. As a result, much of Scottish wind capacity is being wasted (‘curtailed’). In 2024, energy from Seagreen was curtailed in 71 per cent of the hours it was available at a cost of £65 million.

To prevent future bottle necks, ministers will need to ensure that infrastructure is built in a sensible order by aligning Scottish capacity targets with the grid timetable. As it stands, the grid reinforcements that are needed to carry Scottish wind south will not be complete until the 2030s – several years after a wind farm consented today would start generating.

With oil already declining and more green jobs years away, there’s a risk that Aberdeen loses the highly skilled engineering base that took half a century to build. In the year to mid-2023 alone, 4,400 Aberdonians voted with their feet and left for overseas destinations.

In the short-term, decommissioning work (making safe old rigs, wells and pipes) can help bridge the gap and draw on the skills that the city already has. The part of the North Sea currently serviced out of Aberdeen is expected to account for 60 per cent of national decommissioning spending over the next 10 years, with demand for workers increasing to a peak in 2029.

To get the most out of this inherently temporary work, the Government should attach domestic content conditions to the tax relief that funds much of decommissioning and treat dismantling capacity at ports as national infrastructure to ensure as much of the work as possible is based in Scotland, rather than hubs on the other side of the North Sea.

Decommissioning activity, grid investment and wind infrastructure all need to be timed against one another so that workers and the firms employing them can clearly see where the next five years of work comes from.

This kind of coordination would be a major departure from the reliance on market timing that has characterised the North Sea hydrocarbon industry, and that underpins the UK Government’s competition-led, ‘place-blind’ approach to renewable energy subsidies. But to future-proof Aberdeen’s workforce the UK and Scottish Governments will have to be more hands-on: no single operator, regulator or local authority holds all the levers.
Read ‘Second wind’ to find out more about how green industries can contribute to local economic growth in places like Aberdeen.

articles.title: Jackdaw was well handled – but government needs a coherent net zero strategy
articles.standfirst:
Jackdaw was well handled – but government needs a coherent net zero strategy melissa.ittoo Thu, 22/10/2026 - 16:18 Miatta Fahnbulleh made a good case for the government decision on the Jackdaw gas field. 4 Comment Jill Rutter Rosa Hodgkin Institute for Government Yes Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey during a visit to Shell UK's St Fergus Gas Terminal in Peterhead, Aberdeenshire. Policy making Net zero Energy Climate change Environment Labour Burnham government Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
No

The secretary of state for energy security and net zero finally retook the decision on the exploitation of the Jackdaw gas field. It was a decision long in the making after the Scottish courts found that the initial decision by the then Conservative government had failed to take proper account of the impact of licencing the field on the UK’s ability to deliver net zero.

The government aced its Jackdaw communications

The announcement itself was testament to the political skill of the Burnham operation. It made clear that the decision was – as it had to be – for the secretary of state. Miatta Fahnbulleh was clear about the implications – this was about energy security, tax revenue and jobs, not reducing gas prices set by the international market. She, the chancellor and the secretary of state for Scotland shared the press release, and the publicity, with the prime minister, emphasising the positives for the Scottish economy.

Meanwhile, hypothecating future revenues to an “Energy Wealth Fund”, which will sit within the National Wealth Fund and invest in green energy infrastructure, made it clear that exploiting UK supplies for residual gas could (in theory at least) help speed the reduction in fossil fuel dependence. Jackdaw’s shelf life means that the UK will stop using gas quite some time after the field has to be decommissioned.

The government lined its ducks up – and they quacked appreciatively. And this is useful in the run-up to the budget to show what “Burnham pragmatism” means in practice and that government is prepared to listen to business concerns.

Critics of the plan missed the target 

Authorisation has inevitably triggered criticism from green campaigners and Green politicians. Some has been about the UK losing ground on climate leadership. This is a genuine concern, but the UK was already on shaky ground after cuts to the aid budget and a raid on international climate finance paid for the bus fare cap two days into Burnham’s premiership.

But the second criticism was that there were alternatives – more investment in electrification, decarbonising power, upgrading homes, all of which could create wider benefits, more jobs and speed the green transition.

That posed a false dichotomy: Jackdaw or the green transition. But in truth they were not competing: all net zero scenarios still have the UK using gas into the 2040s. The choice on Jackdaw was UK or imported gas. That was the supply side question the secretary of state had to answer. The government now has – at the margin – a little bit more resource to put into the transition that matters which, looking ahead, is primarily on the demand side.

Related content

Jackdaw and Rosebank

Jackdaw and Rosebank

What are Jackdaw and Rosebank, and what position has the government taken on North Sea licences?

Read our explainer

Rosebank is a very different decision

There have been two readings of the implications of the Jackdaw decision for the bigger one on the new oil field at Rosebank. One is that the secretary of state will be able to use similar rationales, and it would not be worth establishing the Energy Wealth Fund for Jackdaw alone. The other is that Miatta Fahnbulleh has been emphasising the differences – not least the lesser domestic security angle when it comes to oil versus gas, and she is rolling the pitch for a no. The key thing is that this is a separate, and quite different, decision which she needs to show she has taken on the merits.

The bigger issue is a credible net zero strategy

Jackdaw should not be a distraction from the much bigger issue of whether the government has a coherent strategy to get the UK off fossil fuels in the longer term. Jackdaw alone does not blow a hole in that strategy, but the strategy had numerous holes already and will look even more patchy if the government rolls back on some of its key levers to drive electrification. There are stories that the Boiler Upgrade scheme may be cut to pay for the uplift in defence spending and that the EV mandate may be watered down (and if getting inside Made in Europe means applying EU style tariffs to Chinese EVs that change may slow anyway).

The government has made a good case for why approving Jackdaw makes sense in the short term, but a plan for getting off fossil fuels that actually adds up when combined with concerns on energy security and affordability – and fits with a strategy to adapt to the climate change that is already baked in – is the real issue. That needs to be the secretary of state’s next priority.

The government has set out its case for approving Jackdaw clearly, but it needs a more credible roadmap for getting the UK off fossil fuels, write Jill Rutter and Rosa Hodgkin Off Net zero

That posed a false dichotomy: Jackdaw or the green transition. But in truth they were not competing: all net zero scenarios still have the UK using gas into the 2040s. The choice on Jackdaw was UK or imported gas. That was the supply side question the secretary of state had to answer. The government now has – at the margin – a little bit more resource to put into the transition that matters which, looking ahead, is primarily on the demand side.
What are Jackdaw and Rosebank, and what position has the government taken on North Sea licences?

There have been two readings of the implications of the Jackdaw decision for the bigger one on the new oil field at Rosebank. One is that the secretary of state will be able to use similar rationales, and it would not be worth establishing the Energy Wealth Fund for Jackdaw alone. The other is that Miatta Fahnbulleh has been emphasising the differences – not least the lesser domestic security angle when it comes to oil versus gas, and she is rolling the pitch for a no. The key thing is that this is a separate, and quite different, decision which she needs to show she has taken on the merits.

Jackdaw should not be a distraction from the much bigger issue of whether the government has a coherent strategy to get the UK off fossil fuels in the longer term. Jackdaw alone does not blow a hole in that strategy, but the strategy had numerous holes already and will look even more patchy if the government rolls back on some of its key levers to drive electrification. There are stories that the Boiler Upgrade scheme may be cut to pay for the uplift in defence spending and that the EV mandate may be watered down (and if getting inside Made in Europe means applying EU style tariffs to Chinese EVs that change may slow anyway).

The government has made a good case for why approving Jackdaw makes sense in the short term, but a plan for getting off fossil fuels that actually adds up when combined with concerns on energy security and affordability – and fits with a strategy to adapt to the climate change that is already baked in – is the real issue. That needs to be the secretary of state’s next priority.
The Treasury needs to take the lead on how we adapt to the heat.

articles.standfirst:
How John Healey should approach his budget headache sam.macrory Thu, 22/10/2026 - 15:34 IfG experts set out how the chancellor should approach a difficult budget. 6 Comment Ben Paxton Dan Haile Thomas Pope Rosa Hodgkin Institute for Government Yes On 28 October John Healey will deliver his first budget as chancellor. Public finances Budget Tax Public spending Defence and security Economy Labour Chancellor of the exchequer Prime minister Burnham government HM Treasury
No

John Healey’s first budget as chancellor is a chance to define the fiscal approach of the Burnham administration. The prime minister has said he will “pull every single lever” to ease the cost of living, while Healey has insisted that he and Burnham are “lockstep in our commitment to meeting the fiscal rules.”

Having inherited the tight spending plans of his predecessor and recommitted to Labour’s 2024 manifesto commitments on personal taxation, Healey also faces high borrowing costs and unfavourable international headwinds. The budget challenge is a particularly difficult one. This is how IfG experts think that the chancellor should approach his task.

Related content

Budget 2026

Fiscal headroom is not the best test of this budget’s credibility

Conflict in Iran, Ukraine and Russia has resulted in higher global energy prices which will reduce the buffer the chancellor has against his fiscal rules (as will lower than forecast levels of net migration). These are an indicator of fiscal sustainability both in terms of what they measure and as a reflection of whether the government can deliver on its fiscal commitments. At the spring forecast, the government had a buffer against the current budget rule of £24bn. 2 https://obr.uk/efo/economic-and-fiscal-outlook-march-2026/  A margin of this size should normally mean the government does not feel forced to respond to shocks just to meet its fiscal rules. 

However, on this occasion the government should not allow ‘headroom’ to fall by much. This is for two main reasons. First, now is not a good time to increase borrowing, especially for day-to-day spending. The interest rates on UK government debt are already high, and the government could see further increases in its cost of borrowing if it chose to aggressively loosen policy now. Second, taking corrective action on the buffer now, however politically painful, will be much less painful than at future budgets close to an election.

Related content

Current UK fiscal rules

It would also be wrong to promise a bumper ‘headroom’ number based on a tight spending envelope that the government is unable to deliver. The credibility of this budget should be judged against whether the chancellor addresses the medium-term challenges the government faces in terms of spending pressures, high costs of servicing government debt and a tax system in dire need of reform.

Healey should not delay tough spending choices 

Healey should use this budget to set out an overall envelope for next year’s spending review that reflects the spending needed to deliver the government’s priorities, and what he judges to be affordable. 

Of course, Burnham may prefer to avoid surfacing difficult decisions at his administration’s first budget or have more time to work out his priorities and roll the pitch for tax rises to fund them at a future fiscal event. This would be a valid political choice, but it would come with a cost. Departments need to match their spending plans with Burnham’s political vision, a job which is only complicated by prolonging uncertainty over their future budgets. Delay also means leaving the inevitable difficult spending decisions to date closer to the general election.

The choices facing Burnham and Healey are far from easy. They inherited tight spending plans for 2029/30, with last autumn’s budget cuts leaving total day-to-day spending plans flat in real terms between 2028/29 and 2029/30 (though Rachel Reeves then topped up funding for special educational needs and disabilities [SEND] in March 2026). 

The spending plans for 2029/30, which rely on ambitious assumptions about productivity improvements from upfront investment in the first half of this parliament, look under further pressure from policy announcements since the Spring. June’s Defence Investment Plan left £900m of cuts in 2029/30 from other departments still to be found, and in the shorter-term Burnham’s summer policy spree was not fully funded. 

Increasing defence spending further from 2.7% to 3% of GDP by 2030 would cost around £7bn in 2029/30. The IFS also estimate that higher forecast inflation will erode the real-terms value of departmental budgets by £8–15bn in 2029/30.  4 Boileau B, Harvey-Rich O, Snape D, Public service spending: plans and pressures, Institute for Fiscal Studies, 2026, https://ifs.org.uk/publications/public-service-spending-plans-and-pressures  Add in other pressures – such as 2.7% annual increases in NHS spending and SEND reform not reducing demand by as much as expected  – and pencilled-in cuts to unprotected departments in 2029/30 look substantive.

Delivering improvements to public services within these spending plans, while also finding extra funding for Burnham’s priorities such as adult social care or youth employment, is unrealistic.

Burnham and Healey cannot avoid confronting these pressures. The only question is whether they do that now, or at the upcoming spending review in summer or autumn – when departments’ budgets for 2028/29, 2029/30 and 2030/31 will be set. 

Related content

Public Services Performance Tracker 2026

Budget 2026

John Healey's first budget as chancellor will be the biggest indication yet of the priorities of Andy Burnham's government.

Explore our budget analysis

The chancellor should use this budget to set out a tax strategy

Previous chancellors have far too often adopted an un-strategic approach to tax, looking for convenient revenue raisers that the public won’t notice and introducing ill-thought through giveaways into the system. 9 http://instituteforgovernment.org.uk/publication/john-healey-tax-budget-2026  The result is a messy system that undermines growth and the government’s other objectives much more than it should, while unmoored speculation damages confidence.

Healey should use his first budget to lay out a tax strategy setting out:

•    This government’s views on the current system and its weaknesses
•    Principles he will use to shape the future system
•    His priority areas for reform
•    A confirmation of what won’t change

The chancellor doesn’t need to specify exactly what measures he will introduce in future budgets, but sharing a higher-level set of principles and priorities will provide more certainty and allow Healey to articulate how his tax plans are contributing to the government’s broader priorities, like growth in every postcode. The alternative is a repeat of the same disconnection between rhetoric and policies seen from his predecessor and many before her. 

Healey should set out a targeted and time limited energy support plan

As winter approaches, global energy markets remain disrupted by conflict in the Middle East, Ukraine and Russia. As a result, energy bills facing businesses and households are set to rise. Cornwall Insight have estimated that the Ofgem price cap will rise by £276 (16%) in January and more recent estimates suggest the increase could be even greater. 10 https://www.cornwall-insight.com/predictions-and-insights-into-the-default-tariff-cap/  Bills are approaching, but still below, the level at which the government capped prices in 2022-23 through the Energy Price Guarantee (without which bills would have been much higher) and the risk of further disruption remains high. 

We have argued that the chancellor should provide support to households who are struggling to pay energy bills 11 https://www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/publication/managing-economic-consequences-iran-war , but that this should be targeted and time-limited to avoid the expense of previous schemes (£35bn in total across 2022-23) 12 Levell P, O’Connell M, Smith K, ‘Urgent need to learn lessons from expensive energy support packages: better design could have saved £4.5 billion’, Institute for Fiscal Studies, 31 January 2025, https://ifs.org.uk/news/urgent-need-learn-lessons-expensive-energy-support-packages-better-design-could-have-saved  and to preserve the price signal for those who can use less power. This should be delivered alongside support to encourage electrification of heating and cars, which is the best way to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Cuts to government support in these areas would not help households cope with rising energy costs. The government also needs to consider businesses that face high energy costs, and as prices rise it may feel it needs to further on the support offered in April for energy intensive businesses. 

A package for households will be the headline-making test of Burnham’s promise to pull every possible support lever at this budget, but it is the choices about helping businesses and the policies to build energy resilience that will reveal the coherence of the government’s strategy on energy security and net zero.

articles.title: Fixing NEETs support should be part of wider health and disability benefits reform
articles.standfirst:
Fixing NEETs support should be part of wider health and disability benefits reform sam.macrory Thu, 22/10/2026 - 14:40 The Milburn review is welcome, but Burnham should not create a separate benefits system. 5 Comment Ben Paxton Heloise Dunlop Institute for Government Yes Public finances Welfare Labour Prime minister Burnham government
No

Alan Milburn has successfully built a political consensus around the need to address the rising numbers of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET). His interim report laid the foundations for change, and now Andy Burnham has set out a narrative about the kind of support he wants young people to receive. This proactive approach is welcome. As our recent work has found, leading public opinion through a clear political vision is a pre-requisite for reform of the health and disability benefits system. 

Recent reports suggest Milburn’s review may propose creating a separate benefits system for young people.  14 https://www.ft.com/content/c6e911dd-440b-4852-925c-448faeb52d98?syn-25a6b1a6=1  There is a strong case for some targeted interventions for this group, including those whose health affects their ability to work, but building a separate benefits system for young people – who only make up around one in ten health and disability benefit claimants – would be a time-consuming distraction that creates further complexity. Instead, the government should focus on delivering a system that works for all working age adults. 

Milburn has identified the right problems with support for young people 

Tackling the NEET problem is important. Not earning or learning as a young person has life-long scarring effects – which have huge long-term consequences for the economy, public finances and people’s health, income and wellbeing. 

The interim report of Alan Milburn’s review identified several system failures driving the rising NEET rate. These include a social security system that incentivises people to claim health and disability benefits while providing too little employment support, mental health services which are unable to meet rising demand and an education system that is not giving young people the skills and opportunities to transition into work. Crucially, Milburn highlighted poor coordination between services and fragmented accountability at a local level as key barriers to improvement. This clear diagnosis of the problems should pave the way for the review’s final report to put forward bold solutions. 

Improving the health and disability system for NEETs alone would be a missed opportunity

Many of the problems Milburn identifies as driving higher NEET rates also affect other working age adults. This includes the physical and mental health conditions affecting young people claiming personal independence payment (PIP) being similar (aside from ADHD and autism, which are much more prevalent among young people but still account for a minority of claimants).   

There are some important problems are specific to NEETs. These include a lack of work experience and inadequate adult technical training provision, with the lower proportion of young people in education or training one of the key reasons for higher NEET rates in the UK than other European nations. 

Schools, FE colleges and employers have an important role to play in addressing these issues, but the government should be making the whole health and disability benefits system, including wider support for those receiving benefits, more personalised. This should enable more tailored support that accounts for the specific needs of young people – such as more intensive support to help young people enter and stay engaged in work, as is being done through the Youth Guarantee already – while also better targeting support for all adults.

DWP should avoid a new system that complicates join up of support 

Pouring time and resource into setting up a new benefits system for young people risks being a distraction. Universal Credit’s slow and painful, though ultimately successful, roll out shows the extreme end of potential risks and time involved – but even more minor changes often face significant challenges.

Getting the rules, requirements and administration of a new system right would not be straightforward. And it would add a whole extra layer of complexity to other changes to the health and disability benefits system, such as merging the Work Capability Assessment into the PIP assessment and any reforms to PIP following the Timms review.

A new, separate system for 16–24 year-olds would also create an arbitrary transition point at age 25. A common critique of the existing system is that the transition from the child benefit and education system to adult social security and training is mismanaged. Creating another transition to separate benefits system would add complexity and potentially introduce unhelpful incentives. It would also risk creating discontinuity in the support people receive.

Another risk is that a separate system for young people makes local join-up harder, with a lack of integration has been one of the weaknesses of past governments’ approach to employment support. The Starmer government made welcome attempts to rectify this, with the economic inactivity trailblazers and devolution of the Connect to Work programme, and Burnham has said he wants to go further. Imposing a new top-down national support programme for NEETs – with inflexible, ringfenced funding distinct other employment support – would make it harder for areas to deliver the joined-up local support NEETs desperately need. 

Instead, central government should set the system outcomes, and local areas (mayoral strategic authorities where they exist) should be empowered to design and deliver support. This would not only help bring together the many organisations that can help best support NEETs, but also help join-up support for all working-age adults.

Burnham should not shy away from ambitious reforms to support for NEETs. But this should be just the first step of building a better system of support for all working age adults whose health limits their ability to work.

articles.title: US Holiday cheer, at a higher price
articles.standfirst: We forecast holiday retail sales to rise 4.2% in dollar terms and 2.2% in volume after adjusting for inflation. That would beat last year’s volume, when tariffs hurt sales and shifted purchases forward into October, but it trails a typical holiday season, reflecting the hit to spending power from higher energy prices.
paragraphs: This holiday season will remain deeply bifurcated. High-income consumers will keep a floor under spending, helped by the surge in equities this year.

We forecast holiday retail sales to rise 4.2% in dollar terms and 2.2% in volume after adjusting for inflation. That would beat last year’s volume, when tariffs hurt sales and shifted purchases forward into October, but it trails a typical holiday season, reflecting the hit to spending power from higher energy prices.

High inflation is holding down real disposable income growth, high diesel prices are raising shipping costs, and Federal Reserve rate hikes are raising borrowing costs for those planning to spend by credit card.

This holiday season will remain deeply bifurcated. High-income consumers will keep a floor under spending, helped by the surge in equities this year. Our research shows recreational goods and services, household furniture, and clothing will likely benefit most from a positive wealth effect.

articles.title: In Wyoming, Are Two Homestead Exemptions Enough?
articles.standfirst: No one enjoys paying taxes, but the property tax serves an important purpose, and Wyoming has already implemented significant property tax relief. Proposition 1 would undercut local finances to a degree that would likely force reliance on worse taxes (local or state) and prompt spending cuts that reduce homeowners’ property values.
paragraphs: If having one property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. exemption is good, then having two is preferable, and three is better still. Or at least, that seems to be the logic of many states, where lawmakers and voters keep piling on new property tax relief measures that rarely cohere and sometimes work at cross purposes. But in Wyoming—Big Wyoming, as they say—it’s “go big or go home,” with voters deciding this November whether to create a choose-your-own-adventure system with three different homestead exemptions.

Taxes should be simple, neutral, transparent, and stable. Wyoming, however, is merely the latest state to offer an alternative: what if we made the taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. system more complex, arbitrary, opaque, and volatile?

In 2024, lawmakers adopted a long-term homeowner exemption, which now stands at 50 percent of the first $3 million in market value on primary residences of owners or spouses 65 or older, who have paid Wyoming residential property taxes for at least 25 years, with the condition that they must live in the home at least eight months per year.

In 2025, lawmakers adopted a 25 percent exemption on the first $1 million in market value, both land and structures, for owner-occupants of single-family residential housing who reside in a home at least eight months per year. Those claiming the 50 percent long-term homeowner exemption may not simultaneously claim the 25 percent exemption.

Lower-income households, moreover, can receive property tax refunds. Those with household incomes at or below 125 percent of their county or the statewide median household income, with assets (beyond their home, one vehicle, and retirement accounts) less than about $160,000, receive a refund of the lesser of 75 percent of the previous year’s property taxes or 50 percent of the median residential property tax liability in their county. Those with incomes between 125 and 145 percent of the median household income, and still under the asset limit, receive 65 percent of those amounts. These refunds are subject to appropriations.

This year, voters will decide whether to adopt a third exemption with Proposition 1, worth 50 percent of the assessed value of the home itself (excluding the value of land), with no cap, for those who have been Wyoming residents for at least one year and who lived in the home for at least six months of the preceding tax year. Under anticipatory legislation enacted this year, the new exemption could not stack with the long-term homeowner exemption, but nothing prevents it from being claimed in tandem with the 25 percent exemption, which would allow eligible homeowners to claim an exemption for 25 percent of all value (land and structures), plus another 50 percent of the home’s value.

Owner-occupants of duplexes and other multi-family buildings would be eligible for the new 50 percent exemption but are not eligible for the existing 25 percent exemption. Those who have lived in Wyoming for less than a year are eligible for the 25 percent exemption but wouldn’t be eligible for the new initiative-created exemption. Those who live in a home for at least six months but less than eight months per year could qualify under the new exemption but not the existing ones. And whereas both the 25 percent exemption and the long-term exemption are capped, the new exemption is not. The exemptions also have different application dates, further complicating matters. The existing exemption applications are due March 1, the Proposition 1 application would be due the fourth Monday in May, and refund applications are due the first Monday in June.

This is the wrong way to do tax policy. In tandem, these three exemptions wipe out a significant share of Wyoming’s residential real property tax, forcing Wyoming governments to rely even more heavily on taxes on the oil, gas, and mining industries—a concerning lack of diversification, particularly for industries with high volatility and potential long-term decline.

Consider a $400,000 property, consisting of $325,000 in home value and $75,000 in land value, taxed at the statewide average levy (about 68.5 mills on 9.5 percent of market value). Without any homestead exemptions, annual property taxes would run $2,603. If the homeowners qualify for the existing 25 percent exemption, that trims the property tax bill to $1,952. If Proposition 1 passes, their tax bill gets slashed to $895, with homestead exemptions eliminating almost two-thirds of the household’s property tax liability. If their income is less than 125 percent of the county’s median, they’ll get a refund of up to $671 of that, leaving a net annual tax bill of $224 on a $400,000 property.

That may sound like an incredible deal for homeowners, but it severely undercuts the property tax, and it may seem like a worse deal as local governments scramble to find revenue to fund basic services.

Property taxes, as Gov. Mark Gordon explains in outlining his opposition to Proposition 1, pay for local services that directly benefit homeowners, and they offer a level of local control that other taxes do not. Properties in a community are more valuable because of the services—roads, schools, courts, parks, police, and emergency services—that local governments provide, and if a locality gets the balance wrong, voters can force a correction. If the state eventually has to come in and backfill an eroded property tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates., that local control—and the ability of localities and their voters to make decisions that benefit the community and local property values—will be lost.

No one enjoys paying taxes, but the property tax serves an important purpose, and Wyoming has already implemented significant property tax relief. Proposition 1 would undercut local finances to a degree that would likely force reliance on worse taxes (local or state) and prompt spending cuts that reduce homeowners’ property values.

Jared Walczak is a Senior Fellow at the Tax Foundation, where he spent five years as Vice President of State Projects, and president of Walczak Policy Consulting.

articles.title: Options to Reform the Tax Treatment of Exempt Hospitals
articles.standfirst: Nearly half of all hospitals are exempt from paying US corporate income taxes. As healthcare spending rises, lawmakers have questioned whether hospitals are providing as much in community benefits as they derive from tax exemptions.
paragraphs: TaxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities.-exempt hospitals provide a substantial share of medical care in the United States. Of the 6,100 hospitals operating in the country in 2026, nearly half are nongovernment, tax-exempt community hospitals. As hospitals consolidate into larger systems and their revenues rise, the value of their tax exemptionA tax exemption excludes certain income, revenue, or even taxpayers from tax altogether. For example, nonprofits that fulfill certain requirements are granted tax-exempt status by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), preventing them from having to pay income tax. and the cost of forgone revenue grow.

Not-for-profit hospitals are tax-exempt. They do not usually pay federal income taxes, state income taxes, or local property taxes. They may also use tax-exempt bond financing and benefit from tax-deductible charitable donations.

A variety of studies have attempted to measure the value of these tax exemptions. Recent estimates covering 2018 through 2022 put the value of the federal corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. exemption for hospitals at $8.3 billion to $11.5 billion per year. Several studies have also compared the value of hospitals’ tax exemptions with the benefits they provide for their communities.

Lawmakers in both parties have scrutinized the hospital tax exemption in recent years, questioning whether the community benefits provided by tax-exempt hospitals justify the value of their tax exemptions. Some have debated requiring hospitals to report more information on the community benefits they provide or even limiting tax exemptions for the largest hospital systems.
Below, Tax Foundation models and analyzes several options to reform the tax treatment of exempt hospitals.

We estimate that applying the 21 percent corporate income tax to large hospital systems would raise $147.6 billion in federal revenue over ten years. More targeted reforms, like applying taxes on investment income or recapturing tax benefits in excess of community benefits, would raise less revenue. If policymakers choose to reform the tax treatment of tax-exempt hospitals, they face complex choices along the way, such as how many hospitals would be covered, how community benefits would be defined, and which tax benefit to prioritize within a reform effort.

A tax-exempt organization is one that is generally exempt from federal income tax on income related to its exempt purpose. The first corporate income tax exemption came in 1894, with the imposition of a temporary corporate income tax that was subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court the next year. Congress again exempted charitable organizations from an excise tax on corporations in 1909, and that exemption carried through to the modern income tax first levied in 1913.

Hospitals were not included in the 1909 or 1913 laws by name, but in practice received tax exemptions as nonprofits “affiliated with either religious groups or philanthropic foundations.” A 1956 revenue ruling from the Internal Revenue Service established the “charity care” standard by which hospitals could earn and retain their federal tax exemption. The IRS replaced the 1956 ruling with a broader “community benefit” standard in 1969, which is still in place today.
Hospital systems today are much larger and more sophisticated than they were a century ago. In 2024, 2,271 hospital filers collectively reported:
These figures heavily reflect the influence of the top 100 tax-exempt health filers ranked by tax year 2024 revenue, as demonstrated in the chart below:

In all, hospital filers reported a combined $87.9 billion in net income in 2024. If the hospital tax exemption did not exist, much of that net income would be subject to the 21 percent US corporate income tax rate. Hospitals would also be subject to state corporate income taxes, local property taxes, and federal unemployment taxes.

Table 1 below summarizes several studies that measured the value of hospital tax exemptions between 2011 and 2022. The estimates are not directly comparable with Tax Foundation estimates as they use different years, methods, and definitions of tax benefits.

We estimate the conventional revenue effects of five different ways to reform the tax treatment of large hospital systems, along with several variants. Each reform option is imposed on hospital systems with $1 billion in average total revenue over the three preceding years (indexed for inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin for future years). The $1 billion threshold would cover 287 systems in 2027, making up about 85 to 89 percent of the sector revenue, income, assets, bonds, and gifts.
The options above are illustrative, and policymakers reforming the tax treatment of exempt hospitals might choose different parameters.

Congress could levy a 21 percent income tax on large systems based on book (financial statement) income rather than taxable income. A 21 percent book income tax on large hospital systems would increase revenue by $224.7 billion on a conventional basis, compared to $147.6 billion if levied on taxable income. About half of the difference in these two measures is 100 percent bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. for machinery and equipment, with the other half being regular MACRS depreciation deductions faster than deductions allowed under financial rules.

Lawmakers could also levy the 21 percent income tax on individual hospitals surpassing the $1 billion threshold rather than on consolidated hospital systems. A tax on individual hospitals would raise less revenue, as fewer entities would meet the threshold.

The 4 and 8 percent excise tax rates mirror the top two rates of the existing university endowment tax as it was restructured in 2025, while the 21 percent rate would match the corporate income tax. Policymakers could also decide whether to apply a graduated rate structure, although higher marginal rates could increase incentives for tax avoidance.
The charitable deduction could be restricted incrementally, rather than a full denial of charitable deductions for covered systems.

Policymakers could apply limits on hospital tax-exempt bond financing for existing bonds or only for bonds issued moving forward. Our option only applies prospectively, so existing bond and bond refundings are not included in the tax base. The revenue effect therefore starts small and grows slowly over time as the share of bonds issued since the options took effect rises.

Congress could measure tax benefits or community benefits in different ways. A narrower definition of community benefits, such as charity care alone, would produce more revenue than a broader definition.

Policymakers, academics, and hospital representatives have fiercely debated how to measure community benefits. The hospital sector takes a broad view, including charity care as well as research, education, Medicaid shortfalls, Medicare shortfalls, and bad debt. The IRS takes a narrower view in its Schedule H reporting requirements for hospitals. The IRS includes free care, unreimbursed Medicaid, community health programs, and community building activities but excludes items like bad debt and Medicare shortfalls.

The nonpartisan health think tank Lown Institute produces a widely cited annual report, the Lown Hospitals Index, with a narrower measure still of “meaningful” community investment: financial assistance, subsidized health services, community health improvement services, cash and in-kind contributions, and community-building activities. The Lown Index notably excludes Medicaid shortfalls, as well as education and research funding.

For the recapture option, we model two definitions of community benefits: charity care alone and the broader community-investment measure developed by the Lown Institute. The broader the measure of community benefits, the fewer hospital systems who have tax benefits greater than community benefits, resulting in less revenue from recapture.

Our estimates do not include certain behavioral effects for hospitals. For example, hospital systems would reasonably change their behavior in response to any of these options, especially for systems near the $1 billion threshold we chose for the tax.

Some systems may sell or spin off affiliated hospitals to avoid the tax. We used a threshold based on gross revenue, but thresholds using a net income measure could encourage profitable hospitals to acquire revenue-losing hospitals so that their consolidated entity falls under the threshold. Other hospitals may even shift to for-profit status or seek acquisition by a for-profit entity. We exclude such behavioral responses from our revenue estimates.

Other options incorporate limited behavioral effects; for example, when restricting the charitable deduction for donations to large hospital systems, we assume that overall giving will decline in response to the higher, after-tax cost of charitable giving but we do not assume any shift in the composition of giving (i.e., from donors shifting their giving from covered systems to other charities).

While each option would raise federal revenue and increase horizontal equity between hospitals and similar private sector health care providers, they would involve tradeoffs. Each option would need to be designed to minimize possible impacts on capital investment. Preserving full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. within the corporate income tax base would be an important feature of an income tax design, for example.

From a principles perspective, each of these options would move the tax code toward greater neutrality between similarly situated taxpayers in the health sector. Applying tax rules already in place for most other taxpayers earning similar forms of income is the most defensible approach, especially if it was done in concert with other changes in the tax code.

For example, more broadly limiting tax-exempt bond issuance, imposing stricter rules on nonprofit tax-exempt earnings, and limiting the scope of all charitable deductions would move in the same direction as these sector-specific options. If policymakers wish to keep some tax benefit for hospital operations, tailoring them to the specific societal benefit (such as charity care or other operations) would be an improvement over the status quo.

Our estimates suggest that incremental options focused on the top of the sector would raise revenue and only focus on the largest hospital systems. Reforming the treatment of tax-exempt hospitals is also an opportunity to improve the horizontal treatment of health providers in the tax code. Policymakers have a range of reform options to consider, but the design details matter to ensure we benefit from the neutrality improvements while minimizing unintended consequences on the sector and patients.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

To construct our estimates, we used IRS Statistics of Income (SOI) Exempt Organization study files from tax years 2019 to 2022 and IRS Form 990 e-file returns from tax years 2022 to 2024 to construct a model of hospital filers. We omitted the pandemic years 2020 and 2021 to avoid pandemic-era noise in the data.

We used Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ownership data to group filers into systems under common control from control trees on Schedule R, resulting in 2,452 total hospital filers in 1,771 total systems from tax year 2019 to tax year 2024 (2,271 filers and 1,045 systems in tax year 2024). Systems exclude gifts between members and exclude university hospitals, which tend to file returns with their affiliated universities. As a check, we cross referenced our estimates of the 25 largest systems with their audited consolidated revenue, and the median value came within 4 percent of the audited figures.

SOI and CMS cost report data provide information on financials, Schedule K bonds, Schedule H community benefits, and itemized sources of revenue. Our growth paths for each modeled item follow CMS projections of national hospital spending through 2034, and from there Congressional Budget Office’s February 2026 baseline for nominal GDP, the 10-year Treasury rate, and CPI-U where applicable.

A system is covered under each option if its total average revenue over the three preceding years exceeded $1 billion as of 2027, indexed to CPI-U after that and rounded down to $10 million, reaching a threshold of $1.2 billion in 2036. In 2027, 287 systems would be covered, holding between 85 percent and 89 percent of sector revenue, income, assets, bonds, and gifts.

We use the Tax Foundation General Equilibrium Model to capture interactions with individual and payroll taxA payroll tax is a tax paid on the wages and salaries of employees to finance social insurance programs like Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance. Payroll taxes are social insurance taxes that comprise 24.8 percent of combined federal, state, and local government revenue, the second largest source of that combined tax revenue. revenue, charitable deductions, and depreciation allowances.

The 21 percent corporate tax swaps book depreciation for tax depreciation for investment prospectively using BEA hospital asset mix data. Bonus depreciation for eligible investment is assumed to be taken up 80 percent of the time when profitable and 45 percent in loss years.

The 4 percent investment excise tax includes net investment income as under IRC Section 4940: interest, dividends, royalties, and investment income booked as “other revenue.” Realized securities gains are also included.

The option ending tax-exempt bond financing uses Schedule K data to derive new money bonds net of refundings (refundings of pre-2027 bonds are exempt). Coupons are estimated at the CBO 10-year Treasury rate plus 1.9 points (the average gap between A-rated corporate bond yields and 10-year Treasury yields from 2010 to 2025). Holders of the taxable bonds follow Federal Reserve figures for ownership of corporate bonds.

We use data on gifts to covered systems split by donor type using Giving USA shares for individual, corporation, and foundation and/or donor advised fund giving, with individual gifts run through the Tax Foundation General Equilibrium Model to capture existing charitable giving. Corporate gifts are counted above the existing 1 percent floor at 21 percent. We assume foundation and donor advised fund giving is included in the denial of deduction base, though this is a policy design choice and an avoidance mechanism that could lower the estimate under certain designs.

Federal benefit recapture uses the method established by the Lown Institute, defining community benefit as charity care, community health, cash and in kind-contributions, subsidized services, and community building. Federal benefits are defined as taxable income under a corporate tax base at 21 percent plus bond financing savings. The proposal recaptures 100 percent of benefits above the community benefit per system, tested each year for each system with no carryforward. We exclude state and local tax benefits in our estimates.

Garrett Watson is Vice President of Federal Tax Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. His work has been featured in The Washington Post, The Atlantic, Politico, the Associated Press and other major outlets.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.
