articles.title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
articles.standfirst: For the first time, the Treasury calculates how much the UK could have raised by investing North Sea proceeds.
paragraphs: The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig in the North Sea.
After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.
Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding housed in the National Wealth Fund.

A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.
It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go?
It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time.
"The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said.
"If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."
On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth.

The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's.
"Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.
It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.
It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era.
The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories.
Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.
The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.
I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund.
Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic.
It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future.

While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.

UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.
Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that.
Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is, what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?

articles.title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
articles.standfirst: The vulnerabilities with PHP, a programming language widely used across the internet, have been described as the most significant ever found by AI.
paragraphs: International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.

Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leading bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.
The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.
Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.
The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.
Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.
And in a post on X, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.
Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are "temporarily down for maintenance" without specifying the reason.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz.
Calif, along with PHP Foundation, were part of a program started by OpenAI called Patch the Planet.
Through that program, they were given access to the AI company's advanced AI tools in order to find and fix flaws in web development language.

OpenAI said in a blog post that the discovery was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It added an internal researcher at the company had also discovered the issue around the same time as the other firms.
The flaws had gone undetected for more than a decade. By August, after a few weeks of using advanced AI tools, they were discovered.
"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.
It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.

While PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch," details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.
It forced PHP Foundation to rush out its announcement of the vulnerability and its huge scale.
The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.
Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note.
Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning.

"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.
Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.
The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.

"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.
He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".
Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".

The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".
It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.
The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.
PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.
Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

articles.title: Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
articles.standfirst: The economic figures released on Wednesday show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his Budget.
paragraphs: The chancellor was on an early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped.
From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms.
The National Debt has topped £3 trillion for the first time in the official figures.
The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months.
Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase.
These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week.
On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures.
The public finances remain under pressure, however, from the double whammy of rising inflation and borrowing costs.
While inflation was of course expected to increase as petrol and diesel prices surged, in some cases, to records, other measures of underlying inflation also increased.

From airfares to computer game download prices, there are the first signs of stickier forms of price pressure and of higher inflation becoming more embedded, suggesting elevated price rises are not temporary. Capital Economics now expects the main measure of inflation to peak at 4.2% next year.
The Bank of England carefully watches services inflation and core inflation, and this ups the odds significantly for a rise in interest rates next month.
The services sector, which includes everything from law and banking to retail, hospitality and tourism, makes up the vast majority of the UK's economic output.
The latest inflation figure also applies as the uprating to tens of billions in welfare payments next April.
By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.
The figure also confirms that the Triple Lock will see the State Pension increase by 3.9% next April.
There is one form of relief here - food price inflation remains largely unaffected by the energy shock.
While higher inflation at a time of frozen tax thresholds will raise more tax in cash terms, it will also increase the cost of public services, including likely union pay demands.
All the while, UK borrowing costs have risen alongside most of the advanced world as the US-Israel war against Iran has intensified.
The Jackdaw gas field decision is seen as the start of a run of "pro growth" pre-Budget announcements.
It sends a directional message, but will not fundamentally change the trade off between cost of living breathing space, and delivering a Budget that convinces the markets and investors.
The fact the borrowing costs gap has narrowed a bit with other G7 nations, and the IMF praised pencilled-in plans to shrink borrowing, provided a platform for the chancellor's Budget.
The latest economic numbers amply illustrate the challenge of actually delivering them.

articles.title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
articles.standfirst: Inflation accelerated to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
paragraphs: UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest in a year on Wednesday, adding to the pressure on Chancellor John Healey ahead of his first Budget in a week.
The pace of UK price rises accelerated to 3.5% in the year to September, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.
The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, which means borrowing for the financial year to date is running £6bn above official forecasts.
Healey has promised a Budget which will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes - income tax, National Insurance and VAT - while sticking to the party's fiscal rules.

Inflation, the rate at which prices are rising, jumped from 3.1% in the year to August to 3.5% in the year to September. It is the highest inflation has been since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies.

The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.
The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.
Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.
ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.
As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.
September's inflation figure is also important because it suggests how benefits will increase next April.
It means the state pension will most likely rise by 3.9%, in line with average wage rises from May to July, due to the triple lock.

The inflation figure for September also dictates how other benefits will rise in April. By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.
With a week to go until he delivers the Budget, Healey said: "We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide."

He said the International Monetary Fund last week had praised the UK government for its "fiscal discipline", and that the government has just given the go-ahead for getting more gas from the North Sea's Jackdaw field.

The Budget on 28 October will "keep up this momentum", he said, by sticking to the government's self-imposed fiscal rules, and by driving "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space".
But the inflation figure came as the ONS said the government borrowed £24.5bn in September, £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, as higher inflation helped to push up debt interest costs.
The overshoot means, cumulatively, the government has borrowed £6bn more this year than the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which scores government spending plans, had forecast.

Despite overall debt topping £3tn for the first time, debt as a proportion of the UK's economic output - the measure used by the government to judge whether it is in line with its fiscal rules - fell.
The Conservatives said higher inflation and borrowing showed Labour had "lost control of the economy".
Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith called for Healey to use his Budget to "tackle the deficit, and reduce the red tape and net zero costs that are driving up the cost of living for families".
He added that the Conservatives would cut taxes, the costs of benefits and "wasteful" spending to "make our country prosperous again".

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the borrowing figures "painted a dismal picture" ahead of Healey's Budget. She said the amount borrowed in September was higher than analyst expectations as well as spending watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)'s forecast.
"This reinforces our view that the Chancellor will deliver a cautious Budget on 28 October that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal choices for next year," she said.
What are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

articles.title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
articles.standfirst: The prime minister provided little detail, and there are questions over shifting the fees onto unit costs.
paragraphs: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.
These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.
Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.
But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill.

During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".

He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".

No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate, so people pay for what they use.
This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.

For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.
Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.
Average standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas.
When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills.
Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure.
The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households.
Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, but Citizens Advice has warned about the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers.
Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised.

But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices."
Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy prices forecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January.

In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament".
Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries.

articles.title: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.standfirst: A spokesperson said it was removing inaccurate AI images and pausing the rollout of the tool.
paragraphs: A chip muffin and bacon and egg soda - menu items well known in parts of the UK, but not to the AI which made this
Just Eat has apologised after it was ridiculed online over a series of mistakes with AI-generated pictures for some of its restaurants' food items.
The online food delivery platform had been testing out the tech to showcase food which didn't have images yet - but not all turned out as planned.
Instead the AI invented several bizarre concoctions, from bacon and eggs floating in a glass of cola - a confusion between "soda" and "soda bread" - to chips poking out of muffins.
A Just Eat spokesperson said the firm was "in the process of removing" the incorrect images, and would stop making more until the AI was further developed.
Salt and pepper chips usually involves frying chips with onions, garlic and chillies - a little bit more exciting than this suggests
"We work with tens of thousands of small restaurants on their food imagery, including funding professional local photographers," the spokesperson told the BBC.
"We've been trialling AI-enhanced images, and as with any new technology, it isn't always quite right the first time."
What some parts of Manchester call a "chip muffin" - also known as a chip butty - causing the AI to invent a dish which seemingly involved baking potato into bread
The incident highlights the difficulties companies can still face when using AI to speed up or simplify work processes, especially when it is used to interpret words in a specific context.
Members of the Just Eat UK subreddit have flocked to the site over the past few days to post the latest unintentionally hilarious spins on takeaway food items.
Any picture generated using AI on the delivery app appears with a label indicating so, and the BBC has spotted many of the more unusual takes still up on menus.
A "cheese roll" was inexplicably turned into sushi
A Belfast cafe, meanwhile, had its bacon and egg soda bread dish represented as a glass of fizzy drink with a cooked egg and bacon floating in it.

Spelling mistakes on menu items have sometimes added to the confusion, with the Instagram account @uknewestfoods posting a picture of garlic bread in the shape of a plane - presumably because of a misspelling of the word "plain".

Meanwhile, a "cheese roll" - bread and cheese - instead became slabs of cheese rolled into a sushi roll.
While some on social media said they found the images "hilarious", another was less interested in the AI-generated dishes, saying: "Well, that lot just helped my diet".
Meanwhile, one person on Instagram questioned why customers would ever want to see AI images of a restaurant's food even if they were closer to the real thing.
"I want to see what the dish actually looks like as it helps me decide who to order from or what to order," they said.
"These 'perfect' AI versions just lead to disappointment if that's what you think your meal will look like."

articles.title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
articles.standfirst: Kashim Chowdhury was contracted for 183 hours a week, more than the number of hours in seven days.
paragraphs: Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by working multiple full-time public sector jobs
The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood.
He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.
The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.
The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.

He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had jobs elsewhere.
At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector.

In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.
Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.
Chowdhury said the jobs were a "lifeline" during a time his mother's health had declined.

Asked by defence barrister Pieter Briegel what extent stress in his life was due to the number of jobs, he replied: "The jobs at the time were my lifeline at the time, that was what I survived on at that particular moment.

"And they gave me a link to the outside, they were the only thing I had to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time," he told the court.

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".
A succession of Chowdhury's line managers have told the jury that he performed poorly in his roles.

Abigail Mounde, who was Chowdhury's line manager at the Department for Business and Trade previously told the court: ''Any basic tasks I asked him to do he either did late or not to the standard I would have expected."
Chowdhury was asked whether he accepted the criticism of his performance, including the allegation he failed to deliver work on time. He replied: "I reject them all."
The prosecution also alleges Chowdhury used sick notes from his doctor as part of the cover-up.

But the prosecution said while he was telling some employers he was sick and unfit to work because of "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" he was not giving sick notes to other employers. The prosecution said this ''underlines the dishonesty involved in the whole affair".
His line manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, arranged a video call in May 2023, to support him returning to work after a period of absence.
In previous evidence she told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin.
She told the court that as the call went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."
Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ told the court: ''This almost laughable incident demonstrates quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit.''
The trial continues.

articles.title: What is happening to UK prices?
articles.standfirst: UK inflation rose in September, pushed up by higher petrol and diesel prices.
paragraphs: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, the highest rate in nearly a year and above the Bank of England's 2% target.
The rise was slightly higher than economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.
Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months.
Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%.
The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026, while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed.
The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation.
The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), and the latest figure is published every month.
The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%.
Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises.
But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy.
For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals.
Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment.

Although CPI inflation of 3.5% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
That was the highest rate for 40 years.
While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly.
The higher figure for September was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 29.8% compared to September last year.
Food price inflation remained at 1.3%.

But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran.
Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine.

Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026.
But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario.

When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July.

As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the 4% increase in household energy bills from 1 October when the latest Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher.

As part of his pledge to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living, Prime Minister Andy Burnham scrapped VAT on household electricity bills in October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation.
Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs.
Core CPI was 2.8% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to August.
The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023.
In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario.
At its September meeting, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.
The Bank also looks closely at what is happening to wages and unemployment.
The latest official figures show that regular pay in the UK grew ahead of inflation in the three months to August.
Average annual growth in pay, excluding bonuses, during the three-month period was 3.7%.
After taking inflation into account, it means regular pay grew by 0.8% between June and August.
The US and eurozone countries have also been trying to limit price increases, but also face challenges with inflation.
The inflation rate for countries using the euro was 3.8% in September, according to EU data - up from 3.2% in August.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in recent months to 2.5%.
US inflation was in 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August, with prices there also affected by higher fuel costs.
The Federal Reserve cited "too high" inflation when it raised interest rates for the first time in three years in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%.
The move came despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

articles.title: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroad
articles.standfirst: With graduate jobs hard to come by, more young adults are reported to be considering emigrating.
paragraphs: Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseas
Last year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place.
"I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails."

More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey of 15,000 final year university students.
Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high.
UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report.
For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading?
While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show.

In addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme, British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years.
Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than London

Rachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for accountancy giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First.

She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London.
Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched.

"People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life."
Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures from the UK's Office for National Statistics.
It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived.
After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US.
Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunities
Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University.
West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching.

"I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live.
"In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences."
The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult.
One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends.
Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from Finland
This is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design.
Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020.
"Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently."
Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon.
"To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities."
Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas.
"When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational."
Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London.
"I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better."

articles.title: Inflation Could Climb Above 5% in Early 2027
articles.standfirst: Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent the previous month.  Monthly price growth between August and September in 2026 was high at 0.4...
paragraphs: Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent the previous month. Monthly price growth between August and September in 2026 was high at 0.4 per cent compared to 0 per cent in 2025, leading to the increase of 0.4 percentage points in annual inflation.

The monthly inflation of 0.4 per cent corresponds to an annualised rate of 4.9 per cent and flows on from the high monthly inflation of 0.5 per cent in August. This suggests that the continuing energy supply issues caused by the American war on Iran are feeding into general price inflation. These effects are likely to escalate until a resolution to the conflict is found. Under our preferred forecast scenarios, inflation looks set to reach
The Bank of England will face pressure to tighten policy as inflation continues to increase.
If we look at the broad categories of inflation over the last 12 months, we see:

Services inflation this month is pretty much in line with wage data reflecting a cooling labour market: the latest ONS figures on wage increases excluding bonuses, covering June to August 2026, came in at 3.7 per cent.
The biggest contributors to the change in headline inflation between August and September were:

However, these overall contributions combine the “base effects” of inflation dropping out from the previous year with the new inflation “dropping in”. We need to unwrap these to get the true picture. Figure 1 (below) shows the sectoral contributions to overall inflation, with the previous year’s monthly inflation dropping out (blue) and the current month’s new inflation dropping in (brown). The overall impact is the sum of the two, shown by the burgundy line.

Focusing on the new monthly inflation (brown), eight sectors registered an increase in prices this month, with two registering falls (interestingly these two were Transport and Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages). The blue dropouts from the previous year are negative or close to zero in eight sectors, and positive in two (also Transport and Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages). Overall, the burgundy line, showing the total effect for each sector, is significantly negative in one sector, and significantly positive in three sectors, as listed above.

We can look ahead over the next 12 months to see how inflation might evolve as the recent inflation “drops out” as we move forward month by month. Each month, the new inflation enters the annual figure and the old inflation from the same month in the previous year “drops out”. We depict the following scenarios for future inflation dropping in:

The Iran war makes the future path of inflation highly uncertain. In my initial blog, The Possible Effects on UK Inflation in 2026 of the US-Iran Conflict, published on 23 March, I contrasted the possible effects of two scenarios, a “good scenario” with a short conflict that left most of the energy infrastructure in the Gulf intact and an “ugly” scenario with a prolonged conflict in which most of the infrastructure is destroyed. With the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and now the additional closure of the Bab-el-Mandeb, we seem to be heading into the “ugly” scenario, with a major inflationary spike. In addition, the direct conflict between Saudi Arabia and Ansar Allah (the Houthis) has led to the destruction of significant pipelines and refineries in Saudi Arabia. Unless the conflicts are resolved soon, there is likely to be more inflation coming our way and also negative impacts on output and employment across much of the world as we move into 2027.

I have therefore revived our old friend from 2022, the “sanctions” scenario, now renamed the “Hormuz” scenario. This and the very high scenario seem to be most relevant at present, and we also depict the high and medium scenarios for reference. The low scenario seems unlikely to be relevant so we have not depicted it.

If we look at the very high and Hormuz scenarios, inflation might be at 4.2-4.7 per cent in December 2026. Even the medium and high scenarios suggest that inflation will be at 3.4-3.7 per cent by December. So, under all scenarios, inflation looks set to rise in the final quarter of 2026.
For further analysis of inflation in the United Kingdom, see:
Seasonal Adjustment of CPI and CPIH, Huw Dixon and Monica George Michail. NIESR Policy Paper 45, May 2025

articles.title: Japan’s low-leverage economy should withstand rate hikes
articles.standfirst: The rate hikes we expect over the next few months are unlikely to derail Japan’s economy from its modest but steady growth path. Most firms and households will be able to withstand a rise in interest rate costs thanks to their healthy balance sheets.
paragraphs: The rate hikes we expect over the next few months are unlikely to derail Japan’s economy from its modest but steady growth path. Most firms and households will be able to withstand a rise in interest rate costs thanks to their healthy balance sheets.

Most companies will likely maintain a reasonable spread between return on assets and interest rate costs thanks to their low leverage and rising profitability. However, an analysis of small firms shows that a 1ppt rise in effective interest rates could increase the share of loss-making small firms from 27% to 31%.

On aggregate, the Japanese are net savers and rate hikes will have a net positive impact by raising deposit rates. However, people in their 30s and 40s tend to be net debtors due to large, overwhelmingly floating-rate mortgages, making them vulnerable. Although higher rates will weaken already stagnant residential investment, their impact on overall economic growth should be limited.

The economy’s overall resilience to higher interest rates may allow the Bank of Japan to hike its policy rate beyond 1.75% to prevent further weakening of the yen and/or the de-anchoring of inflation expectations driven by prolonged cost-push inflation. However, the potential damage to vulnerable small firms and stretched household finances could make the government more cautious, exerting pressure on the bank.

articles.title: Expensing Concentrates the Corporate Tax Burden on Economic Profits
articles.standfirst: As scrutiny over data center investment and AI rises, some commentators are concerned about how expensing interacts with these ongoing investments. Most of these concerns misunderstand what expensing does.
paragraphs: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) improved the corporate taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. system with permanent bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. for machinery and equipment investment and immediate expensing for research and development (R&D) costs. But now, as scrutiny over data center investment and AI rises, some commentators are concerned about how expensing interacts with these ongoing investments. Most of these concerns misunderstand what expensing does. Expensing stops the tax code from discouraging marginal investment, but it doesn’t subsidize investment that isn’t worthwhile on its own merits, nor does it eliminate taxes on profitable projects.

Full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. allows firms to immediately deduct what they expend on capital investment in the same year the capital investment starts being used. Aligning the timing of the deduction to the timing of the expense preserves its full value; firms fully recover investment costs, as opposed to taking deductions over time and experiencing the erosion brought on by inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin and opportunity cost. This treatment eliminates the burden of the tax system on the normal return to investment, the amount needed to break even. It does not eliminate tax on the supernormal return, which arises when firms earn economic profits.
Imagine two firms that each undertake a $100 investment in a world of 2 percent inflation and a 3 percent real discount rate (which we approximate with a 5 percent rate for simplicity).

Firm A’s investment will just break even, returning $105 in year 2, equal in present value terms to the $100 upfront cost. It’s a marginal investment, and the firm wouldn’t undertake it if the tax system imposed a burden on marginal investment. Firm B’s investment will earn economic profits, returning $110 in year 2. It is not a marginal investment, but is something so profitable the firm would undertake it even under a biased tax system.

Now we’ll add taxes, using the 21 percent corporate tax rate and an illustrative depreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco system that requires the firms to use straight-line depreciation over the two-year period, deducting $50 in year 1 and the remaining $50 in year 2. Firm A’s investment broke even before taxes, but the requirement to delay depreciation deductions imposes a tax burden on the normal return to investment, making the project no longer pencil out. Firm B still clears a profit, even in the presence of depreciation.

Waiting to take the depreciation deduction in year 2 reduces its real value: the $10.50 of tax savings in year 2 ($50 depreciation deduction x 21 percent corporate rate) is only worth $10.00 today. This erosion in the real value of the deductions flips Firm A’s after-tax net present value negative, while it costs Firm B $0.50 of its after-tax net present value.

But if the tax system instead permitted the firms to deduct the investment cost upfront, the tax burden on the break-even investment would be eliminated. Firm A would break even, while Firm B still earns a profit of $3.76 in present value, down $1.00 from the no-tax scenario and up $0.50 from the depreciation scenario. Expensing concentrates the tax burden on the supernormal returnSupernormal returns are payoffs to investment greater than the typical market rate of return. They are often approximated as company profits that exceed 10 percent. This additional return on capital or labor is above breaking even on an investment relative to the amount of risk and time that investment required. (21 percent of $4.76) and leaves the normal return untaxed.

Expensing would not make an unprofitable investment worthwhile. For example, consider Firm C, with the same $100 upfront investment cost but a return of $104 in year 2. In present value, the project loses $0.95 before taxes. Under full expensing, it would still lose $0.75, so Firm C still would not invest. Expensing makes the tax code neutral toward investment; it does not turn a pre-tax loss into an after-tax gain (see the discussion on potential interactions with interest deductions below).

Table 4 separates each firm’s tax into the normal and supernormal return components. Depreciation taxes both, while expensing removes the burden on the normal return and places it entirely on the supernormal return. Expensing thus removes most of the corporate tax’s adverse impact on economic efficiency and growth, while still generating revenues from projects with positive economic profits.

Some argue that in the presence of deductions for business interest paid, full expensing more than eliminates the burden on the normal return and leads to negative effective tax rates. Under the current tax code, business interest deductions are limited to 30 percent of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA). Further, the concern over negative effective tax rates typically excludes consideration of the tax that applies to the interest income received by lenders, as Stephen J. Entin explains for Tax Foundation:

Some students of taxation claim that the two deductions result in a negative tax rate on some businesses, because between the two write-offs the business would appear to be writing off more than the cost of the asset. But that argument looks only at one side of the financial transaction (the borrower’s side) and misses a key point. The interest payment deducted from the borrower’s income is added to the lender’s income. Looking at lender and borrower together shows there is no excess deduction. Some of the earnings of the asset are passed on to be taxed on the lender’s tax form instead of on the business’s tax form. The earnings are still taxed. There is no negative tax on the investment and its returns. (Note: some limited lending comes from tax exempt groups, but their endowments are relatively inflexible and are not generally funding new investment, at the margin, which determines the amount of capital formation. The issue with the non-taxable entities is whether they deserve that status; it is not a reason to avoid expensing.)

As Entin explains elsewhere, simply disallowing interest deductions while still taxing lenders on the interest they receive would lead to double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income.. Consistent reform of interest deductions would move toward cash flow taxation: either disallowing deductions for borrowers and excluding interest income for lenders, or the reverse, permitting deductions and ensuring full taxability. But reforming the treatment of interest is not a prerequisite for a tax system built on expensing.

Expensing is the right policy because it eliminates the tax burden on the normal return to investment—the margin that matters most for growing the capital stock—and it concentrates the burden of the corporate tax on economic profits. Profitable data center investment may be like the economic profits case, and expensing still taxes its economic profits in full. Expensing does not make a higher corporate tax rate fully harmless, as the statutory rate and the burden on supernormal returns affect incentives for profit shiftingProfit shifting is when multinational companies reduce their tax burden by moving the location of their profits from high-tax countries to low-tax jurisdictions and tax havens. and innovation, but it right-sizes the corporate tax system.

Erica York is Senior Economist with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Her analysis has been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post, Politico, and other national and international media outlets.

articles.title: 2026 Economics Nobel Laureate Robert Hall Helped Lay Foundation for Pro-Growth Tax Reform
articles.standfirst: Hall’s research helped economists understand how taxes distort investment decisions, while his work with Rabushka shows how to minimize those distortions. Although the US remains far from a pure consumption tax, Hall’s work informs efforts to reduce the tax burden on investment, improve neutrality, and promote long-run economic growth.
paragraphs: Last week, economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” The award recognizes their foundational contributions to New Keynesian macroeconomics, including how individual decisions by households and businesses shape broader economic outcomes.

Robert Hall is also well known in the taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. policy world. In a landmark 1967 paper written with Dale Jorgenson, Hall helped establish how tax policy affects business investment decisions. Businesses invest when the expected return exceeds the cost of depreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco, financing, and taxes. This combined hurdle is known as the user cost of capital.

The Hall-Jorgenson framework shows quantitatively how tax policy can impact both the level and timing of business investment, providing the foundation for why delaying depreciation deductions raises the cost of investment by raising the cost of capital. Immediate expensing, on the other hand, removes the tax penalty on marginal investment imposed by inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin and the time value of money.

Additionally, Hall is known for being the co-author of the Hall-Rabushka flat tax. While some focus on the tax proposal’s flat rate design—the original proposal used a 19 percent flat taxAn income tax is referred to as a “flat tax” when all taxable income is subject to the same tax rate, regardless of income level or assets. rate—it is also, at its core, a tax aimed at consumption.

Policymakers can target a consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible. base in many different ways; a value-added tax (VAT) targets value added at each stage of production, while the Hall-Rabushka flat tax splits the base out to tax businesses on their cash flow and individuals on their wages.

Businesses deduct the cost of investment and households pay tax on wages above an exemption, without being taxed twice on investment returns such as interest, dividends, and capital gains. The proposal therefore eliminates the income tax’s bias against saving and investment by providing expensing and avoiding additional taxes on investment returns.

Hall and Rabushka’s work inspired subsequent proposals to tax consumption progressively, including the X-tax proposed by economist David Bradford. The X-tax keeps a cash flow tax for businesses and applies a graduated tax rate for household wages with a top household rate matching the business tax rate. This design helped inform the design of destination-based cash flow taxes (DBCFTs) as a policy option to reform the business tax code.

While the US remains a hybrid tax system between income and consumption tax bases, Hall’s tax policy legacy contributed to the policy motivation behind the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which moved the US tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. toward consumption by reviving 100 percent bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs.. The 2025 reconciliation law made 100 percent bonus depreciation permanent and restored domestic R&D expensing, keeping that progress in the tax code.

Hall’s research helped economists understand how taxes distort investment decisions, while his work with Rabushka shows how to minimize those distortions. Although the US remains far from a pure consumption tax, Hall’s work informs efforts to reduce the tax burden on investment, improve neutrality, and promote long-run economic growth.

articles.title: The Return of the Energy Shock
articles.standfirst: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of...
paragraphs: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of the year, following the February, May and July 2026 blogs. Three things have changed since July:

The July blog made a testable claim: our recommended Intermediate Energy MRN projected 3.0 per cent for June 2026, easing to 2.7 per cent by August, before rising to a 4.5 per cent peak in February 2027. The outturns were 2.6 per cent in June and 3.1 per cent in August. The model was 0.4 percentage points too high in June and 0.4 points too low in August, and the sign of the error flipped exactly as the geopolitics did. In June the peace announcement was pulling energy prices down faster than the model’s training data allowed for; by August the collapse of that deal was pushing them up faster. We flagged the first possibility explicitly in July (“a June print materially below this range would suggest the peace-deal energy price fall is passing through faster than the model anticipates”). We did not anticipate the second, and nor, on the evidence of its July Report, did the Bank of England, whose central projection assumed oil prices would drift from $76 to $71, and inflation would peak at 3.2 per cent in the fourth quarter of 2026. Two lessons follow. The first is that the MRN carries no oil price assumption at all; it extrapolates from the energy history it has seen. So its twelve-month path is best read as an unconditional projection of where the data were pointing at end-August. The Bank’s and NIESR’s forecasts are conditional on an assumed path for oil prices. Part of the gap between us is therefore a difference in what is being forecast, not only in how; the fair test is whether the unconditional path keeps moving the right way when the world moves, as it did between June and August. The second is that readers of our May blog will recall that the then-current MRN had inflation “well beyond 5 per cent in early 2027”; the July update, trained during the brief peace, pulled that back to 4.5 per cent. The present round returns to the May reading.

Figure 1 shows the current forecast of two classes of MRN model: the Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which uses CPI level and month-on-month change, ONS UK energy CPI, the monthly Brent average and, new in this round, Bank Rate; and the Intermediate Energy MRN, which adds real GDP, PPI, the 10-year gilt yield and the sterling effective exchange rate to that set. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects annual CPI inflation of 3.7 per cent in September 2026, 4.1 per cent in November, 4.4 per cent in December, and then a step up to 5.4 per cent in January 2027, holding at 5.4 per cent in February and March before easing to 4.3–4.4 per cent in April–May and drifting back up to 4.9 per cent by July and August 2027. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN follows a similar path but peaks later and higher, at 5.7 per cent in June 2027. The Average MRN peaks at 5.3 per cent in February and does not fall below 4.5 per cent at any point in the forecast window. The quarterly averages are 3.9, 5.2 and 4.8 per cent for the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first two quarters of 2027, respectively.

We must state two things about this path clearly. The first is that the peak has moved up by almost a full percentage point since July, from 4.5 per cent to 5.4 per cent, while its timing has stayed put in the first quarter of 2027. That revision is almost entirely the energy channel doing what it is designed to do: the price of Brent crude oil is 50 per cent higher than when the July models were trained, UK wholesale gas prices have risen 78 per cent since the Bank’s July Report, and the Ofgem energy price cap has gone from £1,477 in Q2 to £1,663 in Q3 and £1,723 for October–December, with Cornwall Insight now forecasting £1,999, a 16 per cent rise, for January 2027. The second is that part of the January step is arithmetic rather than economics. The CPI fell by 0.5 per cent month-on-month in January 2026; so, roughly half a point of the first quarter peak is that base effect. It is real, in the sense that the headline rate will print it, but it does not imply a fresh burst of price pressure in that month.

This is the first round in which we forecast the policy rate, and the two classes disagree in a way we think is informative rather than embarrassing. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which sees inflation, energy and the rate itself, but nothing of the real economy, has Bank Rate rising from 3.75 per cent to 4.0 per cent by February 2027 and 4.5 per cent by June. The Intermediate Energy MRN, which also sees GDP, producer prices, gilt yields and sterling, has it falling to 3.5 per cent by November, 3.25 per cent by January and 3.0 per cent by March, before settling at 3.25 per cent. The average of the two dips to 3.5 per cent through the winter, touches 3.25 per cent in March, and is back at 3.75 per cent by June 2027.

Read the two classes as the two sides of the Monetary Policy Committee’s own argument. At its 17 September meeting the Committee held at 3.75 per cent by six votes to three, with Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill voting for an immediate quarter-point increase on the grounds that slack “may have already peaked” and that raising rates is “a better risk-management strategy when faced with uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects”. The six who held pointed to “very limited evidence of emerging second-round effects” and to slack “still evident in a range of indicators”, with Alan Taylor arguing that policy “should respond to evidence of propagation rather than mechanically to volatile ticks in headline energy prices”. The Simple class, which has no measure of slack and reacts to headline energy, is the hawkish minority’s direction of travel. The Intermediate class, which can see weak activity and the restrictiveness of financial conditions, is the majority’s. We do not claim the network understands this debate; we claim that the two feature sets encode the two positions, and that is exactly why we report both rather than only the average.

The September 2026 inflation number from the ONS is due on 21 October and is the first direct test of these forecasts. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects 3.7 per cent, the Simple Energy + MPC MRN 3.9 per cent and the Average 3.8 per cent, all well above August’s 3.1 per cent, reflecting the motor-fuel surge the Bank has already documented. A September number in the 3.6–3.9 per cent range would validate the near-term path; something nearer 3.3 per cent would suggest the VAT cut and the G7 reserve release are biting faster than the model allows. The second test is the 6 November MPC decision: the Simple MRN class implies the hawks gain ground, the Intermediate MRN class implies the first cut arrives by November, and the two cannot both be right. The third is the Ofgem announcement for January 2027, due in late November, which will fix the single biggest input into our peak in the first quarter of 2027. The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook and the NIESR Autumn Economic Outlook both appear before our next update, and we will report how the MRN stands against their revised paths.

1 The modelling approach is described in Binner, J. M., Kelly, L. J. and Tepper, J. A. (2025) ‘Professional Forecasters vs. Shallow Neural Network Ensembles: Assessing Inflation Prediction Accuracy’, Journal of Risk and Financial Management, 18(4), 173 (MRN methodology). https://doi.org/10.3390/jrfm18040173.

articles.title: Is the minimum wage to blame for falling youth employment?
articles.standfirst:
This blog was originaly published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.  Once a year the Low Pay Commission (LPC) assemble in their Canary Wharf office to decide the following year’s minimum wage rates. I went along to share my thoughts on falling youth employment. I said that we can’t confidently blame the minimum wage. But the … Continued
The post Is the minimum wage to blame for falling youth employment? appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This blog was originaly published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.

Once a year the Low Pay Commission (LPC) assemble in their Canary Wharf office to decide the following year’s minimum wage rates. I went along to share my thoughts on falling youth employment. I said that we can’t confidently blame the minimum wage. But the LPC should still tread carefully and refrain from shrinking the gap between the youth rate and the adult rate next year.
Youth employment rates are ringing alarm bells, having fallen further than for older workers in recent years, as shown below.1

Employment rates among 18-24 and 25-64-year-olds fully recovered after Covid, but the trend for young people then diverged. The youth employment rate fell from 2022 onwards, now standing almost 6 per cent below 2019 levels. By contrast, the rate among 25-64-year-olds held up, reached a new high in 2023, and only then drifted down to 1 per cent below 2019 levels.
Before we get to the minimum wage, it’s worth heading off some challenges to this negative picture.

Firstly – it’s not about studying. Student numbers are flat. This means that the share of young people not in employment or education (the NEET rate) has almost certainly been rising – which is also what the LFS tells us.

What about population growth? If the employment rate is jobs divided by people, then maybe it’s more people, not fewer jobs? If we focus on the numerator for a moment – the number of jobs – it looks like there might be some truth to that. The number of 18-24-year-olds in PAYE employment recovered post Covid and then stayed pretty flat.

Flat jobs and a rising population might be less worrying if we thought the population increase was coming from groups we’d expect to work at lower rates. We know there’s been high migration recently – so maybe it’s just that lots of people arrived with low employment rates?

But that’s not what’s been happening. Firstly, the number of jobs held by young UK nationals has been falling since 2022 – it’s not that population growth from overseas is making a flat picture on jobs look bad.2

Second, the number of UK nationals has probably been growing since 2022, due to a mini baby boom twenty years ago.3 This means jobs among UK nationals would have had to have been growing since 2022 for the employment picture to be stable among that group.

So, the picture is pretty much the same as where we started. There has been a serious fall in youth employment since 2022, which isn’t accounted for by rising education participation, or by population or migration changes.
Honestly, we don’t have great answers. Lots of the obvious candidates don’t line up neatly with a deterioration that began in 2022.

Earlier in the year we dug into rising NEET rates and found that half of the post-2019 increase can be put down to a general labour market slowdown. The rest seems to be to worsening health, but that’s a slower moving trend, not something that accelerated in 2022 specifically. It’s tempting to reach for AI as an explanation, but Claude and ChatGPT weren’t very widely used until fairly recently, so they don’t really help with the 2022 question.

What about the minimum wage? There have certainly been big increases. Between April 2022 and April 2026, average weekly earnings rose 24 per cent, the adult minimum wage rose 34 per cent, and the older youth rate rose 59 per cent.

Lots of people have put two and two together: the minimum wage went up, youth employment went down, what more do you need to see? Well plenty else changed over that period, and it’s hard to strip that out. The IFS did some great analysis on the recent youth rate changes and couldn’t rule out a zero effect. And you find zero effects in some other studies.

What if this is all structural change, not policy? Perhaps the shape of the economy shifted against the young. Retail and wholesale jobs never recovered post-Covid and have been falling since 2022, while hospitality jobs have fallen since 2023. Together those sectors account for 2-in-5 youth jobs, and they stopped adding jobs just as more young people needed work. You can tell a story of big forces here: online shopping; automated warehouses; and a preference for screens to seeing our mates.

But maybe the minimum wage is why they shrank – it makes what they sell more expensive and causes firms to save on low-wage (disproportionately young) labour. That said, it’s not true that recent job shedding is all happening in low-paid sectors. This implies that either recent sectoral changes aren’t being driven by policies affecting low-paid labour costs (like the minimum wage, and employer NICs), or that those policies are having an effect, but there just happen to be other drivers affecting higher-paying sectors at the same time.
So, what to do if you are the Low Pay Commission? They have to make an actual pounds and pence decision for next year’s minimum wage rates – they can’t get away with the hand waving I’ve done here.

I think in the face of big uncertainty about policy effects, and when the labour market is weak, the right choice is caution. We can’t say that the minimum wage is causing the youth employment downturn. But absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. And with the UK’s high minimum wage rates, low hourly pay isn’t the problem it once was. So, I think the LPC should avoid another convergence hike to the youth rates this year.

One LPC Commissioner looked me in the eye and said give me a number. I’d eaten several of their biscuits so I could hardly say no. So my specific recommendation for 2027 was to uprate the whole framework – the adult rate and the youth rates – in line with average wages.

1 Data aside #1: I say ‘employment rate’ because we are using proxies based on tax and population data, because the ONS’s LFS still isn’t very useful for monitoring trends. The 18-24 rate is simply PAYE jobs among this age group divided by the population. This means it doesn’t include any self-employed people in that age group, but there aren’t many so that’s ok. The 25-64 rate nets 18-24-year-olds off the fully-fledged estimates we produce for 16-64-year-old employment rates which do include self-employment.

2 Data aside #2: These charts are counting PAYE jobs not people – because that’s what HMRC published – and there’s a probable discontinuity in 2021 from IR35 changes boosting the number of PAYE jobs per person in the PAYE system. But it’s safe to look at trends before and after this point.

3 Data aside #3: Unfortunately, as far as I’m aware the ONS doesn’t publish population by age by nationality explicitly. But we can make a reasonable guess by ageing forward younger cohorts (specifically – we add up the population aged 16 from previous years). This will differ from the true change in 18-24 UK nationals to the extent that the non-UK share of 16-year-olds and net migration patterns among young UK nationals have changed in this period.
