articles.title: Performance Tracker 2026: Cross-service analysis
articles.standfirst:
Performance Tracker 2026: Cross-service analysis melissa.ittoo Thu, 15/10/2026 - 14:27 63 Report chapter Stuart Hoddinott Institute for Government Yes Public services NHS Schools Public sector Public spending Local government Criminal justice Police Prisons Labour Prime minister Chancellor of the exchequer Health and social care secretary Home secretary Starmer government Burnham government Number 10 HM Treasury Home Office Department of Health and Social Care Ministry of Justice Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
Public services performance tracker 2026 - cross service analysis
No Despite progress in some areas, Starmer's reform agenda did not live up to expectations and leaves Burnham with difficult choices.

The ‘honeymoon period’ enjoyed by Keir Starmer’s Labour Party in the summer of 2024 was possibly the shortest lived of any recent government – certainly one coming off the back of a landslide general election win. Walking into their new departments, ministers were confronted with a raft of problems inherited from their Conservative predecessors.

In the health department, Wes Streeting quickly declared the NHS “broken”. 18 Streeting W, ‘The NHS is broken: Health and Social Care Secretary statement’, speech at the Department of Health and Social Care, 5 July 2024, www.gov.uk/government/speeches/statement-from-the-secretary-of-state-for-health-and-social-care  In the Ministry of Justice, Shabana Mahmood was confronted with a prison estate with functionally no available capacity, requiring an immediate response. 19 Ministry of Justice, HM Prison and Probation Service, Youth Custody Service and The Rt Hon Shabana Mahmood MP, ‘Lord Chancellor sets out immediate action to defuse ticking prison ‘time-bomb’’, press release, 12 July 2024, www.gov.uk/government/news/lord-chancellor-sets-out-immediate-action-to-defuse-ticking-prison-time-bomb

Angela Rayner was bequeathed a local government system in the middle of a genuine financial crisis. Bridget Phillipson found knotty, long-standing problems across the education brief, from children’s social care to special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

Unlike the last Labour government, Starmer could not rely on a growing economy and consequent large tax receipts to provide unprecedentedly large funding increases to public services. And the outgoing Conservative government had laid him a trap too, signing off in 2024 with an unrealistically tight spending envelope that implied spending cuts that would – almost without question – worsen performance across many services for the years ahead.

Once in office, Labour rapidly abandoned those plans. Starmer and his chancellor, Rachel Reeves, raised taxes in the 2024 autumn budget to fund larger settlements than the Conservatives’ spending plans. That additional funding, combined with effective, targeted policy, meant that performance in some services – general practice and the police – has improved since the election. As a result, Starmer’s successor Andy Burnham, prime minister since July 2026, has a slightly better inheritance on public services than his predecessor.

New prime minister, same problems

But the overall picture remains difficult. Burnham faces many of the same problems Starmer did, but now there is the added complexity of ongoing reforms in various services, kicked off by the Starmer and Burnham governments. Some are poorly conceived and executed, like Streeting’s abolition of NHS England; others do not align with Burnham’s goals, such as the ambition to create large regional police forces that do not align with other services’ boundaries (a key aim of Burnham’s much vaunted devolution agenda).

Burnham has already articulated a more coherent high-level vision for public service reform than Starmer, characterised by his ‘devolution by default’ approach. He has also outlined more specific goals, such as his intent to finally reform the adult social care sector. But while he has put more personal political capital into both than many before him, he would not be the first prime minister to make grand promises on devolving power and reforming adult social care, only to back away when faced with the realities of office.

Even if he remains committed to those pledges, there will still be many testing moments over the coming months and years that will hinder his reform programme and wider attempts to improve performance. Reeves’ 2025 spending plans were more generous than her Conservative predecessor’s but still imply cuts (for the prison service) and funding increases that may not meet expected demand (in the police and hospitals). Stretching performance targets, extensive reform programmes and the ever-present spectre of another period of higher-than-forecast inflation pile pressure on other budgets.

Priorities for the Burnham government on public services

We lay out three priorities for Burnham on public services in the early days of his government:

  1. Burnham should clarify the principles that will underpin his ‘devolution by default’ reform agenda. 20 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the State – Cabinet Statement’, GOV.UK, 31 July 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html  That is a welcome direction of travel. But he should lay out the principles by which departments decide which powers to devolve and to which level or organisations within government.
  2. Burnham should rapidly clarify which ongoing reforms he wants to stop, adapt, or continue and use the power of the prime minister to ensure they are better co-ordinated than they were under Starmer.
  3. Burnham should use this year’s budget and next year’s spending review to better support his cross-cutting priorities.

This report will first describe the changes in public service performance under the Starmer government, then assess that government’s public service reform agenda and the effect it has had on services. It will then examine Burnham’s proposed approach to managing public services and some of the challenges that he will face over the rest of this parliament. It will finish by making recommendations for how Burnham can improve performance before the next election.

This report draws on analysis of publicly available data and dozens of interviews with government officials, employees in public bodies, staff in front-line services, and experts from other organisations.

Related content

Fixing public services: Sticking with the status quo – implications of current spending plans

Part 1: The Starmer government’s record on public services

How did public services fare under the Starmer government, from July 2024 to July 2026, and what reforms were begun in this period?

Starmer steadied the ship in some services and improved performance in other areas

Smart policy choices and additional money helped the Starmer government to stabilise performance across many public services and improve performance in others, sometimes markedly.

In the NHS, the government hit its first target for elective* waiting times. Patient satisfaction with general practice also increased, likely facilitated by a large expansion of the salaried GP workforce. In both cases, however, performance still lags pre-pandemic levels.

Absence rates fell in schools, though from record levels following an explosion during and after the pandemic. The government has also recruited more teachers since the election and is on course to hit its target, although not necessarily to meet actual demand. The relative performance of England against other countries in reading, maths and science also improved, though this was largely due to reforms implemented by governments over the 2010s. 22 Adam R, ‘England’s teenagers outperform peers in most countries in maths, reading and science’, The Guardian, 8 September 2026, retrieved 30 September 2026, www.theguardian.com/education/2026/sep/08/england-teenagers-outperform-peers-in-most-countries-in-maths-reading-and-science

Local government finance, long in a state of collapse, was another area where Starmer’s government took difficult decisions. It implemented a long overdue redesign of the funding system, directing money towards more deprived local authorities. Combined with larger-than-expected funding increases, local government funding is now due to return to 2010 levels by the end of this parliament, providing councils with some much-needed breathing room. Even that extensive programme may not be enough, however, to return the sector to financial stability. Funding will still be almost 14% lower in real terms on a per person basis in 2028/29 than in 2010/11. Too many councils still rely on one-off funding sources – such as reserves, additional borrowing or asset sales – to fund day-to-day services.

Starmer’s government faced arguably the most difficult immediate challenge in the prison system, which was weeks away from completely running out of spaces. Shabana Mahmood, the then justice secretary, successfully avoided disaster with an initial decision to release some prisoners after 40% of their sentence in September and October 2024 (rather than 50%), while her successor, David Lammy, passed legislation to stabilise the prison population. Prisons are still in a bad state, sometimes severely so – but keeping the system going at all was a significant achievement given how bad the situation was in July 2024, and there were even some signs of improving performance towards the end of the Starmer government.

In policing, the government substantially exceeded its first-year target to increase police officers in neighbourhood roles, which grew by 3,800 in the year to March 2026 against a target of 3,000 – an increase of 22%. Knife crime, another of the Starmer government’s key priorities, fell 10% between 2023/24 and 2025/26.

Facing a record backlog, in 2025 the crown court closed more cases than in any year since 2016. The government has also facilitated the expansion of key workforce groups – in the Crown Prosecution Service and criminal lawyers – after additional investment.

The Starmer government laid the groundwork for potential future improvements in performance

There are also some areas where Starmer’s government launched reform programmes or initiatives that didn’t immediately lead to improvements, but which may contribute to them over time.

Children’s social care is an obvious example. The government closely followed the recommendations made by Josh MacAlister (now the minister for children and families in the Department for Education) in his independent review of the care system. It duly allocated more money for services designed to keep children with their families and out of the care system, such as multi-agency child protection teams in every local area.

Many of the reforms in the January 2026 police white paper are also likely to improve performance, including a National Police Service and reforming the oversight and assessment of police performance. Relatively little progress has been made on the structural reforms to policing so far, but the new performance processes are already up and running and most interviewees thought they would drive meaningful improvements.

The government also launched the first stages of its special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) reforms, aimed at better integrating local services around children and preventing the rise of acute demand for those services.

In these cases, the benefits of these reform programmes may only be felt in several years’ time, not least because much of the money that the Starmer government allocated for those programmes has not yet been spent.

The Sentencing Act would also have likely generated performance improvements in the prisons system over the rest of this parliament, as prisoners were released early, freeing up space. Since the changes the Burnham government has introduced, however, these improvements have become much less likely. Prison capacity will remain significantly more constrained for the foreseeable future, even if further crisis is avoided.

* This is planned care that NHS hospitals provide – for example, hip replacements or cataract removals – and contrasts with the emergency care that they provide.

Related content

Performance Tracker 2025: Children's social care

Starmer also substantially increased capital spending compared to levels in the 2010s. In particular, DHSC and MoJ capital spending reached the highest point in real terms in any year on record (excluding pandemic years for the NHS) in 2025/26. Budgets for both departments are due to remain well above 2010s levels for the rest of the spending review period.

The MoJ is spending a good portion of its allocation on expanding the prisons estate to increase capacity. 44 Ministry of Justice, 10-Year Prison Capacity Strategy, CP 1219, The Stationery Office, 11 December 2024, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/67586f828a1ef8f66413b9c2/24.231_MOJ_10-Year_Capacity_Strat_Pub_v10.1_WEB.pdf  DHSC plans to spend its budget on initiatives including new neighbourhood health centres, upgrading the existing primary care estate, trying to bring down the maintenance backlog in hospitals, and delivering the New Hospitals Programme launched by the Johnson administration. 45 Department of Health and Social Care, 10 Year Capital Plan for Health and Social Care, GOV.UK, 8 July 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/10-year-capital-plan-for-health-and-social-care/10-year-capital-planfor-health-and-social-care

Home Office and MHCLG capital spending is not as high relative to historic levels as those departments but will be above the average level of the 2010s throughout this Labour government.

These boosts in capital budgets were certainly welcome. The preceding coalition then Conservative governments neglected that area throughout the 2010s, leaving many services on their knees on the eve of the 2024 general election (as successive Performance Trackers have shown). However the benefits will take a while to work through the system, as capital projects like building prisons, hospitals or neighbourhood health centres typically take years to conclude, and as services work their way through extensive maintenance backlogs.

This means many of the improvements promised, and funded, at the start of this parliament may only just be felt by the public at the end of this one, if not the start of the next.

Performance improved after the Starmer government filled some key staffing gaps, though other gaps remain

A clear trend across public services under Starmer was improvements in key staffing areas. These are staff groups where insufficient numbers created bottlenecks to effective working within and across systems, but where previous governments had failed to redress shortages.

In the NHS, the Starmer government rapidly expanded the salaried GP* workforce from 10,825 in June 2024 to 14,355 in August 2026, an increase of almost a third (32.6%). That workforce had been growing under the Conservatives, but much more slowly. The average monthly increase was 37.8 between September 2015 and June 2024, compared to 135.7 under the Labour government, though issues remain with how these staff are employed, and there are questions about how durable that growth might be.

Regardless, progress in this area has likely increased access to general practice, led to more GP appointments and contributed to higher patient satisfaction in 2026.

At the same time, however, the government did nothing to reverse the long-term decline in the GP partner workforce: there was a drop of 945 (5.9%) of those staff between June 2024 and August 2026. The fall is far greater since 2015: 30.5%. GP partners are vital for the effective working and sustainability of general practice. Partners are essentially small business owners that have a contract with the NHS to provide services, which it could not deliver itself in total, meaning that the current model of general practice cannot exist without them. They are also the staff that are associated with the largest increases in satisfaction and appointments. Doing nothing to reverse the decline was a major oversight by the Starmer government.

That government also successfully pursued growth in the criminal legal workforce, both in-house in the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and HM Courts and Tribunals Services (HMCTS) and among criminal defence lawyers. CPS crown advocates increased by more than 10% from 2024/25 to 2025/26 thanks to a substantial funding boost in the 2025 spending review, with a further rise expected in 2026/27. HMCTS hit its target staffing level of legal advisers in magistrates’ courts in 2024/25 following a recruitment drive, and there are also signs higher legal aid spending is increasing the number of criminal legal aid barristers and duty solicitors.

Given further increases to legal aid rates under Starmer, we expect that workforce to grow again in 2025/26. Shortages across these roles have been a major constraint on capacity and productivity in recent years, so this growth should help address criminal court backlogs. There is also evidence of increasing numbers of criminal defence lawyers.

In the magistrates’ courts, the Starmer government made some progress growing the number of magistrates, by 2.3% per year between 2023/24 and 2025/26, bringing the total number to just over 15,000. That is still far short, however, of the 21,000 that the MoJ estimates it needs by 2028/29. To meet that, the government would need to grow the number of magistrates by a wholly unrealistic 11.2% per year between 2025/26 and 2028/29.

And while the number of criminal barristers has grown in recent years, the number of criminal King’s counsel (KCs, the most senior barristers) continued to decline and was 24.4% lower in 2024/25 than in 2017/18.

In local government, there were record numbers of child and family social workers in the sector in 2025: 36,186 up from 34,328 in 2024, a 5.4% increase. 46 Department for Education, ‘Children’s social work workforce: Reporting year 2025’, GOV.UK, 19 March 2026, https://explore-education-statistics.service.gov.uk/find-statistics/children-s-social-work-workforce/2025  This may be partly attributable to Labour’s new regulations of agency working in the sector, 47 Department for Education, Agency Rules: Statutory guidance for local authorities on the use of agency child and family social workers, Department for Education, 2024, p. 10, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/670e59e9080bdf716392f380/Agency_Rules_-_statutory_guidance_for_local_authorities_on_the_use_of_agency_…  which were intended to increase the attractiveness of permanent employment over agency working.

The adult social care workforce continued to grow in 2025/26 from 1.57 million filled posts to 1.59 million, a 1.4% increase, though this is far lower than the average growth between 2021/22 and 2024/25, which was 4.2% per year. As has been the case since at least 2020/21, that growth was driven by an increase in staff from outside the UK working in the sector while the number of British staff continued to decline. That has happened despite the government ending the health and care visa route for new care worker applicants based abroad in 2025. Just under a third (32.5%) of staff in the sector are now from outside the UK, compared to 15.5% in 2020/21. 48 Skills for Care, The size and structure of the adult social care sector and workforce in England, 2026, Skills for Care, 24 June 2026, p. 14, www.skillsforcare.org.uk/Adult-Social-Care-Workforce-Data/workforceintelligence/resources/Reports/National/The-size-and-structure-of-the-adult-social…

In schools, the government is on track to far exceed its teacher workforce target (but not necessarily to meet demand for teachers). It has also improved its performance against recruitment targets for shortage subjects, but mostly because the targets were reduced – partly due to falling pupil numbers – rather than because recruitment increased substantially.

Throughout the 2010s, the proportion of hours that were taught by teachers that did not have a qualification in that subject dropped, reaching a low of 11.2% in the 2021–22 academic year. The lack of expert teachers in schools means that that proportion has crept back up, and reached 12.9% in 2025–26, higher than at any point since 2015–16.

* Salaried GPs are employed as permanent staff, but they do not own a practice like a GP partner.

This puts Starmer-era reforms at risk

The Starmer government’s inability or unwillingness to address some of these areas poses a direct risk to its own reforms. A growing GP partner workforce is required to sustainably increase capacity in general practice and achieve the government’s ambition of a ‘GP-led’ neighbourhood health service. In the courts, the government’s proposed reforms to the system would result in the magistrates’ courts handling more cases. Unless it can grow the magistrates workforce, that will put severe strain on that sector. The government’s 2025 changes to the health and care visa and proposed changes to settlement rules may result in a large exodus of social care staff in 2027 and 2028, when their five-year visas expire (workers will be able to renew their visa if they remain with the same employer). If many do choose to leave, they may leave a large hole in the social care workforce.

Improvements in priority areas mask a lack of progress elsewhere

Frequently, services improved most in the areas that ministers prioritised. In the NHS, Starmer’s government tied its agenda almost entirely to improved elective waiting times. In the police, it was neighbourhood policing, knife crime, and violence against women and girls (VAWG). In the courts, growing key parts of the workforce. And in prisons and probation, improving capacity.

In each case, the government has seen improvements in its selected areas. But, given limited funding envelopes, that has often come at the expense of performance elsewhere in those services. That is positive if the priorities are the right ones to deliver the government’s goals. In the criminal justice system, the government chose the right priorities – prison and court capacity – given the most urgent problems it faced and its long-term goals.

In contrast, the NHS’s focus on elective care often led to the system deprioritising the government’s other supposed priorities, such as a shift to community care or a greater focus on prevention. This was a mistake. The elective target has reinforced the NHS’s tendency to disproportionately direct funding and attention towards hospitals. And even within hospitals, the prioritisation of elective performance means there has been minimal improvement in poor A&E performance.

In contrast to those systems, the Starmer government never had a clear hierarchy of priorities in children’s services (such as schools, SEND and children’s social care). Instead, it seemed to pursue its myriad initiatives equally. There was no clear sense of which objectives took precedence between, for example, attainment, absence and inclusion. The government can afford to be more ambitious than previous governments, as falling pupil numbers reduces pressure on the schools’ budget. But it is still spreading resources very thin.

The lesson is that political prioritisation and focus drives attention in services. When forced to decide between an area with high political focus and another area services will direct time and resources towards the politically important one. They will also allow other areas (such as A&E and the community shift in the NHS or improving purposeful activity in prisons) to drift, even if they have an explicit target or strategy to improve.

Interdependencies within systems meant that improvements in one area created problems elsewhere

There is also an emerging pattern of successes in one part of a service leading to deteriorations elsewhere, generating a form of public services whack-a-mole.

In the NHS, the government has increased the use of ‘specialist advice’ – when a GP consults with a specialist colleague in a hospital before making a referral for elective care – to divert cases away from the elective waiting list. That has improved elective performance but arguably pushed pressure into community and primary care. There is some evidence that it is also leading to lower quality care. 49 Tilley C, ‘Exclusive: Watchdog links patient deaths to controversial NHSE policy’, Health Service Journal, 18 August 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/patient-safety/exclusive-watchdog-links-patientdeaths-to-controversial-nhse-policy/8124080.article

In the criminal justice system, the much-publicised early release scheme and sentence reform to reduce pressure on prisons pushed demand into the already-stretched probation service. Rising numbers of police charges, the result of greater activity among forces, continue to pile cases on to courts already struggling with record backlogs – while the Starmer government’s proposals for the courts system would reduce pressure on the crown courts, but would increase the workload for the magistrates’ courts.

Many areas are still struggling

Despite progress, Starmer’s government did not put public services on a trajectory that would return performance to pre-pandemic levels or, in many cases, meet the commitments ministers made. In many services, improvements on key targets often obscured a more nuanced picture.

Despite claiming to want to shift resources and care away from hospitals and into the community, the government continued to de-prioritise that sector. As a result, the waiting list for children’s community services is rising uncontrollably, with more than 25% waiting a year or more for care compared to 14% at the time of the election.

While access to publicly funded adult social care crept up under Starmer, more than a third fewer people access care than in 2009/10, when accounting for population growth. Access also grew far less slowly than spending, reflecting rapidly rising costs of providing care, without commensurate increases in quality. The Starmer government ducked reforming the sector, instead passing the decision to Louise Casey. Untouched, the largely broken system continued to exert pressure elsewhere: delayed discharges from hospitals stayed unacceptably high, slowing flow through hospitals and contributing to high A&E waiting times and likely slowing the reduction of the elective waiting list.

While the government’s reforms to local authority funding was the correct step, it continued to rely on one-off funding sources – such as borrowing and asset sales – to fund local government services. That has kept council ‘bankruptcies’ (section 114 notices) out of the press but has merely served to push the crisis into the future. Local government borrowing is rising, and faster among the councils in most financial distress. It will take them decades to repay those loans, while imposing interest costs on residents in the meantime.

Mirroring the situation in 2024, Burnham inherits a prisons system that is rapidly running out of places. Some of the decisions he has taken since coming into office have exacerbated those issues, as discussed in more depth below. The probation service is also under immense strain, with a further wave of early releases contributing to staff’s workload.

Starmer’s public service reform agenda was less than the sum of its parts

In his time at the head of the Labour Party, Keir Starmer made much of his plans to reform public services. In 2023, he said that services could not expect “vast sums of money” and argued instead that it was “reform or bust” if Labour wanted to improve public services. 50 Helm T and Savage M, ‘Keir Starmer: We can’t win power by spending. We need to reform and create wealth’, The Observer, 15 July 2023, retrieved 21 September 2026, www.theguardian.com/politics/2023/jul/15/keirstarmer-we-cant-spend-our-way-back-to-power  However, despite some positive changes to funding and a handful of promising pilots, Labour took power without a strong theory of how to carry out reform across services in practice.

Changes to funding flows were a big step forward

Starmer’s government set longer term funding settlements for more services than in recent years. This was a key step in supporting his reform principles. Longer term funding allows services to plan spending across multiple years, supporting longer term thinking on preventative services.

This started at the top. Starmer and Reeves’ decision to conduct a multi-year spending review was a wise one and was long overdue. The Conservative governments fell into a pattern of more ad hoc, single-year settlements, leaving departments unable to plan beyond the following March. Even the 2021 spending review – ostensibly set for multiple years –ended up more as a succession of single-year settlements as higher-than-forecast inflation meant that the government had to keep providing top-ups. Often, though, government preferred single-year settlements because it gave them more flexibility, not tying their hands over the coming years.

Crucially, under Starmer some departments mostly passed the multi-year settlement down to services. In 2025, the government ran the first multi-year local government finance settlement since 2016/17. In the NHS, the government set targets and allocated funding between 2026/27 and 2028/29 through the Medium-Term Planning Framework – setting budgets for integrated care boards. 51 NHS England, Medium Term Planning Framework – Delivering change together 2026/27 to 2028/29, NHS England, 24 October 2025,www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/medium-term-planning-framework-delivering-change-together-2026-27-to-2028-29.pdf  As justice secretary, David Lammy made funding commitments for the crown court up to 2028/29.

This was not, however, a common approach across all services. Departments continued to use single-year settlements for the school systems, general practice, police, prisons and probation units.

Starmer’s government also reduced the number of ring-fenced pots of money for services. Ring-fencing funding reduces local services’ control over funding, requiring them to spend it on areas of importance for central government. Loosening restrictions supported Starmer’s devolution principle, putting more control in the hands of those nearer the front line.

These reforms were most obvious in local government funding, where central government merged funding pots for areas like children’s services. The Starmer government also replaced several conditional grants for policing linked to maintaining officer numbers and replaced them with a single conditional grant focused on officers in neighbourhood roles, increasing local forces’ control over how they spend their money.

In her first stint as secretary of state for housing, communities and local government, Angela Rayner also launched the Fair Funding Review 2.0. This was an overhaul and update of the funding formulae that determine how government allocates grant funding to councils. The government ensured that those formulae would direct more funding to more deprived parts of the country, redressing the larger cuts that those local authorities experienced in the 2010s.

Finally, the Starmer government launched five place-based budgeting pilots – initiatives that aimed to combine disparate funding streams in a local area, 52 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Place Based Budgets’, GOV.UK, 13 July 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/place-based-budgets  in line with recommendations we have previously made. This type of funding arrangement would also support better integration of services. These provide a foundation on which Burnham could build a better integrated funding system for local areas.

There were other, smaller programmes that reflected an emergent approach to public service reform

The Cabinet Office launched the ‘Test, learn, and grow’ (TLG) programme. This is an iterative approach to public service reform in which local areas are encouraged to try new ways of designing and delivering services, keeping what works, leaving what doesn’t and disseminating what they have learnt to the rest of the sector. 53 Gill C, ‘What is Test, Learn and Grow?’, blog, Cabinet Office, 18 June 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, https://testlearnandgrow.blog.gov.uk/2026/06/18/what-is-test-learn-and-grow  This is a positive approach to reform, moving away from top-down prescriptions from departments and towards a more decentralised model. The government has trialled this in 10 areas across the country, with each area tackling a specific ‘challenge’, such as encouraging uptake of Best Start family hubs. 54 House of Commons, Hansard, ‘Public Service Reform: Test, Learn and Grow Programme’, 16 July 2025, https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2025-07-16/debates/25071645000010/PublicServiceReformTestLearnAndGrowProgramme

The Starmer government also designated Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) the ‘prevention demonstrator’. That status afforded GMCA greater flexibility over services. It is using that flexibility to attempt to integrate its health, employment support, family support and housing services to better fit residents’ needs. In practice, they have rolled out multi-disciplinary neighbourhood teams and Live Well centres, which provide space for co-located services and community and voluntary groups. 55 Greater Manchester Combined Authority, ‘GM Live Well’, Greater Manchester Combined Authority, (no date), retrieved 21 September 2026, https://greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/what-we-do/live-well  Given this is a programme that Burnham oversaw in his time as mayor of GMCA, this could act as a blueprint for his approach, as prime minister, to reform across England.

The thinking behind these and myriad other initiatives was positive but they ended up being poorly co-ordinated. In interviews, staff working in local services welcomed the principles and ethos of these small programmes, but they also expressed frustration. They argued that many were broadly attempting to do the same thing but with little co-ordination between them. As a result, front-line staff often struggled to distinguish between these programmes, resulting in duplication of work reporting into different well-meaning Whitehall teams.

Likewise, there was too little buy-in from senior politicians and senior civil servants, preventing them from becoming the blueprint for a wider public service reform agenda. Both programmes are in their early stages, and the Burnham government should ensure it supports them with sufficient analytical capacity and capability to ensure that lessons are captured effectively.

Missions did not drive meaningful public service reform

Starmer’s first attempt at a reform agenda was his five missions. Labour’s missions were inspired by the work of the economist Mariana Mazzucato (though she would distance herself from Starmer’s version of the missions). 56 Mazzucato M, ‘Labour has abandoned the missions that brought it to power. Here’s how Burnham could revive them’, The Guardian, 28 June 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jun/28/labour-keir-starmer-government-five-missions-failed-andy-burnham-mariana-mazzucato  Missions were supposed to focus on solving long-term, complex problems that often require working between departments.

Three of Starmer’s missions – the NHS, safer streets and opportunity missions – broadly map on to the work of the NHS, the police and education settings respectively. Each mission was given a ‘milestone’, a target the government wanted to achieve by the end of the parliament. These were:

  • NHS mission: 92% of patients seen within 18 weeks of a referral for elective care.
  • Safer streets mission: 13,000 more personnel in neighbourhood policing roles.
  • Opportunity mission: 75% of five-year-olds reaching a good level of development. 57 Prime Minister’s Office, 10 Downing Street, Plan for Change: Milestones for mission-led government, CP 1210, The Stationery Office, 5 December 2024, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6751af4719e0c816d18d1df3/Plan_for_Change.pdf

The government argued that these targets would drive better cross-departmental working. But the missions never got off the ground. For more than a year, until the appointment of Darren Jones as both chief secretary to the prime minister and chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, there was no clear minister in charge of driving the missions across government from the centre. ‘Mission boards’ were set up – as inter-ministerial groups that were intended to drive missions across Whitehall – but these never fulfilled their delivery roles. Perhaps most damning was that at the 2025 spending review there was little or no sign that the missions had meaningfully guided how spending was allocated.

There were some attempts to co-ordinate activity across government. But this largely happened in an ad hoc way, led by groups of staff in particular departments rather than co-ordinated from the centre. Ironically, that led to multiple, uncoordinated teams in different departments trying to co-ordinate. 58 Institute for Government interview.

It didn’t help that Starmer appointed the secretaries of state of the lead departments as chairs of the ‘mission boards’, not least as he had said he would chair them himself. If chaired by the prime minister or the chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, the boards could have provided a more robust scrutiny role, pushing the lead department from the outside to work more effectively across government. That they did not rests with Starmer. He did not use the power of the prime minister to focus attention or co-ordinate cross-departmental work.

Partly, the milestones themselves hindered progress. In the health and safer streets missions, responsibility for reaching the milestone target largely fell within the control of the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) and the Home Office respectively.

If instead Starmer had widened the NHS mission to be a health mission and chosen a longer term outcome as the metric for its success – for example, improving healthy life expectancy – then it could have encouraged DHSC to co-operate more with departments such as DfE, DfT, Defra and MHCLG, where responsibility for many of the wider determinants of health sit.

On the opportunity mission, the target for 75% of reception-aged children to be reaching a ‘good level of development’ (GLD) by 2028/29 was poorly conceived. The metric is pass–fail, assessed by teachers, unmoderated and only applies to one cohort (2028/29 reception age). As the Institute for Government has argued previously, this can encourage ‘gaming’. Placing duties and targets on local authorities might incentivise them to co-ordinate local SEND, education and other preventative services (like early development checks conducted by health visitors) better and earlier. But there is little evidence that the target was meaningfully changing how DfE and DHSC, for example, worked together.

The safer streets milestone was arguably the best of the three. As we argue in the policing section, despite being an input target, it has been effective in increasing the number of personnel in community roles, and visible community policing helps to drive public trust and supports intelligence gathering.

In the end, then, Starmer’s missions failed to act as either a framework for reforms or as a catalyst for better cross-departmental working.

Starmer’s rhetoric around reform was contradicted by the government’s actions

Missions were not the only way, however, that Starmer could have driven reform across public services. He could have also ensured that the many reform programmes started by departments aligned with his broader vision for what he wanted services to achieve. But his government failed to do that as well. First, it took the government a year to articulate even the thinnest vision of what they wanted public services to achieve, publishing their three principles of public service reform at the 2025 spending review. These were:

  1. To integrate services, so they “are organised around people’s lives”
  2. To shift the focus of services towards prevention
  3. To devolve power to local areas “that understand the needs of their communities best”. 59 HM Treasury, Spending Review 2025, CP 1336, The Stationery Office, 11 June 2025, p. 27, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/686270a608bf2f53761219fc/E03349913_HMT_Spending_Review_June_2025_TEXT_PRINT_CS.pdf

These were welcome principles and aligned with our previous recommendations for how the government should manage services. But on their own, these were insufficient as a framework to drive reforms. Starmer’s government also never made clear how these interacted with the missions. Ideally, these principles should have been stated right after, or even before, the election, and informed subsequent decisions.

Worse, while the Starmer government did follow these objectives in some cases, the overall trend of reforms often pushed in the opposite directions: far from devolving power, for instance, its instinct across 2024 and 2025 was to centralise power, 60 Home Office, Sarah Jones MP and The Rt Hon Shabana Mahmood MP, ‘White paper sets out reforms to policing’, news story, 26 January 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/white-paper-sets-out-reforms-to-policing , 61 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Health Bill: oversight of the health system fact sheet’, GOV.UK, 19 May 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/health-bill-oversight-of-the-health-system-fact-sheet  making prevention and integration more difficult. Reforms were driven by individual Whitehall departments and ministers, with little consideration of how they hung together as a whole. This was made worse still by the fact that, by the time of the spending review in June 2025, DHSC, DfE, and MHCLG were all steaming ahead with their own reform programmes.

Maybe worse, Starmer did not require that departments co-ordinate the large-scale structural reorganisations that departments launched or continued in local government, the NHS, the police, and at a strategic authority level. That was a missed opportunity – and unaligned boundaries between those services makes it much harder for them to work together, as Burnham’s government has now recognised. Starmer should have used the rare opportunity of concurrent reorganisations to correct that wrong, supporting his aim of integration. Instead, he allowed them to create a newly incoherent map.

Starmer made some of the same mistakes as his predecessors

Aside from Starmer’s failures to use missions as a basis for public service reform and to follow through on his promises of large-scale public service reform, he also fell into more familiar, damaging approaches to managing public services, which echoed his predecessors.

Starmer’s reforms threaten to further erode management and administrative capacity in services

We have argued before that most services have too little management and administrative capacity, which limits services’ ability to plan strategically and therefore contributes to sluggish productivity growth. This is particularly true in the NHS, where a far smaller proportion of the workforce is employed in management roles than in the private sector (3% vs 11%). But it is also the case in the police and most likely the criminal courts and local government.

A lack of analytical staff across most services also harms preventative, joined-up initiatives, which require deep understanding of local demographics and needs. As with previous governments, Starmer’s administration made no systematic attempt to improve analytical capacity across services.

The Starmer government also assumed that the roll-out of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies over the course of this spending review period would result in productivity improvements in public services. 62 HM Treasury, ‘Departmental Efficiency Plans’, GOV.UK, 11 June 2025, www.gov.uk/government/publications/departmental-efficiency-delivery-plans/departmental-efficiency-plans  Crucially, though, for the government to successfully implement AI systems in services, it will need sufficient management and technical capacity in public services.

For the most part, Starmer’s reforms worsened that situation through the pursuit of back-office savings.*

In the NHS, there are three levels where the service is losing management, analytical and administrative capacity. At a national level, the government is targeting 50% headcount cuts from the merger of NHS England and DHSC. It is similarly asking integrated care boards (ICBs) to cut 50% of staff. Finally, on the front line, tight finances in NHS trusts means that they have had to cut non-clinical staff.

This picture is not confined to the NHS. There has been no significant increase in HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS) workforce, despite growing demand and complex changes planned to case listing processes. Local government is also focused on cutting back-office staff through local government reorganisation, despite weak evidence that it will lead to meaningful savings.

Cutting these staff to save money is a false economy that has repeatedly backfired on previous governments.

* There are exceptions. The government increased management capacity in the probation service.

Reorganisations distracted attention from other reforms

Across the courts system, local government, the NHS, the police, SEND and children’s social care, among others, Starmer’s government launched structural reforms – redesigning the organisations that govern and run services, including police forces, councils, and ICBs in the NHS.

Structural reforms can be beneficial. When existing structures impede a government’s ambitions for the service, then it makes sense to redesign them. But it is vital in that case that form follows (desired) function. Similarly, there can be sense in updating structures if the context in which services operate changes substantially. For example, a district tier of local government makes less sense when there is full coverage of strategic authorities across the country.

Structural reforms were probably attractive to ministers because they were relatively cheap compared to other reforms – and could even be pitched as cost saving (though the government tends to overestimate the savings from large-scale reorganisations, and understate the cost of implementing them). They are also highly visible, showing that this or that minister is doing something.

Some of these reorganisations were more justified than others: the creation of a national police force should provide national strategic direction for policing as well as improved co-ordination on professional standards and vetting. But often, Starmer’s government launched structural reorganisations with little clarity of purpose or clear plan for what it was supposed to achieve.

The most egregious of these was the abolition of NHS England and the reorganisation of ICBs. As we’ve written before, the government sprang both on unsuspecting systems, damaging relations with staff. It then constantly changed its rationale, swinging from saving money through redundancies to improving accountability of systems to the centre. More than a year and a half on from Starmer’s announcement, the NHSE abolition is drifting, suffering from no clear political direction.

Even where the rationale is clearer, the government seemed to fail to consider the effect that these would have on other priorities. Reorganisations distract from other goals. With limited staff time, it was short-sighted of Starmer’s government to expect that staff would be able to deliver priorities like a neighbourhood health service, better inter-agency working on SEND, or children’s social care reforms while management and organisational attention is turned towards the redesign of their organisation. Interviewees in local government repeatedly emphasised how difficult it was to improve adult and children’s social care, homelessness and SEND services while also reorganising their council.

Burnham inherits Starmer’s difficult fiscal choices

Many of those problems will not go away now that Burnham is in office. Indeed, some of them may become more unmanageable over the next few years.

Funding increases were slightly front-loaded for the services we examine 

Burnham cannot rely on large funding injections to improve public services over the remainder of this parliament. The Starmer government increased total day-to-day funding substantially in 2024/25 and 2025/26 compared to pre-election spending plans. After 2025/26, however, the spending profile is flatter.

Funding for the services that we examine in this report follows a similar pattern for the first two years but then has more generous annual increases than the total spending envelope between 2026/27 and 2028/29. Partly that is because other areas have cuts baked in over the rest of this parliament, notably asylum spending in the Home Office 63 HM Treasury, Spending Review 2025, CP 1336, The Stationery Office, 11 June 2025, p. 63, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/686270a608bf2f53761219fc/E03349913_HMT_Spending_Review_June_2025_TEXT_PRINT_CS.pdf  and a reduction in Covid-related passenger subsidies for the Department for Transport (DfT). 64 Ibid., p. 80.  And partly it is because funding for police and local government include rising council tax receipts, which outstrip government-wide spending.

As a result, real terms funding increases will slow from an average of 2.8% per year between 2023/24 and 2026/27 to 2.0% per year between 2026/27 and 2028/29 for the services that we look at. In contrast, the same numbers are 2.6% and 1.0% for the overall spending envelope.
