Mirroring the situation in 2024, Burnham inherits a prisons system that is rapidly running out of places. Some of the decisions he has taken since coming into office have exacerbated those issues, as discussed in more depth below. The probation service is also under immense strain, with a further wave of early releases contributing to staff’s workload.

In his time at the head of the Labour Party, Keir Starmer made much of his plans to reform public services. In 2023, he said that services could not expect “vast sums of money” and argued instead that it was “reform or bust” if Labour wanted to improve public services. 142 Helm T and Savage M, ‘Keir Starmer: We can’t win power by spending. We need to reform and create wealth’, The Observer, 15 July 2023, retrieved 21 September 2026, www.theguardian.com/politics/2023/jul/15/keirstarmer-we-cant-spend-our-way-back-to-power However, despite some positive changes to funding and a handful of promising pilots, Labour took power without a strong theory of how to carry out reform across services in practice.

Starmer’s government set longer term funding settlements for more services than in recent years. This was a key step in supporting his reform principles. Longer term funding allows services to plan spending across multiple years, supporting longer term thinking on preventative services.

This started at the top. Starmer and Reeves’ decision to conduct a multi-year spending review was a wise one and was long overdue. The Conservative governments fell into a pattern of more ad hoc, single-year settlements, leaving departments unable to plan beyond the following March. Even the 2021 spending review – ostensibly set for multiple years –ended up more as a succession of single-year settlements as higher-than-forecast inflation meant that the government had to keep providing top-ups. Often, though, government preferred single-year settlements because it gave them more flexibility, not tying their hands over the coming years.

Crucially, under Starmer some departments mostly passed the multi-year settlement down to services. In 2025, the government ran the first multi-year local government finance settlement since 2016/17. In the NHS, the government set targets and allocated funding between 2026/27 and 2028/29 through the Medium-Term Planning Framework – setting budgets for integrated care boards. 143 NHS England, Medium Term Planning Framework – Delivering change together 2026/27 to 2028/29, NHS England, 24 October 2025,www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/medium-term-planning-framework-delivering-change-together-2026-27-to-2028-29.pdf As justice secretary, David Lammy made funding commitments for the crown court up to 2028/29.
This was not, however, a common approach across all services. Departments continued to use single-year settlements for the school systems, general practice, police, prisons and probation units.

Starmer’s government also reduced the number of ring-fenced pots of money for services. Ring-fencing funding reduces local services’ control over funding, requiring them to spend it on areas of importance for central government. Loosening restrictions supported Starmer’s devolution principle, putting more control in the hands of those nearer the front line.

These reforms were most obvious in local government funding, where central government merged funding pots for areas like children’s services. The Starmer government also replaced several conditional grants for policing linked to maintaining officer numbers and replaced them with a single conditional grant focused on officers in neighbourhood roles, increasing local forces’ control over how they spend their money.

In her first stint as secretary of state for housing, communities and local government, Angela Rayner also launched the Fair Funding Review 2.0. This was an overhaul and update of the funding formulae that determine how government allocates grant funding to councils. The government ensured that those formulae would direct more funding to more deprived parts of the country, redressing the larger cuts that those local authorities experienced in the 2010s.

Finally, the Starmer government launched five place-based budgeting pilots – initiatives that aimed to combine disparate funding streams in a local area, 144 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Place Based Budgets’, GOV.UK, 13 July 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/place-based-budgets in line with recommendations we have previously made. This type of funding arrangement would also support better integration of services. These provide a foundation on which Burnham could build a better integrated funding system for local areas.

The Cabinet Office launched the ‘Test, learn, and grow’ (TLG) programme. This is an iterative approach to public service reform in which local areas are encouraged to try new ways of designing and delivering services, keeping what works, leaving what doesn’t and disseminating what they have learnt to the rest of the sector. 145 Gill C, ‘What is Test, Learn and Grow?’, blog, Cabinet Office, 18 June 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, https://testlearnandgrow.blog.gov.uk/2026/06/18/what-is-test-learn-and-grow This is a positive approach to reform, moving away from top-down prescriptions from departments and towards a more decentralised model. The government has trialled this in 10 areas across the country, with each area tackling a specific ‘challenge’, such as encouraging uptake of Best Start family hubs. 146 House of Commons, Hansard, ‘Public Service Reform: Test, Learn and Grow Programme’, 16 July 2025, https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2025-07-16/debates/25071645000010/PublicServiceReformTestLearnAndGrowProgramme

The Starmer government also designated Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) the ‘prevention demonstrator’. That status afforded GMCA greater flexibility over services. It is using that flexibility to attempt to integrate its health, employment support, family support and housing services to better fit residents’ needs. In practice, they have rolled out multi-disciplinary neighbourhood teams and Live Well centres, which provide space for co-located services and community and voluntary groups. 147 Greater Manchester Combined Authority, ‘GM Live Well’, Greater Manchester Combined Authority, (no date), retrieved 21 September 2026, https://greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/what-we-do/live-well Given this is a programme that Burnham oversaw in his time as mayor of GMCA, this could act as a blueprint for his approach, as prime minister, to reform across England.

The thinking behind these and myriad other initiatives was positive but they ended up being poorly co-ordinated. In interviews, staff working in local services welcomed the principles and ethos of these small programmes, but they also expressed frustration. They argued that many were broadly attempting to do the same thing but with little co-ordination between them. As a result, front-line staff often struggled to distinguish between these programmes, resulting in duplication of work reporting into different well-meaning Whitehall teams.

Likewise, there was too little buy-in from senior politicians and senior civil servants, preventing them from becoming the blueprint for a wider public service reform agenda. Both programmes are in their early stages, and the Burnham government should ensure it supports them with sufficient analytical capacity and capability to ensure that lessons are captured effectively.

Starmer’s first attempt at a reform agenda was his five missions. Labour’s missions were inspired by the work of the economist Mariana Mazzucato (though she would distance herself from Starmer’s version of the missions). 148 Mazzucato M, ‘Labour has abandoned the missions that brought it to power. Here’s how Burnham could revive them’, The Guardian, 28 June 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jun/28/labour-keir-starmer-government-five-missions-failed-andy-burnham-mariana-mazzucato Missions were supposed to focus on solving long-term, complex problems that often require working between departments.

Three of Starmer’s missions – the NHS, safer streets and opportunity missions – broadly map on to the work of the NHS, the police and education settings respectively. Each mission was given a ‘milestone’, a target the government wanted to achieve by the end of the parliament. These were:

The government argued that these targets would drive better cross-departmental working. But the missions never got off the ground. For more than a year, until the appointment of Darren Jones as both chief secretary to the prime minister and chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, there was no clear minister in charge of driving the missions across government from the centre. ‘Mission boards’ were set up – as inter-ministerial groups that were intended to drive missions across Whitehall – but these never fulfilled their delivery roles. Perhaps most damning was that at the 2025 spending review there was little or no sign that the missions had meaningfully guided how spending was allocated.

There were some attempts to co-ordinate activity across government. But this largely happened in an ad hoc way, led by groups of staff in particular departments rather than co-ordinated from the centre. Ironically, that led to multiple, uncoordinated teams in different departments trying to co-ordinate. 150 Institute for Government interview.

It didn’t help that Starmer appointed the secretaries of state of the lead departments as chairs of the ‘mission boards’, not least as he had said he would chair them himself. If chaired by the prime minister or the chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, the boards could have provided a more robust scrutiny role, pushing the lead department from the outside to work more effectively across government. That they did not rests with Starmer. He did not use the power of the prime minister to focus attention or co-ordinate cross-departmental work.

Partly, the milestones themselves hindered progress. In the health and safer streets missions, responsibility for reaching the milestone target largely fell within the control of the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) and the Home Office respectively.

If instead Starmer had widened the NHS mission to be a health mission and chosen a longer term outcome as the metric for its success – for example, improving healthy life expectancy – then it could have encouraged DHSC to co-operate more with departments such as DfE, DfT, Defra and MHCLG, where responsibility for many of the wider determinants of health sit.

On the opportunity mission, the target for 75% of reception-aged children to be reaching a ‘good level of development’ (GLD) by 2028/29 was poorly conceived. The metric is pass–fail, assessed by teachers, unmoderated and only applies to one cohort (2028/29 reception age). As the Institute for Government has argued previously, this can encourage ‘gaming’. Placing duties and targets on local authorities might incentivise them to co-ordinate local SEND, education and other preventative services (like early development checks conducted by health visitors) better and earlier. But there is little evidence that the target was meaningfully changing how DfE and DHSC, for example, worked together.

The safer streets milestone was arguably the best of the three. As we argue in the policing section, despite being an input target, it has been effective in increasing the number of personnel in community roles, and visible community policing helps to drive public trust and supports intelligence gathering.
In the end, then, Starmer’s missions failed to act as either a framework for reforms or as a catalyst for better cross-departmental working.

Missions were not the only way, however, that Starmer could have driven reform across public services. He could have also ensured that the many reform programmes started by departments aligned with his broader vision for what he wanted services to achieve. But his government failed to do that as well. First, it took the government a year to articulate even the thinnest vision of what they wanted public services to achieve, publishing their three principles of public service reform at the 2025 spending review. These were:

These were welcome principles and aligned with our previous recommendations for how the government should manage services. But on their own, these were insufficient as a framework to drive reforms. Starmer’s government also never made clear how these interacted with the missions. Ideally, these principles should have been stated right after, or even before, the election, and informed subsequent decisions.

Worse, while the Starmer government did follow these objectives in some cases, the overall trend of reforms often pushed in the opposite directions: far from devolving power, for instance, its instinct across 2024 and 2025 was to centralise power, 152 Home Office, Sarah Jones MP and The Rt Hon Shabana Mahmood MP, ‘White paper sets out reforms to policing’, news story, 26 January 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/white-paper-sets-out-reforms-to-policing , 153 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Health Bill: oversight of the health system fact sheet’, GOV.UK, 19 May 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/health-bill-oversight-of-the-health-system-fact-sheet making prevention and integration more difficult. Reforms were driven by individual Whitehall departments and ministers, with little consideration of how they hung together as a whole. This was made worse still by the fact that, by the time of the spending review in June 2025, DHSC, DfE, and MHCLG were all steaming ahead with their own reform programmes.

Maybe worse, Starmer did not require that departments co-ordinate the large-scale structural reorganisations that departments launched or continued in local government, the NHS, the police, and at a strategic authority level. That was a missed opportunity – and unaligned boundaries between those services makes it much harder for them to work together, as Burnham’s government has now recognised. Starmer should have used the rare opportunity of concurrent reorganisations to correct that wrong, supporting his aim of integration. Instead, he allowed them to create a newly incoherent map.

Aside from Starmer’s failures to use missions as a basis for public service reform and to follow through on his promises of large-scale public service reform, he also fell into more familiar, damaging approaches to managing public services, which echoed his predecessors.

We have argued before that most services have too little management and administrative capacity, which limits services’ ability to plan strategically and therefore contributes to sluggish productivity growth. This is particularly true in the NHS, where a far smaller proportion of the workforce is employed in management roles than in the private sector (3% vs 11%). But it is also the case in the police and most likely the criminal courts and local government.

A lack of analytical staff across most services also harms preventative, joined-up initiatives, which require deep understanding of local demographics and needs. As with previous governments, Starmer’s administration made no systematic attempt to improve analytical capacity across services.

The Starmer government also assumed that the roll-out of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies over the course of this spending review period would result in productivity improvements in public services. 154 HM Treasury, ‘Departmental Efficiency Plans’, GOV.UK, 11 June 2025, www.gov.uk/government/publications/departmental-efficiency-delivery-plans/departmental-efficiency-plans Crucially, though, for the government to successfully implement AI systems in services, it will need sufficient management and technical capacity in public services.
For the most part, Starmer’s reforms worsened that situation through the pursuit of back-office savings.*

In the NHS, there are three levels where the service is losing management, analytical and administrative capacity. At a national level, the government is targeting 50% headcount cuts from the merger of NHS England and DHSC. It is similarly asking integrated care boards (ICBs) to cut 50% of staff. Finally, on the front line, tight finances in NHS trusts means that they have had to cut non-clinical staff.

This picture is not confined to the NHS. There has been no significant increase in HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS) workforce, despite growing demand and complex changes planned to case listing processes. Local government is also focused on cutting back-office staff through local government reorganisation, despite weak evidence that it will lead to meaningful savings.
Cutting these staff to save money is a false economy that has repeatedly backfired on previous governments.
* There are exceptions. The government increased management capacity in the probation service.

Across the courts system, local government, the NHS, the police, SEND and children’s social care, among others, Starmer’s government launched structural reforms – redesigning the organisations that govern and run services, including police forces, councils, and ICBs in the NHS.

Structural reforms can be beneficial. When existing structures impede a government’s ambitions for the service, then it makes sense to redesign them. But it is vital in that case that form follows (desired) function. Similarly, there can be sense in updating structures if the context in which services operate changes substantially. For example, a district tier of local government makes less sense when there is full coverage of strategic authorities across the country.

Structural reforms were probably attractive to ministers because they were relatively cheap compared to other reforms – and could even be pitched as cost saving (though the government tends to overestimate the savings from large-scale reorganisations, and understate the cost of implementing them). They are also highly visible, showing that this or that minister is doing something.

Some of these reorganisations were more justified than others: the creation of a national police force should provide national strategic direction for policing as well as improved co-ordination on professional standards and vetting. But often, Starmer’s government launched structural reorganisations with little clarity of purpose or clear plan for what it was supposed to achieve.

The most egregious of these was the abolition of NHS England and the reorganisation of ICBs. As we’ve written before, the government sprang both on unsuspecting systems, damaging relations with staff. It then constantly changed its rationale, swinging from saving money through redundancies to improving accountability of systems to the centre. More than a year and a half on from Starmer’s announcement, the NHSE abolition is drifting, suffering from no clear political direction.

Even where the rationale is clearer, the government seemed to fail to consider the effect that these would have on other priorities. Reorganisations distract from other goals. With limited staff time, it was short-sighted of Starmer’s government to expect that staff would be able to deliver priorities like a neighbourhood health service, better inter-agency working on SEND, or children’s social care reforms while management and organisational attention is turned towards the redesign of their organisation. Interviewees in local government repeatedly emphasised how difficult it was to improve adult and children’s social care, homelessness and SEND services while also reorganising their council.
Many of those problems will not go away now that Burnham is in office. Indeed, some of them may become more unmanageable over the next few years.

Burnham cannot rely on large funding injections to improve public services over the remainder of this parliament. The Starmer government increased total day-to-day funding substantially in 2024/25 and 2025/26 compared to pre-election spending plans. After 2025/26, however, the spending profile is flatter.

Funding for the services that we examine in this report follows a similar pattern for the first two years but then has more generous annual increases than the total spending envelope between 2026/27 and 2028/29. Partly that is because other areas have cuts baked in over the rest of this parliament, notably asylum spending in the Home Office 155 HM Treasury, Spending Review 2025, CP 1336, The Stationery Office, 11 June 2025, p. 63, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/686270a608bf2f53761219fc/E03349913_HMT_Spending_Review_June_2025_TEXT_PRINT_CS.pdf and a reduction in Covid-related passenger subsidies for the Department for Transport (DfT). 156 Ibid., p. 80. And partly it is because funding for police and local government include rising council tax receipts, which outstrip government-wide spending.

As a result, real terms funding increases will slow from an average of 2.8% per year between 2023/24 and 2026/27 to 2.0% per year between 2026/27 and 2028/29 for the services that we look at. In contrast, the same numbers are 2.6% and 1.0% for the overall spending envelope.
An expert panel presents the key findings of the IfG’s annual Public Services Performance Tracker.

Despite that additional investment in the first two years of this parliament, there have not been large performance improvements. Partly that is a result of comparison. Marginal performance improvements may not feel like a large success. But it is likely that performance would be much worse than current levels if the Starmer government had stuck to pre-election spending plans. It is almost certain, for example, that there would have had to be much more emergency financial support for local authorities.

The NHS received relatively large funding increases compared to other services over the spending review period, approximately 3% real-terms annual increases. But those increases are still modest by historical standards and have been targeted at reducing the large backlog in elective demand that built up during the pandemic. Much of that has been to support short-term activity, rather than address wider causes of demand, or to create capacity elsewhere in the system. Meanwhile, other areas – urgent and emergency care, primary care and community care – have had to cut their cloth to a far greater extent.

The optimistic case is that there could be tailwinds for Burnham from some of the spending that happened in 2024/25 and 2025/26. Sectors will often use additional funding to hire more staff and it can take a while for those staff to either join the permanent workforce (if they require training) or to become as productive as their more experienced colleagues. Other areas have spent money on longer-term investments – such as in children’s social care – which may bear fruit over the coming years.

Similarly, large increases in capital spending could have a longer time lag before impact is felt. For example, the prisons building programme has just begun and the government is due to open hundreds of neighbourhood health centres over the coming years.
It may be the case that Burnham comes under increasing pressure to top up service budgets to improve performance before the next election.

All the services that we look at likely* had near to sufficient additional funding between 2023/24 and 2026/27 to compensate them for increases in underlying demand. Of those, prisons and schools funding outstripped demand by the most, with a 2- and 3.3-percentage-point difference respectively between the increase in demand and the increase in funding per year.

The picture looking forward – for the years between 2026/27 and 2028/29 – is less rosy for some services. There is sufficient funding to compensate general practice and hospitals for anticipated changes in demand.
But for criminal courts, the police, schools and local government, settlements look much less generous. In those areas, funding increases are likely to be very close to demand increases.

By far, however, the least generous settlement is in prisons, where we project that there will be a real-terms decline in spending in 2027/28 and 2028/29. That is despite an expected increase in demand for prison spaces in those years.

Across the entire parliament, schools, general practice, local government and courts will have funding that should allow them to meet additional demand with slack left over to improve performance. Settlements will be much tighter in hospitals, police and prisons, relative to the increases in demand they face.

All else being equal, performance is likely to improve in most services compared to 2024. However, the baseline was so low in 2024, with services dealing with so many backlogs in demand, that those relatively small performance increases are unlikely to return services to pre-pandemic performance levels – let alone those seen in 2010, when Labour last left office. And as analysis across each sector shows, those settlements are unlikely to be sufficient to improve performance by as much as the government has promised.

By looking at anticipated increases in demand, our analysis may not capture all pressures on services’ budgets, however. There are other reasons to believe that funding may not be sufficient to improve performance over the course of this parliament.

Most forecasters anticipate a bout of inflation from the US’s war in Iran, as happened in 2022 and 2023 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Bank of England now expects inflation to be 1.5ppts higher in early 2027 than it expected back in February. As happened earlier this decade, services would find themselves with cash settlements that went a lot less far in real terms, especially if there are knock-on effects for public sector pay. That would present the Burnham government with a difficult choice about whether to reopen the envelope.

Not doing so, however, could result in another round of widespread industrial action as inflation reduces the real-terms value of staff pay. The 2022 and 2023 inflation shock saw walk-outs from resident doctors, consultant doctors, nurses, ambulance staff, teachers and criminal barristers, causing widespread disruption. Indeed, there are already indications of poor industrial relations, with both consultant doctors 159 Roberts M and Pym H, ‘Consultants in England vote in favour of NHS strikes’, BBC News, 6 July 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c79yyyxzergo and probation officers 160 Dunton J, ‘Probation officers vote in favour of strike action’, Civil Service World, 12 August 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, www.civilserviceworld.com/professions/article/probation-officers-vote-in-favour-of-strike-action recently voting in favour of strike action.

* We say “likely” because there is only outturn data for one service (criminal courts) for 2025/26 and none for 2026/27, as it is ongoing. Estimates for the other services are based on assumptions that we explain in the Methodology.

Apart from inflation, there are other financial pressures on services not captured by our demand analysis above. Rising SEND demand is putting further pressure on schools’ and local authorities’ budgets. The Starmer government’s decision to salami slice services’ capital budgets to fund increased defence spending may contribute to slower productivity growth.

Many departments have assumed that improvements in technology, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), will result in large efficiency gains 165 HM Treasury, ‘Departmental Efficiency Plans’, GOV.UK, 11 June 2025, www.gov.uk/government/publications/departmental-efficiency-delivery-plans/departmental-efficiency-plans – though the NHS has alluded to the riskiness of this assumption by calling AI a “big bet” in its 10-year health plan. 166 Department of Health and Social Care, Prime Minister’s Office, 10 Downing Street, The Rt Hon Sir Keir Starmer KCB KC MP and The Rt Hon Wes Streeting MP, Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England, CP 1350, The Stationery Office, 3 July 2025, p. 114, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6888a0b1a11f859994409147/fit-for-the-future-10-year-health-plan-for-england.pdf Our own research did not reveal any particular ‘AI revolution’ in services. Some showed early signs of AI adoption – specifically the use of AI-assisted transcription tools in the probation service and among local authority social workers – though it was not frequently raised as a reason for performance improvements.
So if those ‘big bets’ do not return any productivity wins, services may find themselves with a less generous settlement than expected in the last years of this parliament.

Some of the government’s own priorities may put pressure on the envelope. Even after reallocating capital budgets, the government still needs to find an additional £4.7bn of funding to meet its defence commitments over the next four years.

Burnham has also committed to reforming adult social care. He is not alone in such a commitment. That has been the position of many previous prime ministers, who have then gone on to duck the difficult decisions. But if he does go ahead, it seems likely that it will involve the state paying for some more care. Burnham’s party conference speech made clear that he does not anticipate launching his national care service (NCS) until after the next general election, 167 Burnham A, ‘Andy Burnham’s speech to Labour Party Conference 2026’, Labour Party, 29 September 2026, https://labour.org.uk/updates/stories/andy-burnhams-speech-to-labour-party-conference-2026 pushing some of the costliest measures (such as free personal care for those aged 65 and over) beyond the scope of this spending review. But even with that delay, he may want to direct more funding towards his proposed workforce reforms that are due to be enacted before the election.

Starmer had to contend with an unenviable international situation, which made his domestic choices more difficult. Following the election of Donald Trump to his second term, six months after the 2024 general election, and the continued threat of aggression from Russia, Starmer deemed it necessary to increase defence spending. That required fiscal trade-offs. Having not responded quickly to the Trump presidency by, for example, raising more tax revenue in the 2025 budget or cutting spending in a targeted way to fund additional defence spending, Starmer announced that he would ask all departments to cut their capital budgets by 1% to fund additional defence spending in the summer of 2026. 168 Stacey K, ‘Rows over defence investment plan have badly harmed cabinet relations’, The Guardian, 9 June 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/jun/09/rows-over-defence-investment-plan-have-badly-harmed-cabinet-relations That is a decision that risks undermining one of his biggest achievements: providing certainty and stability over capital spending.

Trump’s war in Iran also increased the risk of an inflationary spike, albeit one that has not yet materialised and which did not affect any of the forecasts while Starmer was in government. That, however, may change as the Burnham government braces for the official forecasts that will accompany the November 2026 budget.
Andy Burnham faces many of the same issues that held performance back under Keir Starmer, from backlogs to inflation and geopolitics.

Another positive of the Starmer government’s time in office is that it increased capital spending compared to the 2010s. That is much needed after historically low levels of capital spending in that time generated record maintenance backlogs in services. That in turn contributed to lower productivity, as staff struggled to use the estate and equipment effectively.
Early indications, though, show that this problem continued under the Starmer government.

Maintenance backlogs remain incredibly high across all the services for which we have data, in all cases more than the entire size of their parent departments’ capital budgets. These are also likely an underestimate, as they do not capture backlogs across all parts of services. For example, the DHSC row does not include the sizeable maintenance backlog that we know exists in primary care, but for which we have no reliable data.

These backlogs cause severe problems. Hospitals are forced to close wards and operating theatres, delaying access to care. 191 Department of Health and Social Care, 10 Year Capital Plan for Health and Social Care, GOV.UK, 8 July 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/10-year-capital-plan-for-health-and-social-care/10-year-capital-plan-for-health-and-social-care In his review of the courts system, Brian Leveson identified the maintenance backlog as a driver of rising inefficiency in the courts system, reducing the number of available courtrooms. 192 Leveson B, Independent Review of the Criminal Courts: Part 1, Ministry of Justice, 9 July 2025, p. 59, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/686be85d81dd8f70f5de3c1f/35.49_MOJ_Ind_Review_Criminal_Courts_v8b_FINAL_WEB.pdf Leveson welcomed the MoJ’s decision to increase the maintenance budget for courts,* but this was still only from £120m in 2024/25 to £148.5m in 2025/26 (in cash terms).

Where we have annual data – for the NHS and roads – we can see that the backlogs grew under the Starmer government, by 5.6% and 9.9% in real terms respectively, indicating that even the additional capital spending his government allocated has not reversed the trend.
That is because the scale of the underinvestment over decades, but particularly during the 2010s, was so large that even relatively high capital spending for a few years will struggle to reverse it.
For the other services we cover (schools, courts, prisons and probation) data about the size of backlogs is less current, meaning that they may have changed since then.
* Technically, this is the ‘court and tribunal capital maintenance and project funding’ budget, so includes funding for initiatives other than maintenance.

Since the 2024 election, services have continued to have to deal with high levels of complex demand. Often, this reflects people’s difficulties accessing appropriate support elsewhere in the state or private sector. Given sufficient time, funding and political will, a government could address these problems. But making headway on, for example, improving population-wide mental health would have been very difficult within a two-year window, particularly given how long many of these effects have been building up across the population.

Interviewees across many of the services we cover report that there is more complex demand from worsening mental health, and that there are very few appropriate NHS services to meet that demand or prevent it from arising in the first place. Instead, it is often left to NHS A&E and ambulance staff, and to police to deal with people in acute mental health crises. In children’s social care, local authorities are providing secure residential accommodation to children who would have previously been treated in tier 4 children and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS), which have been cut over time. 193 Royal College of Psychiatrists, ‘Bed days for children and young people in CAMHS tier 4 wards’, Mental Health Watch, (no date), retrieved 21 September 2026, https://mentalhealthwatch.rcpsych.ac.uk/indicators/bed-days-for-children-and-young-people-in-camhs-tier-4-wards There is also a spillover into the education system, with lack of access to CAMHS services likely contributing to rising demand for education health and care plans (EHCPs). Prisons and probation similarly report spillover demand from the lack of community mental health provision.

Interviewees frequently raised the low quantity and quality of housing as a driver of demand for public services. Most obviously, this manifests as rising demand for local authority-provided homelessness services: assessments for homelessness services rose from 72,450 in the first quarter of 2020 to a high of 84,525 in the third quarter of 2024, just after the 2024 general election. Demand has flattened since then – 81,390 people were owed some support in the first quarter of 2026. 194 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Statutory homelessness in England: January to March 2026’, GOV.UK, 13 August 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/statutory-homelessness-in-england-january-to-march-2026/statutory-homelessness-in-england-january-to-march-2… But this is still 12.3% higher than the last pre-pandemic quarter.

Local authorities are increasingly forced to place more people who present as homeless into temporary accommodation. That leads to worse health and educational outcomes for children. 195 Dearden W, The impact of temporary accommodation on children and their families, Bevan Foundation, 9 September 2025, www.bevanfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/The-impact-of-temporary-accommodation-on-children-and-their-families-report-1.pdf
A lack of housing also puts more pressure on prison and probation services: people who become homeless while being supervised by probation services are often recalled to prison.

More indirectly, and over the longer term, poor-quality housing puts more pressure on the NHS. People living in damp, cold, noisy or mouldy housing are more likely to present to the NHS. 196 Kulakiewicz A and Wilson W, Housing and health: A reading list, CBP-09414, House of Commons Library, 17 October 2022, https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-9414 Historically, cold living conditions have been the primary driver of housing-related demand. But as the climate crisis worsens, overly-hot housing may also drive further NHS demand.

We have argued in the past that governments between 2010 and 2024 took decisions on resource allocation that pushed public services into a ‘doom loop’ where constant firefighting and tight budgets prevented a focus on the long term, and forced services to cut spending and initiatives that might lower future acute demand.

That is a difficult cycle to break, particularly in the absence of additional funding to enable ‘double running’ of preventative and acute spending before services reach a more sustainable equilibrium.

Because of that doom loop – as well as the poor quality of the estate, increasingly complex demand, and pandemic era backlogs described above – Burnham and his ministers leading key public services will need to tackle performance problems in numerous areas.

In the prisons system, Burnham has already had a taste of how public service crises consume political attention. One of the earliest announcements he made was to change the prison early release reforms, then due to take effect in October 2026. As a result, 1,000 fewer prisoners will be released early over the first 10 months of the programme. That has also been a test of his ability to make difficult decisions and trade-offs, with the result showing that he buckled to press and political pressure rather than choosing the option that would put the prisons population on a more sustainable footing.
The prisons system is likely only the first of several areas where performance may well worsen before the next election.

In the school system, many of the current reform programmes hinge on optimistic forecasts about the government’s ability to slow the growth of education, health and care plans (EHCPs), which are assigned to children with recognised special needs or disabilities and through which parents and schools attract additional funding. Not only does that threaten the viability of schools reforms, but the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) identifies SEND pressures as a threat to the deliverability of the government’s entire spending envelope. 197 Office for Budget Responsibility, Economic and fiscal outlook – March 2026, Office for Budget Responsibility, 3 March 2026, p. 64, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/69a6d7b62e1f4fbda4252208/economic-and-fiscal-outlook-march-2026-web-accessible.pdf

In the NHS, A&E performance has not improved substantively since the election and attempts to improve performance have focused on diverting demand and increasing staff resources in A&E departments rather than on freeing up hospital flow – a key factor determining performance in that area. 198 Comptroller and Auditor General, Managing the flow of patients through hospital from A&E, Session 2026–27, HC 588, National Audit Office, 9 September 2026, p. 4, www.nao.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Managing-the-flow-of-patients-through-hospital-from-AE.pdf That means that many people attending A&E will continue to wait more than 12 hours for care and it would not be difficult for a shock to the NHS to substantially worsen that level.
In general practice, the steady decline in the GP partner workforce could lead to further practice closures and mergers, reducing patient access and leading to lower patient satisfaction.

Community children’s services are worsening, with very long waits for children to receive diagnoses and support for SEND conditions. Ongoing disruption from structural reorganisations presents a further challenge to performance improvements.

Local authorities’ finances are balanced on a knife edge and could well worsen before they improve. Starmer’s government made good changes to the formulae that allocate funding to local authorities. But the sector remains underfunded compared to the demands put on it. EHCPs – funded by local authorities – will continue to rise for the rest of this parliament. Preventative reforms to children’s social care could take years to reduce demand – especially given how difficult they are to implement when head space and resource are consumed by local government reorganisation.

Adult social care reform plans are still sketchy and, in the case of Burnham’s much-trailed national care service, still years away. To contend with rising demand for that and other acute services, councils are forced to paper over the cracks with one-off funding sources such as drawing down reserves, selling assets and borrowing, which drives up the level of debt and interest payments in the sector. That is not sustainable.

In the criminal justice system, successful police recruitment may increase the number of charges, which would in turn add to the backlog of cases waiting to be heard in the courts system. Courts are hearing more cases than they were, but that could result in more pressure on prison places, particularly with the slow progress of the prison building programme. Burnham’s decision to cancel some parts of early release will only add to that pressure.

Since taking office in July 2026, Burnham has made substantial interventions in some services and next to none in others. Compared to Starmer, he was much quicker to provide a diagnosis for why public service performance has been poor, largely attributing it to overcentralisation in Whitehall. That diagnosis also led to a theory of how to improve services that was much clearer and comprehensive than anything Starmer ever published on public service reform. While details on what this entails remain slim, it is a helpful lens for decisions he will need to make.

Burnham articulated that view in a cabinet statement (a document that all cabinet members have agreed to deliver) called, retaining Starmer’s own rhetoric, “Rewiring the state”. In that, he committed to “a radical shift in where powers and resources lie, so that decisions can be made locally”. 199 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the State – Cabinet Statement’, GOV.UK, 31 July 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html That logic extends to public services. The document says that Burnham’s government “will ensure services work together as a single coherent system built around the priorities of people and places”. 200 Ibid. At the heart of this system will be mayoral strategic authorities (MSAs, such as the one that Burnham led in Manchester before becoming prime minister).

This builds on the work of previous administrations, including work done under Starmer. But its ambition is much bolder than previous attempts and, vitally, it has clear and strong support from the prime minister. If implemented, it would mark a watershed moment in how the state manages and delivers public services. Many of the initial steps are welcome and often overdue decisions. We have argued before that the government must use restructures to align ICB, police force and MSA boundaries. Burnham is right to do so now.
Devolving control of employment support is also in line with previous Institute for Government recommendations. We have also long called for reform of the adult social care and homelessness systems.

Some parts of Burnham’s announcement raise concerns. On boundary alignment, Burnham says that police forces and ICBs may be aligned to multiple, rather than just one, MSA. That would be a mistake. Making NHS or police leaders answerable to multiple mayors would confuse accountability. What happens, for example, if neighbouring Labour and Reform mayors disagree about the approach to policing in their joint police force area? Is it feasible to expect a single police force to take a different approach in different parts of the force – and how would they be held accountable if they don’t?

Perhaps surprisingly for such a devolution-focused prime minister, the references to local government are few in the document, and when it is mentioned, the language is thin – for example, talking of improving “financial sustainability” and reforming(with no further elaboration) the most expensive services. Jim McMahon, the minister of state for local government, devolution and growth, has subsequently said that the upcoming devolution white paper will “address the question of the role of local government in a devolved country”. 202 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and Jim McMahon OBE MP, ‘Local government reorganisation: programme review and decisions withdrawal letter to council leaders’, letter, 7 September 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-government-reorganisation-programme-review-and-decisions-withdrawal-letter-to-council-leaders That must provide more clarity as local government is a vital resource for both place-shaping and delivering services. They are closer to their residents than strategic authorities and have decades of capability built up compared to the relatively young – and in much of the country non-existent – strategic authorities.

The statement also makes no mention of regional care co-operatives (RCCs), the organisations the Starmer government began creating to sit above local authorities and commission children’s social care. 203 Department for Education, ‘Regional care cooperatives: policy statement’, GOV.UK, 4 February 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/regional-care-co-operatives-pathfinder-areas/regional-care-cooperatives-policy-statement They also have geographies that do not align with MSAs and instead bring in a mix of local authorities. 204 Department for Education, ‘Regional care cooperatives (RCCs): pathfinder regions’, GOV.UK, 4 February 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/regional-care-co-operatives-pathfinder-areas/regional-care-cooperatives-rccs-pathfinder-regions

Burnham says he wants to reform children’s social care and SEND services. There are already reforms happening in those areas, following an approach we support. He should be clear how much his vision differs from the programmes that are in train, and what he would do differently.

The area notable for its absence was the NHS. Aside from ICB boundaries, there was little explanation about how Burnham plans to run the service. He has not taken a public position on the ongoing NHSE abolition, or the reforms that Streeting launched in the 10-Year Health Plan for England. Yvette Cooper has outlined her priorities, which focus on maternity care, violence against women and girls, and Sure Start. 205 Cooper Y, ‘Labour conference speech’, speech at Labour Conference, Labour List, 30 September 2026, retrieved 13 October 2026, https://labourlist.org/2026/09/yvette-cooper-labour-party-conference-2026 All worthy focuses, but far away from the previous administration’s priorities towards which the NHS is still working.
As previously described, Burnham inherits a system going through many different reform programmes. Some are particularly problematic for Burnham’s devolution-first approach.

The way schools are organised at a subnational level is an anomaly among public services. For more than two decades, schools have been shifting from the local authority-maintained sector into the academy sector (state-funded schools not overseen by local authorities but run by trusts, either single-academy trusts or multi-academy trusts, or MATs).

At the start of 2026, 55% of state-funded schools were academies, including 84% of secondary schools and around half of primary and special schools and alternative provision. The Starmer government aimed to complete that process, with all schools becoming parts of ‘trusts’.*, 206 Department for Education, Every Child Achieving and Thriving, CP 1508-I, The Stationery Office, 23 February 2026, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6996ee6a047739fe61889e05/Every_child_achieving_and_thriving_web_accessible_version.pdf

The problem for Burnham’s agenda is that MATs can be spread across the entire country. That means that a single MAT might have schools in multiple MSA areas and, conversely, that a single MSA will have many trusts operating schools in their area (plus schools subject to local authority oversight, unless the plan for all schools to become part of a trust is followed through on). That will make it more difficult to bring local accountability into the schools system.

As we argue in the schools report, the Burnham government should develop a clear long-term vision for how the schools system should be structured, including a view on which functions should be controlled locally, by whom, and which would benefit from being controlled or delivered at scale.

In addition, and as previously shown, reform programmes in the NHS and the police are centralising powers into Whitehall departments. It makes no sense to give secretaries of state more control over appointments and firing of local leaders, or to define what objectives they should be pursuing, at the same time as making those services more accountable to mayors. At best, this confuses accountability. At worst, it completely undermines any attempt to improve local integration and accountability. Burnham should urgently clarify whether those reforms will go ahead.

* The Starmer government did not elaborate on what it meant by ‘trust’. Academies are not the only type of school which can be in trusts, but they make up the vast majority of schools in trusts and there have been no openings of foundation schools (the other type of school in trusts) since 2014.
There are some areas of ongoing reforms that align well with Burnham’s agenda.

Though light on detail, the community and prevention shifts in the NHS could match on to Burnham’s goals quite well. A GP-led neighbourhood health service that’s aligned with local authorities could improve co-ordination between primary, community and adult social care and would be a positive vision of an agenda that currently feels unmoored. Meanwhile, GMCA is a test case for a mayoral-led, preventative approach to health. The rest of the NHS should watch carefully.

Relatedly, the move to pool some NHS budgets in integrated health organisations could support better local decision making and improve accountability over spending, though there has been little progress on this agenda.

SEND reforms are intending to better join up provision at a local level. As we have previously written, there are many remaining questions about how this will happen in practice, but increased mayoral accountability could help for elements of the reforms that benefit from bringing scale.

MSAs could help commission for specialist services where local authorities and other smaller organisations do not provide enough scale to shape the market or benefit from the savings that come from commissioning on a larger level. For example, as MSAs set the strategic direction for skills in their area, they may be well placed to support workforce planning for the SEND sector. RCC reforms are, in many ways, intended to provide scale for children’s residential care. But, as previously argued, these are currently poorly aligned with MSA boundaries.
A positive outcome of Burnham’s first reshuffle was that some junior ministers overseeing reform programmes across public services remained in post.

In the DfE, he kept Josh MacAlister and Georgia Gould in their roles as minister for children and families and minister for school standards, respectively. MacAlister is leading the ongoing children’s social care reforms and Gould is handling the SEND reforms, both of which are moving in the right direction. Keeping them in post will support effective delivery.
Similarly, keeping Karin Smyth as minister of state for secondary care in DHSC and Sarah Jones as minister for policing and crime in the Home Office supports continuity in important reform agendas.

Angela Rayner was one of the most effective secretaries of state in Starmer’s government during her first stint in MHCLG. Similarly, Jim McMahon was an effective minister for local government. Bringing them back into those roles means they can pick up where they left off on local government reorganisation, the fair funding review and housebuilding, among others.
As we have argued throughout this report, services are still focused on implementing reforms launched by the Starmer administration.
The Starmer government handled the process of abolishing NHS England abysmally. Yvette Cooper, Burnham’s health secretary, urgently needs to grip this process.

It would be a mistake to stop the abolition of NHSE at this point. But both she and Burnham need to provide political direction about the future form of the NHS super-structure and how that aligns with Burnham’s vision of a more devolved system.

As previously argued, NHS and police reforms are putting more powers in the hands of those secretaries of state. This seems to be a direct contradiction with his ‘devolve by default’ approach to public services. Burnham should pause the Health Bill and adjust the proposed police reforms to ensure that accountability flows support his vision.

Specifically in the Health Bill, Burnham should clarify whether the secretary of state should be able to: 207 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Health Bill: oversight of the health system fact sheet’, GOV.UK, 19 May 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/health-bill-oversight-of-the-health-system-fact-sheet
Among other provisions. If Burnham does not think the secretary of state should have those powers, he should make clear which organisations or individuals should instead.

The prime minister must also decide whether to press ahead with other planned reforms, such as the Courts Modernisation Bill, which is due to restrict the number of jury trials. This involves a substantial shift in the workforce required in criminal courts – particularly a major recruitment of additional magistrates. The sooner departments and other stakeholders have clarity on which reforms the government will be pursuing, the less time and energy will be wasted on proposals that do not go anywhere.

One of the biggest oversights of Starmer’s public service reforms was the failure toco-ordinate subnational reorganisations. It is welcome that Burnham has set a goal to align boundaries, but there are still urgent questions the government needs to address.

Unless there are exceptionally good reasons not to, the government should align the boundaries of ICBs, police forces and strategic authorities on a 1:1:1 basis – he should not allow an ICB or police force to contain multiple SAs, as is currently suggested.

This will not be painless. Twelve ICBs have already merged into six, and it is likely their boundaries will have to be redrawn if the government pursues better boundary alignment, causing more disruption for staff. Some in those services argue that operational concerns should trump boundary alignment. But that is a parochial view of how services should be organised and ignores the benefits to the wider state from having a more coherent cross-service set of structures. Cooper and Mahmood should accept short-term disruption and difficulties navigating the implications for services’ operational concerns to support long-term stability and improved working between services.

Proponents of a smaller number of police forces and ICBs argue that cutting the numbers from 43 and 42 respectively to the 30 or so MSAs (rather than the 10–15 and 26 proposed respectively) will result in fewer savings, as it will mean smaller cuts to back-office staff, nullifying the point of the reorganisations. That is a short-termist approach, prioritising often overly optimistic headcount cuts over the real productivity benefits that would come from a system that effectively supports better integration and co-operation.

There is a strong case to include regional care co-operatives – the initiative launched by the Starmer government to co-ordinate the commissioning of children’s social care between local authorities – into this system. The government is still in the early stages of these reforms, and is piloting RCCs in two areas in England. Under current plans, it is likely every RCC will cover multiple strategic authorities, as there will be only eight RCCs across England (though some local authorities are opting out of being part of RCCs). Burnham should instead aim to align RCCs with MSA footprints.

Schools is a harder problem to solve. The current direction of travel is to academise all remaining local authority-maintained schools. But multi-academy trusts often have schools across the country, meaning they do not neatly sit in any mayoral geography. To determine how schools fit into this emerging place-based system, the government should set out a clear long-term vision for the structure and governance of the schools system, including which functions and responsibilities should be controlled locally, by whom, and which would benefit from being controlled or delivered at scale. It should use this vision to guide decisions about future academy conversions and wider public service geographies.

The Starmer government created clear priorities that focused systems’ attention, in some services at least, but which were inconsistent with its stated overall priorities. In the NHS, for example, the elective target is an odd priority to choose if the government’s overarching goal is to move care outside of hospitals and make the service more preventative. Burnham should clarify if he wants to go ahead with this as the NHS’s primary focus.

We have argued in the past that the Starmer government’s structural court reforms will free up relatively little capacity. Worse, it distracts from other ways that the government could improve courts’ efficiency.

And in policing, there is a specific focus on increasing charges for violence against women and girls, rather than other kinds of positive outcomes outside of court. This could create a perverse incentive to charge offenders, rather than diverting them from prosecution. For some offences, a charge will always be the appropriate outcome if possible, but out-of-court resolutions are cheaper and often more effective at reducing reoffending, including in some cases of domestic abuse. 208 Armitage R, ‘CARA: Cautioning and relationship abuse for domestic abuse: Evaluating the impact of Cautioning and Relationship Abuse programmes for perpetrators of domestic abuse’, Leeds Beckett University, (no date), retrieved 30 September 2026, www.leedsbeckett.ac.uk/research/centre-for-justice-law-and-policy/cara It may also cause further problems in magistrates’ courts, which would be forced to handle a greater volume of cases.

So far, the Burnham government has identified employment support and 16-19 skills as services that it would like to devolve to mayors. That leaves many other services over which mayors do not currently have control or influence, including most of those that we look at in this series of reports. Some of those services and functions are more amenable to devolution than others. It is much easier to imagine giving mayors more control over the police, for example, than over specialist hospitals or prisons.

As a first step, Burnham should set out principles for when central government will look to devolve power over services or bring them up from, for example, local authorities into MSAs. That will provide a framework to help departments decide where there could be opportunities for greater devolution.

Answers to these questions may not always provide a clear conclusion but they should help government to decide whether a service should be devolved and at which level of government (local authority, strategic authority, regional or national) responsibility should sit. In some cases, devolution will not be the easy or right answer. While there are real advantages to a more local probation service, for example – with strong connections with local support services, employers and communities – prisons must continue to be run as a largely national system, given security restrictions, the need to move prisoners around, and the unpopularity of having a prison locally at all. And yet the two systems must work very closely together, to prepare offenders for release, understand potential risks and threats and support effective rehabilitation. The government must weigh these benefits carefully.
A set of principles is the first step towards greater devolution and would increase the chance of consistency of approach across departments.

Burnham should clarify the role that he expects local authorities to play in a world where mayors have increased powers. Jim McMahon has said that detail may be forthcoming in the upcoming devolution white paper. 209 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and Jim McMahon OBE MP, ‘Local government reorganisation: programme review and decisions withdrawal letter to council leaders’, letter, 7 September 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-government-reorganisation-programme-review-and-decisions-withdrawal-letter-to-council-leaders

It is important that the white paper does address these issues. Though currently under-resourced and often treated as the delivery arm of central government, local authorities are a vital piece of any government’s attempts to devolve power and integrate services. Not only do they provide many services themselves, but councils are also one of the closest parts of government to people’s lives. They also have their own democratic mandate, and therefore potentially different interests to the mayors that sit a level above them in MSAs.

Compared to MSAs, they also have several advantages. There is already complete national coverage, with an upper-tier local authority in every area of England.* They understand their residents and local needs in a way that few other parts of the state do. They also have a far larger workforce than MSAs, employing more than one million people nationwide.**, 210 Local Government Association, ‘Local government workforce’, Local Government Association, June 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, https://www.local.gov.uk/our-support/workforce-and-hr-support/local-government-workforce-data/local-government-workforce While there is no good data for the MSA workforce, recent analysis from the Local Government Chronicle (LGC) estimates that the number is somewhere beneath 10,000.***, 211 Topham E, ‘Revealed: Stark differences in strategic authority staffing’, Local Government Chronicle, 5 August 2026, retrieved 21 September 2026, https://www.lgcplus.com/politics/devolution-and-economic-growth/revealed-stark-differences-in-strategic-authority-staffing-05-08-2026/

That is not to say that the current local government workforce would easily be able to absorb more powers and responsibilities. More than 15 years of severe financial pressure means many local authorities have cut the management, analytical and administrative staff needed to deliver effective devolution. But even with those cuts, local authorities are arguably better placed than the average strategic authority to deliver more services.

In short, Burnham cannot and should not ignore local government in the rush to strengthen mayors’ responsibilities. Local government should be at the centre of any future devolved system of delivering public services. Burnham should clarify what role he sees councils playing and how they will work alongside MSAs to deliver more devolved services.

Burnham could also intervene to use the neighbourhood health service – announced by the Starmer government – as a vehicle for a more devolved health offering, aligned with strategic authority boundaries and closely integrated with public health, adult and children’s social services.

* Following the completion of local government reorganisation, there will also be a consistent unitary model across all of England.** Though the local government workforce also includes teachers and other staff that do not work in councils themselves.*** Though interviewees in that article stress that is not representative of their full workforce, as they often have support from their constituent local authorities.

As noted, there are some parts of the Starmer government’s agenda that we think were genuinely innovative and have laid the groundwork for Burnham’s goals for public services. Where that is the case, his government should not abandon them.

In particular, the ‘Test, learn, and grow’ (TLG) programme was attempting to implement a new way of working in services that could help circumvent the continued risk aversion in both central government and in front-line services.

The place-based budgeting pilots and the ‘prevention demonstrator’ in GMCA were both trialling better pooling of budgets to support service integration and allow for a greater focus on preventative spending. Those pilots build on the success of the Total Place agenda at the end of the last Labour government – an approach that we are supportive of. The Burnham government should look to pool more budgets in local areas. Integrated settlements for MSAs are one route to this, particularly if the government devolves more spending powers to mayors. But that should not be where pooling ends and Burnham should consider where it is possible to combine funding streams, along the lines of the Total Place model from the late 2000s. 212 Ibid.

He should also ensure that small pilots and other programmes are better co-ordinated and have clearer, more distinctive purposes than under the Starmer government. It may also make sense to merge some of these programmes – for example, encouraging place-based initiatives such as Changing Futures to come under the TLG banner.

The Burnham government has limited time, funding and capacity to make meaningful improvements to public service performance between now and the next election, particularly given ongoing reform programmes. The next spending review – due to conclude with financial allocations in the summer of 2027 and set departmental allocations for the remainder of the parliament and beyond – is a key moment for the prime minister’s entire agenda.
Burnham should keep the Starmer government’s timetable of a full spending review in 2027. This will allow for a far more measured, productive process than under a condensed timetable.

The Burnham government may use the 2026 autumn budget to top up services’ funding. This is legitimate given new priorities and changing circumstances (for example, on inflation forecasts). But spending is likely to be much more effective if set over multiple years as part of a clear strategy.

The goal of that 2027 spending review should be to provide services with as much certainty and stability as possible. Given the substantial risks to the current settlements, Burnham should ensure that settlements are generous enough to meet potential pressures and sufficient to actually deliver the performance improvements that he has promised.

We have outlined in this report where we think settlements are unrealistic, and potential performance pitfalls throughout the rest of this parliament. Burnham should take these into consideration when he and John Healey set envelopes for next year’s spending review.

Another successful innovation under the Starmer government were the value for money (VfM) reviews that were initially run by the Office for Value for Money (OVfM). Burnham should keep this innovation but should target the next set of reviews at areas that support his agenda.

For example, he could ask the Treasury to conduct a review to support his ambition to eradicate rough sleeping. Other candidates for areas that the Treasury could examine would be the effect on local government financial sustainability from continued use of ‘exceptional financial support’, the effect of limited or poor-quality housing on demand for public services, the interaction between benefits spending and spending on services such as the NHS, adult social care or SEND services, and effective commissioning of adult social care services.
A major failing of the Starmer government was not to use the 2025 spending review to properly drive co-ordination across Whitehall, with missions particularly conspicuous by their absence.
The Treasury should use the 2027 spending review to push departments to think about spending more holistically. This should include:

Regardless of the mechanism the Treasury uses to encourage cross-departmental bids and co-operation, the government needs to improve accountability for Burnham’s priorities. This starts with setting the high-level outcomes that it wants to improve. Unlike the missions, these should be genuine outcome metrics, not merely output or even input metrics. Outcomes are far more likely to require cross-departmental working than narrower output metrics – they are also more likely to force departments to take a longer-term view, rather than incentivising some of the short-term interventions that the NHS has used to improve elective performance.
Also unlike Starmer and his missions, Burnham should retain a close, personal interest in delivering those priorities over the entirety of his time in office.

But to help him do this he must also have a clear mechanism for holding departments and other parts of government to account. This would be easier if the government had a more effective centre (No. 10, Treasury and Cabinet Office). Burnham’s decision to create the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (OPMC) could help here, though he will still need to imbue it with clarity of purpose and administrative authority to make a success of it.

It can be difficult to track progress towards long-term outcomes over the relatively short timeframe of a parliament. The Burnham government should also outline which interim metrics it would expect to improve between now and the general election to demonstrate progress towards chosen outcomes. However, especially where the government’s answer is to devolve funding, the government must resist the mistake its predecessor made of requiring MSAs to conform to a detailed set of inputs and outputs which, in practice, limited how they could use that money.
