Garrett Watson is Vice President of Federal Tax Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. His work has been featured in The Washington Post, The Atlantic, Politico, the Associated Press and other major outlets.

Alex Durante is a Senior Economist at the Tax Foundation, working on federal tax policy and model development. Alex worked as a research assistant at the Federal Reserve Board and served as a staff economist on the Council of Economic Advisers.

articles.title: The Bank of England Should Not Stop Paying Interest On Banks’ Reserves: Here Is Why
articles.standfirst: As the Chancellor looks to find additional sources of revenue in his upcoming Budget, some commentators (e.g., Gerald Holtham) and politicians (e.g., Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice, both of Reform...
paragraphs: As the Chancellor looks to find additional sources of revenue in his upcoming Budget, some commentators (e.g., Gerald Holtham) and politicians (e.g., Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice, both of Reform UK) have suggested that stopping the payment of interest on bank reserves might be a way of doing this. But is this really a sensible thing to do? The Bank of England thinks not and previous work by NIESR suggests not. In what follows, I run through the arguments underlying this view.

It is first worth recalling how we got here. The Bank of England moved from a system of ‘scarce reserves’, where the banks were kept short of reserves and so had to borrow from the Bank at its policy rate, to a system of remunerated reserve balances with reserve averaging in 2006. This change better enabled the Bank to stabilise the interbank interest rate around its policy rate, making monetary policy more effective. But, although the banks chose the level of reserves in this system, it became clear during the global financial crisis that this level of reserves was too low.

In 2009, in response to the global financial crisis, the Bank started buying up government bonds financed by the creation of reserves, a process known as quantitative easing. This led to a much larger level of reserves than the banks would willingly hold. The quid pro quo for this was that the Bank of England were paying interest on these reserves, compensating the banks for interest they would otherwise have lost. This point was made by Bill Allen in this article in Central Banking, who argued that this meant that the Bank of England was able to buy gilts at a cheaper price than would have been the case had they not been paying interest on reserves. Given that, to stop paying interest on reserves now would be an act of bad faith. This point was made even more strongly by Tim Young in this letter to the Financial Times.
But, leaving aside this issue, there are other reasons why stopping the Bank of England from paying interest on reserves would be a bad idea.

First, commercial banks would have a strong incentive to minimise their holdings of reserves. This could leave the banks potentially short of liquid assets to cover unexpected payment outflows, making them less resilient to shocks. And this problem was a key reason for moving from a system of ‘scarce reserves’ to ‘ample reserves’ in the first place. To the extent that liquidity regulation requires banks to hold a given level of reserves, the banks would be led to recoup the cost of holding these reserves from their customers, via lower deposit rates and/or higher charges. Indeed, this has happened in the Euro Area since the ECB stopped paying interest on reserves. As a result, there would be no net gain for society: there may be (short-term) fiscal savings but these would be offset by higher costs for consumers.

Second, the Bank of England would find it harder to carry out monetary policy. By setting the interest rate on reserves, the Bank can directly control the marginal cost of funding for banks. In turn, this will feed through to interest rates throughout the economy, allowing monetary policy changes to affect real decisions. In a world in which no interest is paid on reserves, the Bank would only be able to affect interest rates by ensuring that banks needed to borrow reserves from it. And this would mean creating a shortage of reserves, with the additional risks to financial stability that this would entail. One answer to this critique is that the Bank could adopt a ‘tiered’ structure for reserves where it pays interest on reserves up to a certain level. Although this could be done, as Bill Allen said in this article in Central Banking, it would have to be done very carefully and would still be subject to the other criticisms in this note.

Third, to stop paying interest on reserves while forcing banks to hold them for liquidity purposes effectively represents a tax on the banks, who would have to pay interest on the funds they borrow to finance their reserve balances. While the government can, of course, feel free to tax the banks above and beyond what they tax other companies, it would seem much better to be open about this and apply a direct tax on banks rather than tax them by stealth.

Finally, and perhaps most worryingly, if the government were to instruct the Bank of England to stop paying interest on reserves, this would bring into question the Bank’s independence. Given such an instruction would be motivated by short-term pressure on the public finances, rather than a more reasoned examination of how the financial system functions, this would be a clear case of political interference in the Bank’s operations. And if the Bank of England were seen as subject to political interference, monetary policy credibility could well be lost leading to a rise in inflation expectations. In turn, this would imply higher inflation on average, making it harder for the Bank to bring inflation down without lowering output and raising unemployment, and making us all worse off.

articles.title: A Small Value-Added Tax Could Pay for Tariff Repeal
articles.standfirst: Rather than continuing the Trump administration’s tariff policy, policymakers should explore new solutions that can raise sustainable revenue with fewer distortions, like replacing the tariffs with a value-added tax.
paragraphs: TariffTariffs are taxes imposed by one country on goods imported from another country. Tariffs are trade barriers that raise prices, reduce available quantities of goods and services for US businesses and consumers, and create an economic burden on foreign exporters. revenue has more than tripled as a share of GDP under the tariff increases imposed by President Donald Trump since 2018. The revenues have proven unstable, however, as many new tariffs were imposed under untested legal authorities and subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2026. While the administration crafts replacements, policymakers should devise their own alternative fiscal plan to address the twin problems of economic uncertainty and fiscal instability.

Even with the new tariff revenue, America’s fiscal trajectory is still poor. Annual budget deficits will exceed $2 trillion within a few years and $3 trillion by the end of the budget window in 2036. Interest payments on the debt will exceed $2 trillion by 2035, costing more than defense spending and almost as much as major spending programs like Medicare.

Our new book, Options for Reforming America’s TaxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. Code 3.0: A Policymaker’s Guide to Tax Reform Trade-Offs, considers a reform that would remove all the new tariffs and return US tariff policy to its 2017 baseline. Removing the tariffs would ease the economic burden they create, but would add to the US’s already-high deficits.

Since publication of the book, additional tariffs have taken effect. We now estimate that removing all the new tariffs, including the levies dating back to Trump’s first term, would cost nearly $1.8 trillion in forgone revenue for the federal government from 2027 through 2036. Tariff repeal would reduce marginal tax rates on work and investment in the US, leading to higher output and hours worked.
To replace the lost revenue, lawmakers could consider a value-added tax (VAT).

A VAT is a consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible. collected on the incremental value added at each stage of production of a good or service—it is similar to a retail sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. in that it only burdens final consumer goods, but it is administered along the way during production rather than only at the final sale.

VATs are most commonly administered through a credit-invoice system: businesses collect tax on their sales at every stage but receive credit for the tax paid on their inputs. This removes the tax burden on intermediate transactions and places it on the final sale.

The result is that a VAT is neutral between consumption and saving. Unlike the present income tax, which can discourage capital investment, a VAT, once fully transitioned to, imposes no burden on the normal return to investment (that is, the return required to just break even, as opposed to supernormal returns that exceed the normal return, arising from advantages such as market power, rent-seeking, investment risk, or innovation). VATs are also neutral with respect to trade and different types of capital investment. VATs still impose an economic burden by reducing returns to work, which shrinks hours worked and economic output.

Many think of tariffs as a consumption tax, but they depart from consumption tax design in an important respect: they apply to final consumer goods as well as intermediate transactions. In contrast with a VAT, which imposes no burden on the normal return to investment because intermediate transactions are effectively exempted, tariffs burden investment, in some cases by more than the income tax.

Tariffs can distort returns across sectors and types of investment, leading to capital misallocation. They also differ from other taxes because they carry geopolitical consequences: they invite retaliation, which compounds the economic cost without raising additional revenue for the Treasury, and may encourage countries to pursue trade pacts that exclude the tariff-imposing country. For these reasons, tariffs are a relatively distortive type of tax. Additionally, the new tariffs have been imposed under executive authority (including Section 122, Section 301, and Section 232 tariffs) and face ongoing legal challenges.

Accordingly, a VAT would cause fewer distortions than a tariff. We estimate that the revenue loss from eliminating the tariffs could be fully replaced with a broad-based VAT levied at a rate of 1 percent, while increasing economic output, the capital stock, and hours worked. Tax Foundation’s modeling does not capture the distortive effects tariffs have on the cost of capital, and so likely understates the gains from replacing them with a VAT.

The swap would be revenue neutral on a conventional basis, but after considering the increase in output, it would raise $130.1 billion over the budget window on a dynamic basis. The debt-to-GDP ratio would be virtually unchanged conventionally measured, but dynamically, it would be slightly lower, falling about 1.3 percentage points from 175.9 percent in 2056 to 174.7 percent. Distributionally, the revenue-neutral swap would not result in a significant change in who bears the burden of the tax. On a dynamic basis, all income groups would see gains because of the increase in economic output.

The nation is on track to run record-breaking deficits year after year, and businesses and workers are navigating an uncertain economic environment. Policymakers must navigate difficult trade-offs in designing policy solutions to these twin problems. Rather than continuing the administration’s tariff policy, policymakers should explore new solutions that can raise sustainable revenue with fewer distortions, like replacing the tariffs with a value-added tax.

Erica York is Senior Economist with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Her analysis has been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post, Politico, and other national and international media outlets.

articles.title: Burnham’s proposed electoral reform could have unpredictable effects
articles.standfirst:
Burnham’s announcement that he will be putting electoral reform on the next Labour manifesto was cheered by proponents of proportional representation. But, Tim Bale writes, when political ideals meet political reality, a lot can change. Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles. Far be it from me … Continued
The post Burnham’s proposed electoral reform could have unpredictable effects   first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: Burnham’s announcement that he will be putting electoral reform on the next Labour manifesto was cheered by proponents of proportional representation. But, Tim Bale writes, when political ideals meet political reality, a lot can change.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

Far be it from me – a supporter of proportional representation and even, I confess, compulsory voting – to throw shade on the first Prime Minister in my lifetime to commit to electoral reform. But before we get carried away, we should perhaps remind ourselves that in real-time, real-life politics there is many a slip twixt cup and lip.

When we talk about electoral reform, we are inevitably talking about a series of sometimes less-than-uplifting compromises cobbled together by historically situated actors pursuing their own best interests in conditions of greater or lesser uncertainty. As a result, anything can happen – and, as they say, probably will.

Scrapping first past the post FPTP in favour of a potentially more proportional system (PR) has been something of a pipedream for so long: the 2011 referendum doesn’t count since it was on the Alternative Vote – a non-proportional system that Nick Clegg himself had previously called “a miserable little compromise”? As a result, we have got into the habit of considering reform at a fairly lofty level of normative abstraction, revolving, for instance, around discussion of what would be the fairest way to, say, improve representation, extend participation and promote greater openness – all without sacrificing strong and stable government.
Scrapping first past the post FPTP in favour of a potentially more proportional system (PR) has been something of a pipedream for so long.

It’s therefore been easy to forget that, as soon as it becomes a serious prospect, reality and human creativity are likely to interfere with the wishes of those seeking the fulfilment of their cherished ideals. Fortunately, perhaps, it can also mess with the best laid plans of those who seek to control the process and the outcome to their own advantage.

The likeliest means by which those managing that process will try to ensure they end up as its beneficiaries (or, at the very least, not its victims) will involve, first, deciding the terms of reference and the composition of Burnham’s putative National Commission.

The fact that the Conservative Party has decided not to take part will admittedly make it harder to argue that there is some kind of consensus around whatever it recommends. But it should make it easier for those parties who do get involved to ensure its recommendations, even if they don’t do them as much good as they’d hoped, don’t actively harm them. While Reform UK seem to have gone cold on PR recently, they might therefore want to think again before they join the Tories’ boycott.

Whatever system is adopted, reality has a nasty but nonetheless welcome habit of ensuring that electoral engineering is not an exact science – nor one that can completely take the politics out of democracy.

Once the process begins, parties that do agree to take part will, fairly obviously, push for whichever system that they believe will favour them, be it non-proportional (essentially AV or SV) or proportional (essentially List, MMP or STV). Then, depending on their size, they will also start lobbying for whichever “electoral formula” (essentially, the equation used to allocate seats to parties after votes are cast) tends to advantage either smaller or larger parties.

Once the system is decided upon, however, (and assuming, if only for the sake of argument, that it is a variant of PR) the biggest battle will likely be over the threshold which Parties are required to cross in order to be awarded seats in Parliament: if you go low (as in the Netherlands) you may see even more parties represented at Westminster than is already the case; if you go high (like Germany) you’ll probably get fewer. Indeed, even the most hardened Tory opponents of PR might be reconciled to it if they could only be made to realize the extent to which proportionality can be eroded via the ‘right’ decision on a percentage of the vote required to entitle the recipient to seats.

For all that the process of reform can be manipulated, however, the good news is that experience the world over suggests that whatever emerges from it is unlikely to turn out quite as those doing the manipulation had hoped. Whatever system is adopted, reality has a nasty but nonetheless welcome habit of ensuring that electoral engineering is not an exact science – nor one that can completely take the politics out of democracy. Eastern Europe in particular is littered with the bodies of parties that, in the years that followed the coming of democracy after 1989, sought to establish and then tinker with electoral systems in order to promote their cause and hurt their opponents.

The bad news, though, is that the very process of electoral reform, because it’s often a messy, less principled and more prolonged affair than its proponents assume, doesn’t necessarily help reconnect the public with their political representatives in the way that reformers hope it will. Indeed, it may even alienate them still further – particularly if, following a less than uplifting reform process, the party they vote for in the election that either fails to make it into the parliament because of thresholds or, if it does so, still ends up being marginalized and ignored.
Reformers then should welcome Andy Burnham’s words. But, in the end, it’s deeds that count.

Tim Bale is Professor of Politics at Queen Mary University and is the author, together with Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser, of Riding the Populist Wave and, most recently, The Conservative Party after Brexit.

articles.title: Ending the Triple Lock: A Welcome Step, But It Must Happen Sooner Rather Than Later
articles.standfirst: Ending the triple lock The coalition government introduced the triple lock in 2011. It ensures the state pension rises each year by CPI inflation, average earnings growth, or 2.5 per...
paragraphs: Andy Burnham has pledged to end the triple lock from 2030 to help fund a new national care service. This is a welcome move as it removes the one-way government spending ratchet on the state pension. But it leaves some important issues unaddressed.
The coalition government introduced the triple lock in 2011. It ensures the state pension rises each year by CPI inflation, average earnings growth, or 2.5 per cent, whichever is the highest.
On paper, this sounds like a useful safeguard against pensioner poverty, but in practice it has created a one-way ratchet. The state pension can only rise, but never fall, in real terms.

One of the main reasons for this is that earnings growth tends to lag inflation shocks by a year or two. The state pension is uprated in line with spikes in CPI inflation to ensure no real-terms loss for retirees. But then the state pension is uprated again once workers begin to restore their real earnings power.

In effect, the state pension benefits twice from the same shock. Once from inflation protection and again from the subsequent wage catch-up. The flaw is self-evident, without any anchor, state pension spending quickly becomes unsustainable in a world of inflationary supply shocks.
Andy Burnham has pledged to end the state pension triple lock from 2030. This is a welcome announcement as it removes the one-way spending ratchet. But it leaves some important issues unaddressed.

First, the pledge to end the triple lock is to help fund a new national care service. This is a reallocation of spending as opposed to a consolidation of spending. Second, the policy change takes effect in 2030, outside the window of the current parliament. Brining forward the change to start in the next fiscal year would be a more credible commitment.
The United Kingdom’s public debt stands at around 94 per cent of GDP, the highest since the 1960s. At some point, this debt ratio must be brought down. There are two primary reasons:

The pledge to end the state pension triple lock makes no progress towards a fiscal consolidation that could help reduce the debt ratio. Instead, the funds are being reallocated from one part of the government’s budget to another.
The pledge to end the triple lock takes effect from 2030. This does not fall within the current parliament and therefore raises doubts over whether this is a credible commitment.

The fiscal outlook remains one with heavily back-loaded tax rises pencilled in toward the end of the parliament. This announcement adds to the list of difficult policy decisions whose implementation has been postponed to a future date.
Not only is this unfavourable in terms of rebuilding credibility, but it will also add significantly to the state pension bill.

Using projections from the OBR’s March 2026 Economic and Fiscal Outlook (EFO), holding the triple lock in place until 2030 will cost the government an additional £5.8 billion per year by the end of the decade, relative to simply preserving the real value of the state pension via a CPI uprating.

Uprating the state pension under the triple lock has delivered a cumulative real-terms increase of 17 per cent between 2011–12 and 2025–26. By contrast, average earnings growth has deliver a 5.5 per cent real-terms increase over the same period. The pledge to end the triple lock from 2030 is therefore welcome as it removes this unsustainable spending ratchet on the state pension.

But 2030 lies outside of the current parliament. Bringing forward the change to the start of the next fiscal year could increase the credibility of this policy announcement and potentially save money for the government.
A lasting solution to the UK government’s debt problem will ultimately require a broad and difficult conversation that reaches far beyond the state pension triple lock.

But the Chancellor’s key objective at the upcoming budget, above all else, should be to prioritise spending restraint and put the debt ratio on a declining path in the medium term. And, if this is to happen, the triple lock must go sooner rather than later.

articles.title: Real Property Taxes in Europe, 2026
articles.standfirst: High property taxes levied not only on land but also on buildings and structures can discourage investment in infrastructure, which businesses would have to pay additional tax on.
paragraphs: Early property taxes, first implemented in feudal times, were levied primarily on land and paid mostly by farmers. In modern times, property taxes are also levied on assets like real estate and paid on a recurrent basis by individuals or legal entities.

Ideally, property taxes can give local governments a valuable fiscal incentive to permit new development and offer a way to fund local public services whose value is capitalized into property prices. However, high property taxes levied not only on land but also on buildings and structures can also discourage investment in those assets, which businesses would have to pay additional taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. on. For this reason, businesses may choose to locate away from places with high property taxes.

Two of the 34 European countries covered here, Liechtenstein and Malta, do not levy any recurrent taxes on property at all. Estonia is the sole country on this map to tax only land, meaning that its real property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. is the most efficient.

Of the 32 countries that levy property taxes, 28 allow businesses to deduct property or land taxes from corporate income, which mitigates the tax burden and encourages businesses to invest. Four countries—Austria, Iceland, Italy, and Slovenia—prohibit the deduction of property taxes from business income, leading to double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. of business properties.

Luxembourg and Moldova raise the lowest property tax revenues as a share of their private capital stock, at around 0.05 percent. Switzerland and Estonia follow at 0.08 and 0.09 percent, respectively. The highest property taxes as a share of the private capital stock occur in the United Kingdom (2.04 percent), Iceland (1.43 percent), and France (1.08 percent).

On average, the revenue raised from recurrent property taxes in the 32 European countries covered that have a property tax lies at 0.45 percent of their private capital stocks. In contrast, the United States raises as much as 1.88 percent of its private capital stock in property taxes.

For the 16 European countries that record how property tax revenues are split between businesses and households, households remit around 60 percent of total property tax revenue, ranging from only 7.4 percent of receipts in the Slovak Republic to 71.4 percent in France.

Starting from 2025, Germany is devolving its property tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. to the state level. The state of Baden-Württemberg used this opportunity to apply property taxes only to the value of land. Croatia introduced a recurrent property tax in 2025, levied on the square metres of land and floor area.

Alex Mengden is an Economist at the Tax Foundation, where he focuses on international tax issues and tax policy in Europe. He holds a BA in philosophy and economics from the University of Bayreuth and an MSc in economics from the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich.

articles.title: Budget 2026: When Fiscal and Monetary Policy Collide
articles.standfirst: This year’s Budget, scheduled for 28 October, takes place against a challenging economic and fiscal backdrop. Inflation looks set to go higher, as global energy prices remain elevated while there...
paragraphs: This year’s Budget, scheduled for 28 October, takes place against a challenging economic and fiscal backdrop. Inflation looks set to go higher, as global energy prices remain elevated while there are concerns that this could also derail activity growth. Bond markets have reacted by pushing up US yields to their highest since 2002. The gilt market has followed this trend, putting pressure on debt servicing costs at a time when the debt-to-GDP ratio in the United Kingdom is at its highest in over 60 years. There is a pressing need to make changes to the balance between taxation and spending, and potentially more fundamental changes to the tax system itself.

But matters are made more complicated by the increasingly blurred distinction between monetary and fiscal policy issues. In the first five months of the 2026-27 fiscal year, public borrowing is running around £8.8 billion above the monthly profile consistent with the OBR’s March forecast, driven primarily by higher-than-expected outlays on social benefits and debt interest. If sustained, this will entail higher-than-planned debt issuance at a time when global debt markets are already demanding a higher premium to hold government debt. In large part, the rise in gilt yields is due to expectations of a repricing of monetary policy, with around four 25-basis-point rate increases implied through to mid-2027. This in turn will raise the cost of debt servicing, while the central bank’s balance sheet can itself have significant fiscal implications as the recent decision to slow the pace of quantitative tightening (QT) illustrates.

This does not mean that the United Kingdom is about to experience a period of outright fiscal dominance where fiscal requirements constrain monetary policy actions. But the traditional separation between fiscal and monetary decisions is now becoming harder to sustain: while they remain institutionally separate, their effects on financial markets and the public finances increasingly interact. Indeed, the Bank of England’s September announcement that it would slow the pace of gilt sales held on the balance sheet for monetary policy purposes and introduce a multi-year plan to outline a predictable pace of QT, is a case in point. At a time when market volatility is already high and when the domestic demand for long-dated securities has fallen due to reduced appetite from pension funds, the decision over the pace at which the Bank reduces its gilt holdings has implications that extend beyond monetary policy. It affects the supply of government debt that must be absorbed by private investors and, potentially, the yield that the government must pay to finance its borrowing. What is formally a monetary policy decision can therefore have direct implications for fiscal policy.

One potential consequence is that financial markets could impose a stronger constraint on government spending than the official fiscal rules. Under current legislation “the current budget must be in surplus in 2029-30, until 2029-30 becomes the third year of the forecast period. From that point, the current budget must then remain in balance or in surplus from the third year of the rolling forecast period.” The OBR’s March forecast (made in February before the US and Israeli attack on Iran) suggested that the Government had relatively little headroom against this rule – around £24 billion. NIESR’s August forecast (which took into account the effects of the US-Iran conflict to that point) pointed to no headroom at all. Financial markets will not wait for the deficit rule to be breached. If investors become concerned about the sustainability of public finances, they will raise gilt yields and thereby impose a tighter constraint on fiscal policy whether or not the Government formally fails to meet its fiscal rules.

This raises a more fundamental question about how the fiscal and monetary authorities jointly determine the value of government liabilities. The conventional monetary policy framework assumes that fiscal policy ultimately adjusts to ensure debt sustainability, leaving the central bank free to pursue price stability. But what happens if that fiscal adjustment is not forthcoming? The fiscal theory of the price level (FTPL) provides a useful, if controversial, perspective. FTPL starts from the government’s intertemporal budget constraint, arguing that the real value of outstanding government liabilities must be consistent with the present value of future primary fiscal surpluses. If fiscal policy does not adjust sufficiently to ensure this condition, the theory suggests that the price level adjust instead, with inflation changing the real value of nominal government debt. The implication is not that fiscal policy mechanically determines inflation, but that the sustainability and credibility of fiscal policy are ultimately part of the determination of the price level.

The relevance of this perspective is particularly interesting when government debt is high and monetary and fiscal policy are closely intertwined. If higher interest rates increase debt-servicing costs, while attempts to reduce inflation through tighter monetary policy simultaneously make the fiscal position more difficult, the conventional distinction between an independent monetary authority and a fiscally constrained government becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. The question then is whether fiscal policy will adjust to monetary policy, or whether monetary policy will ultimately have to take account of the fiscal consequences of its actions.

Historical analysis by Bordo et al. suggest that fiscal policy may well have played a role in exacerbating the Great Inflation of the 1970s. They contend that household inflation expectations shifted in discrete steps rather than adapting to realised inflation, with the timing coinciding with major fiscal regime changes such as the Barber budget of 1972 and the Howe budget of 1981. The authors interpret these shifts as evidence that changes in the fiscal regime affected inflation expectations. This provides historical evidence that is relevant to the FTPL perspective because in a regime where fiscal policy is not perceived to stabilise debt, tighter monetary policy need not generate the same disinflationary response as it would under monetary dominance.

The broader lesson is that fiscal and monetary policy cannot always be considered independently. Fiscal rules seek to constrain the Government’s borrowing decisions; financial markets can impose an additional constraint through the price of government debt; and monetary policy seeks to control inflation but simultaneously affects the fiscal cost of servicing that debt. FTPL highlights the possibility that when fiscal policy does not adjust sufficiently to stabilise debt, inflation itself can become part of the mechanism through which the government’s intertemporal budget constraint is satisfied.

The Chancellor thus faces many challenges. Most obviously he must pay heed to the fiscal rules and ensure that the Bank of England remains independent of discussions on fiscal issues. Perhaps more importantly, he must convince the bond market this is the case. But he also needs to assess more broadly whether the interaction between fiscal sustainability, financial markets and monetary policy is consistent with price stability.

articles.title: Lock, stock and two missing grandmas
articles.standfirst:
Morning all, This week, we got a step closer to the end of the triple lock – the State Pension should keep pace with earnings growth, but good riddance to the ratchet! Keep an eye out for fresh analysis from us digging into the long-run savings from this proposed change. We’ve also officially entered Budget … Continued
The post Lock, stock and two missing grandmas appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This week, we got a step closer to the end of the triple lock – the State Pension should keep pace with earnings growth, but good riddance to the ratchet! Keep an eye out for fresh analysis from us digging into the long-run savings from this proposed change.

We’ve also officially entered Budget month. If you haven’t already, please do register to join our discussion next week about how the Chancellor can allay cost of living concerns when he steps up to the dispatch box on the 28th. And look out for details of our Budget preview on the 13th.
Keep reading for the latest on artificial lawyers and generational health drift, not to mention the end of grandmothers and the growing impact of the criminally under-discussed benefit cap.

You’ll be hearing from my chat bot. Lawyers are expensive (and arguably not widely beloved). Is it any wonder then, that new research shows that around one-in-six people with a legal problem have turned to an AI chatbot for help? Among the 3,000 people surveyed who’d had a legal problem, young people were the keenest to reach for AI: more than one-in-four (26 per cent) of 18-24-year-olds with a legal problem used a chatbot, falling to one-in-ten (10 per cent) among 55-64-year-olds. Participants’ transcripts show the range: consumer disputes, landlord-tenant rows, employment problems and family law all featured. As the authors note, these are situations which are “common, stressful, and often difficult to navigate without advice, but that largely fall outside the scope of legal aid”. So, this could go one of two ways. Justice may become far more accessible, as long as the advice dispensed is accurate, especially for those without the resources or know-how to fight their corner. Or our public services may get irreparably gummed up with (occasionally spurious) complaints and appeals. Watch this space…

Goodbye Grandma. Ageing parents enquiring why their offspring haven’t produced another generation yet is a well-worn trope. The authors of a new paper, themselves grandparents-in-waiting, arguably fit the bill. They coined the “Rotten Adult Kid” problem: their term for the phenomenon of people deciding when to have children without thinking about the costs of delay to the would-be doting-grandmothers. As women postpone childbearing, these delays compound intergenerationally. In the US, median age at first grandmotherhood shot up from 44 under 1960 birth patterns to 57 in 2024, cutting the average number of healthy years shared with grandchildren by nearly half. While social interaction and free childcare are important, the paper still drew critique over language such as families becoming “extinct” and grandmothers’ “rights”. Our own research on fertility decline points also to a ‘relationship recession’, financial constraints and housing costs as contributing factors in the dearth of grandkids – not simply insufficiently pushy grandparents-in-waiting.

Unlocking care. Burnham’s big, bold plan to end the triple lock ratchet and pour the savings into a National Care Service has, understandably, grabbed the headlines this week. Handily, a new Joseph Roundtree Foundation briefing lays out in grim detail the scale of the problem he’s trying to solve. Residential care costs between £1,000 and £1,400 a week. Even the poorest, lowest-saving couples who receive the most state support still hand over around £9,000 a year in “user charges” and low-income residents pay only slightly less than high income equivalents. Little wonder Dan Neidle has likened the whole thing to an arbitrary tax handed out by lottery. Free personal care won’t fix all of these problems, but any step towards a more compassionate and fairer system is welcome.

Le Rust Belt. We all want to see Britain growing, and here at RF we’ve long advocated for agglomeration (cities are good!), and the opportunities available within service industries to former manufacturing heartlands. This paper (free version) tracks how France’s rust belt, which lost 400,000 manufacturing jobs between 1975 and the late 2010s, was revived by a booming Luxembourg next door. By 2021, over a third of prime-age workers in border towns commuted across, earning 60 to 65 per cent more (!) than comparable French workers. Most strikingly, the workforce did not stick to manufacturing, with 60 per cent of the increase in cross-border employment driven by services. Employment rates rose by 7 percentage points, the population grew 15 per cent, incomes climbed and reliance on benefits fell (rents rose too, by around a third, the usual price of a booming local economy). Far-right and anti-EU voting also fell relative to similar regions: In the authors’ chipper words, former industrial regions “are not inherently rigid nor doomed to fall to anti-globalization backlash, but can and do adjust”. All relevant to the Government’s vision of regional renewal, but perhaps indicative that a ‘new age of industrialisation’ is not the only, or even the most effective, way to boost living standards.

Catch my drift? We’ve long banked on each generation living longer and healthier than the last. But a Substack warns that 50 could be the new 60 thanks to ‘generational health drift’, as younger generations seem to be seeing worsening health. In the US, those born in the 1950s (i.e. people now approaching their early 70s) have seen worsening mortality across most of their lives, and cohorts born twenty years later have also seen deaths rise in their 30s and early-40s. And it’s not just people dying sooner. In the UK, diabetes among 40-somethings almost doubled, from 3.1 per cent among Baby Boomers to 5.9 per cent among Gen X, while Gen Z have the highest childhood obesity rates. Younger generations reaching retirement age in worse health could magnify the fiscal and societal impacts of population ageing. In the words of the meme: not now, additional demographic burden on our overstretched health service!

I don’t blame you if this one passed you by, but last week the DWP shared the latest data on the benefit cap (which limits how much benefit income people can receive, although working parents and families with a disabled member are exempt). As you might expect, whenever benefit rates have increased – like in April 2024, when LHA was uprated – the number of households hitting the cap rises – because the value of the cap hasn’t changed since 2023. This explains the particularly steep rise in capped households in April of this year, following the welcome removal of the two child limit. That policy change meant that there will be 425,000 fewer children living in poverty by the end of the decade. But the red line in our chart makes clear that the increase in capped households this April was driven by households with children, meaning around 36,000 more households with children have been cut off from the material boost of the ending of the two child limit, and a 37 per cent increase in the number of capped households with children. Before its removal, the two child limit arbitrarily broke the link between a household’s needs and its entitlement. The benefit cap is no different. Families in Scotland can already receive payments from their local council to offset its impact, and any UK government wanting to do more to reduce child poverty should look hard at this capricious cap.

articles.title: Will Labour win the Holborn and St Pancras by-election?
articles.standfirst:
The Holborn and St Pancras by-election has been seized by the Green Party as an opportunity to challenge Labour’s hegemony over that seat. But, Paul Whiteley writes, past data on the correlation between general election and by-election results, Andy Burnham’s popularity, as well as the Party’s change of direction when it comes to Israel mean … Continued
The post Will Labour win the Holborn and St Pancras by-election? first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: The Holborn and St Pancras by-election has been seized by the Green Party as an opportunity to challenge Labour’s hegemony over that seat. But, Paul Whiteley writes, past data on the correlation between general election and by-election results, Andy Burnham’s popularity, as well as the Party’s change of direction when it comes to Israel mean Labour is very likely to win.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

The by-election in Holborn and St Pancras triggered by the retirement of Keir Starmer from the House of Commons takes place on 8 October. Altogether there are 15 candidates standing including representatives of the “big five” parties, Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, Greens and Reform. In addition, there is a candidate from Rupert Lowe’s “Restore Britain” Party and even a “Communist League” candidate.

Some of the candidates are well-known, including Zack Polanski the leader of the Green Party, George Galloway the former left-wing Labour MP who won the Rochdale by-election for the Respect party in March 2024. The Labour candidate replacing Keir Starmer is Sagal Abdi-Wali, the Leader of Camden Council.

In the 2024 general election Keir Starmer captured just under 49 per cent of the vote but the second place went to an independent called Andrew Feinstein who took a share of just under 19 per cent. He was a former Labour party member and was highly critical of Starmer’s lack of action in relation the Israeli retaliation for the Hamas attack in October 2023. The Israeli attacks have been described as a genocide by a United Nations Commission.
There is a lot of continuity between general election results and subsequent by-elections.

The 2021 Census showed that just under 20 per cent of the population in Holborn and St Pancras were Muslims. This religious dimension to the contest and the fact that the constituency has many university students who largely sympathise with the Palestinians explains this voting pattern. Both groups tended to support Feinstein.

The current by-election is being seen as a competition between Labour and the Greens, even though the latter party had a vote share of only 10 per cent in the general election. Despite this it has been suggested that the Green Party leader Zack Polanski could win the contest. The data suggest that’s highly unlikely.

One way of examining if this is possible is to look at the relationship between the Labour vote share in general elections and in subsequent by-elections over time. There have been 62 by-elections in Britain since the 2010 general election, and the chart shows the relationship between the two from 2010 to 2026. The relationship between Labour’s vote share at general elections and subsequent by-elections is very strong with a correlation of 0.78 (If the two variables were identical, the correlation would be 1.0 and if they were completely unrelated it would be zero). We can conclude therefore that there is a lot of continuity between general election results and subsequent by-elections.
The Relationship between the Labour vote share in by-elections and the previous General Election 2010 to 2026

We can use this relationship to forecast a vote share for Labour in the by-election. To improve the accuracy of the forecast we can add current voting intentions data from the YouGov tracking poll to the modelling. At the time of writing this was 23 per cent, more than twice the Green Party vote intentions at 11 per cent. The forecast results from the data is that Labour will get 40 per cent of the vote and win the by-election,subject to the usual caveats and possible errors associated with survey data.

This forecast is a baseline derived largely from historical data, but there are two other reasons why Labour may do better than this in the actual byelection. The first is the Andy Burnham effect which is still being felt as his time in 10 Downing Street has been relatively short. According to YouGov polling last month he was the most popular Prime Minister in the last six years.
The second reason why there is likely to be additional support for Labour relates to the change in policy on the Gaza war.

His net popularity rating (favourable minus unfavourable) was +13 per cent. This compares with a rating of -16 per cent for Kemi Badenoch, -29 per cent for ZaCk Polanski and -44 per cent for Nigel Farage. There is a common pattern to the leadership evaluations of the two insurgent parties, Reform and the Greens. Their leaders tended to be quite popular when these parties first achieved double figures in voting intentions and did well in the recent local elections. But as public scrutiny of them increased, they tended to lose ground. But the popularity of Labour’s leader is still high, so it’s likely that the by-election result will be boosted by a “Burnham effect”.

The second reason why there is likely to be additional support for Labour relates to the change in policy on the Gaza war. Andy Burnham apologized for Labour’s weak stance on the war and took a much stronger line on the attacks by Israel on the Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank. This is likely to change the votes of many people in Holborn and St Pancras who supported Feinstein in the general election.
Overall then we expect that Labour will have a comfortable win in the by-election.
Enjoyed this post? Sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.
All articles posted on this blog give the views of the author(s), and not the position of LSE British Politics and Policy, nor of the London School of Economics and Political Science.
Paul Whiteley is Emeritus Professor of Government at the University of Essex. His research interests are in electoral behaviour, public opinion, political economy and political methodology.

articles.title: Colorado’s Election Day Choice on Income Taxes
articles.standfirst: On Election Day, Coloradans will get to decide on two competing measures on income taxes: an initiated statute that would cap income taxes at the current 4.4 percent rate; and a constitutional amendment that would authorize a graduated-rate individual and corporate income tax, paired with an initiated statute setting new rates, with a top rate of 8.4 percent.
paragraphs: On Election Day, Coloradans will get to decide on two competing measures on income taxes: an initiated statute that would cap income taxes at the current 4.4 percent rate; and a constitutional amendment that would authorize a graduated-rate individual and corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax., paired with an initiated statute setting new rates, with a top rate of 8.4 percent.

Under Amendment 87, Colorado’s constitution would permit a graduated-rate income taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities., and the new higher rates would initially be set at 7.4 percent above $500,000, 7.9 percent above $750,000, and 8.4 percent above $1 million. Rates and brackets could be changed by the legislature at any time.

The proposal also embeds an extreme marriage penaltyA marriage penalty is when a household’s overall tax bill increases due to a couple marrying and filing taxes jointly. A marriage penalty typically occurs when two individuals with similar incomes marry; this is true for both high- and low-income couples. since bracket widths are the same for single filers and married couples filing jointly. A couple earning $25,000 each faces a marriage penalty of $125. A couple earning $500,000 each faces a marriage penalty of $16,575.

Colorado had a graduated-rate income tax until 1987, when it became the first state to switch from a graduated- to single-rate income tax. (Several other states have always had flat income taxes.) Before the transition, Colorado’s top rate had been 8 percent on income above $10,000 for 24 years. The new top rate became 5 percent, which had previously been the marginal rate between $4,000 and $5,000 in income (about $12,200 to $15,250 in today’s dollars).

The flat taxAn income tax is referred to as a “flat tax” when all taxable income is subject to the same tax rate, regardless of income level or assets. rate has been reduced multiple times and now sits at 4.4 percent. This is a feature of flat taxes: a rate on all income is harder to raise and more attractive to cut. Should Amendment 87 pass, the initial replacement rate schedule will only impose higher rates on income above $500,000, but the new rates would be statutory, while the authorization for a graduated-rate tax would be enshrined in the constitution, permitting the legislature to adjust rates later.

Currently, Colorado’s constitution “require[s] all taxable net income to be taxed at one rate, excluding refund tax credits or voter-approved tax credits, with no added tax or surcharge.” As amended, the provision would “require all taxable net income to be taxed with no added surcharge,” which eliminates the prohibition on a graduated-rate schedule but doesn’t entirely make sense. The unusual construction, however, has a purpose: by only eliminating constitutional language rather than adding any, the amendment can be ratified with a simple majority. Ordinarily, Colorado constitutional amendments require 55 percent to pass.

Colorado’s 731,000 small businesses employ almost 49 percent of all Colorado employees, and the vast majority of these businesses are pass-through businesses (e.g., S corporations, partnerships, and LLCs), meaning that their income is taxed on owners’ individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source return. According to Internal Revenue Service data, of the state’s 53,640 filers with adjusted gross incomeFor individuals, gross income is the total of all income received from any source before taxes or deductions. It includes wages, salaries, tips, interest, dividends, capital gains, rental income, alimony, pensions, and other forms of income. For businesses, gross income (or gross profit) is the sum of total receipts or sales minus the cost of goods sold (COGS)—the direct costs of producing goods above $500,000—those subject to higher marginal rates under the proposed tax increase—30,850 receive partnership or S corporationAn S corporation is a business entity which elects to pass business income and losses through to its shareholders. The shareholders are then responsible for paying individual income taxes on this income. Unlike subchapter C corporations, an S corporation (S corp) is not subject to the corporate income tax (CIT). income, and 14,310 have other business or professional income. Households earning $500,000 or more earn 27 percent more in business income than they do in wage income. In other words, high tax rates on those with incomes above $500,000 function, to a considerable degree, as higher taxes on small business ownership.

Higher rates would reduce small business profitability and put Colorado’s small businesses at a competitive disadvantage against out-of-state rivals. The result would be some combination of reduced investment and growth, business attrition, lower wages, and higher prices.

Economic decisions are made on the margin. When the tax rate on the next dollar of income rises, business owners are likely to hire fewer workers, delay capital investment, and scale back expansion plans. They may also try to raise prices. (Whether they have the ability to raise prices will depend significantly on the conditions under which their competitors are operating.)

Colorado’s higher tax rates, moreover, would apply to many people who aren’t what we ordinarily think of as wealthy. Many filers will report $500,000 or more in income only once or twice, such as when they sell their business or an investment property. For them, this is a surtaxA surtax is an additional tax levied on top of an already existing business or individual tax and can have a flat or progressive rate structure. Surtaxes are typically enacted to fund a specific program or initiative, whereas revenue from broader-based taxes, like the individual income tax, typically cover a multitude of programs and services. on retirement or the return on many years of entrepreneurship and risk-taking, where most of the gains are realized at once rather than spread out over the many years of work that went into earning them.

High top rates have backfired elsewhere. In California, where voters approved increases to top rates in 2012, a combination of out-migration, reduced in-state investment, slower economic growth, and tax avoidance strategies eroded an estimated 61 percent of the anticipated revenue gains and did broader harm to the state’s economy. New Jersey’s Department of the Treasury assessed that the 2004 adoption of a new top rate of 8.97 percent above $500,000 increased out-migration by 20,000 over the next five years. And in New York, the Citizens Budget Commission found that the state’s share of the nation’s millionaires fell from 12.7 percent in 2010 to 8.7 percent in 2022, estimating that the state would have collected an additional $10.7 billion in individual income tax revenue in 2022 had the share remained constant.

The measure raises the corporate income tax rate as well, establishing a graduated-rate income tax even though progressive rate schedules make very little sense for corporate income taxes. The size of a business is largely irrelevant to the income of shareholders. A low-income household might have shares of some of the world’s largest businesses in their 401(k), while wealthy households might have an ownership stake in a small corporation.

Colorado, like most states, uses single sales factor apportionmentApportionment is the determination of the percentage of a business’s profits subject to a given jurisdiction’s corporate income tax or other business tax. US states apportion business profits based on some combination of the percentage of company property, payroll, and sales located within their borders., meaning that a corporation is taxed by Colorado based on its share of sales in Colorado. As economists have noted, this functionally means that the corporate income tax functions as a tax on sales into the state, which shows up in higher prices. The tax is not costless for the state, nor simply borne by investors.

In stark contrast to Amendment 87, another measure on the ballot, Proposition 136, would statutorily cap individual and corporate income tax rates at their current rate of 4.4 percent. As a statutory change, it also only requires a simple majority to pass, but it is not particularly binding. Voters could later repeal it with another simple-majority vote, and the legislature can amend statutes, so it imposes no new restriction on the legislature’s ability to raise income tax rates beyond the political constraint of adopting something contrary to a prior vote of the people. The significant constraint is TABOR, which already requires voter approval of any rate increase. Proposition 136 primarily functions as an alternative to Amendment 87, which would override its key provisions if both passed.

If both Amendment 87 and Proposition 136 pass, the one with the most votes would prevail on any conflicting provisions. This means that if both passed with Proposition 136 receiving more votes, graduated rate taxation would be permitted, but the top rate could not exceed 4.4 percent. A straightforward reading of both measures suggests that, if Proposition 136 received more votes, it would strike rates above 4.4 percent, leaving high income entirely untaxed given how the Proposition 87 statute is written. Such an outcome, however, is clearly not intended and would create other textual tensions, so it seems probable that courts would allow all higher income to be taxed at 4.4 percent. The state’s ballot information book (the “Blue Book”), however, acknowledges that the outcome of any conflict of the two measures is unclear and would have to be resolved by the courts.

At a 4.4 percent rate, Colorado is competitive with regional peers, many of which have cut income tax rates in recent years. But states are increasingly diverging on income taxes, with many pursuing low rates while a smaller number of states double down on much higher rates. Voters will get to decide which side of the divide Colorado joins.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.
Jared Walczak is a Senior Fellow at the Tax Foundation, where he spent five years as Vice President of State Projects, and president of Walczak Policy Consulting.

articles.title: September Round-up
articles.standfirst:
Welcome to this month’s round-up – it’s a special one! This month we published First Jobs, New Barriers, our deep dive into how technology can support young people without degrees as they move from education into work. It asks how technology can help young people – especially those without university degrees – get into work. … Continued
The post September Round-up appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This month we published First Jobs, New Barriers, our deep dive into how technology can support young people without degrees as they move from education into work. It asks how technology can help young people – especially those without university degrees – get into work.
For founders and investors in this space, it doubles as a map of where the gaps are – and where we hope they will build and invest. So we’ve decided to give it the full spotlight this issue.

Young non-graduates face the steepest transition into work, yet they’re the least well served by the tools built for it. In our experience as investors, most job-search platforms, mentoring services and career tools tend to target graduates, who already carry a degree, a network and an earnings cushion to soften an early stumble.
Four distinct gaps where there lie problems (in need of solutions)
We break this transition into four elements, each a question a young person has to answer, and each with points of failure a well-designed product could address:

Resilience and confidence. 76 per cent of young people in one survey said their wellbeing affects their ability to look for work. A poor search knocks confidence, which makes the next application harder.
Above, we’ve set out where the gaps are, but the harder question is what actually works to close them.

In the full report we give our view on the design principles that separate tools that reach this group from tools that lose them, and the single constraint that we think decides whether any of them survive contact with the market.
Read the full report for where we think founders should build, and what design principles they should follow to succeed. Read here: First Jobs, New Barriers.
We accept applications from WorkerTech ventures on a rolling basis. You can book a slot in our office hours for an initial conversation.

articles.title: Hope at last for social care reform?
articles.standfirst:
Andy Burnham’s first speech to the Labour Party Conference as Prime Minister set out his ambition to build a National Care Service based on universal principles where everyone contributes and everyone benefits. Melanie Henwood considers what this might look like and whether there is finally hope for lasting and meaningful reform of adult social care. … Continued
The post Hope at last for social care reform? first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: Andy Burnham’s first speech to the Labour Party Conference as Prime Minister set out his ambition to build a National Care Service based on universal principles where everyone contributes and everyone benefits. Melanie Henwood considers what this might look like and whether there is finally hope for lasting and meaningful reform of adult social care.

Andy Burnham’s long-held personal ambitions to reform social care are a surprise to no one, and characterised his approach when he was previously a member of parliament from 2010 t0 2017. His speech in Downing Street on his return to Westminster as Prime Minister in July 2026 included a commitment to “put the care of people at the heart of everything I do.” The failed social care system was identified as a major challenge that has let people down for decades.

So far, so familiar – the story of social care is well known from the time of the Blair government’s Royal Commission on Long Term Care in 1999 (the Sutherland Commission) there have been 12 green papers and white papers, five independent reviews and commissions None have resulted in reform and the current Independent Commission on Adult Social Care being led by Dame Louise Casey is ongoing.

But Andy Burnham’s first speech as Prime Minister to the Labour Party Conference on 29 September set out a direction of travel that had first been trailed two days earlier in the Sunday interview with Laura Kuenssberg. In place of a broken social care system that threatens also to break the NHS, the Prime Minister concluded there is only one real answer – a National Care Service, that will operate on the same universal principles as the National Health Service.

The idea of a National Care Service has surfaced before; Gordon Brown’s government (in which Andy Burnham was then Health Secretary) went into the 2010 General Election pledging to build such a model of free personal care. The opposition attacked the policy proposals as a ‘death tax’ and Labour lost the election.

In 2011 the Dilnot report on fairer care funding commissioned by the coalition government offered a model not of free personal care for all, but a capped cost approach that would limit people’s lifetime liability to £35,000. The principle of a capped cost approach (although not the financial amount) was accepted and introduced in the 2014 Care Act, although implementation was repeatedly deferred and ultimately shelved in 2025 by the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves.

Make no mistake about the scale of ambition here – to deliver something as comprehensive and universal as this, with no care charges, which is fully funded and affordable, would be an achievement comparable to the Beveridge Report and creation of the welfare state in 1948.

Andy Burnham is not – it would appear – suggesting a further iteration of a capped cost approach, but a National Care Service as “a landmark policy as significant as the creation of the NHS itself.” Make no mistake about the scale of ambition here – to deliver something as comprehensive and universal as this, with no care charges, which is fully funded and affordable, would be an achievement comparable to the 1942 Beveridge Report and the creation of the welfare state and NHS in 1948.

Burnham’s personal commitment and passion are not in doubt; he is driven not least by the experience of his own family, including his late father. Nothing is going to happen overnight, and Burnham has indicated that the model will be integral to the next Labour manifesto for the general election anticipated in 2029. That might offer little hope for today’s older citizens and others who draw on social care services or who expect that they will need to in the near future; it sounds like more promise of jam tomorrow that have plagued this area of policy for years. But there is some benefit in this potential window of three years that Burnham describes as “laying the ground” for the national care service that would be introduced in the next parliament. In that time, he and the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care will be advised by Baroness Casey and “will seek to build the maximum national consensus around her recommendations.” Building consensus and forging a way through the weeds of previous failed attempts at reform will be hard won; Burnham himself acknowledges the likely personal political cost but has set his determination to bring about lasting change as a test of his leadership.

Successive governments of all colours have grappled with the dilemma of reforming social care. None has managed to get close to implementing reform. The Prime Minister referred to the failings as an “indictment of my generation of politicians, myself included. Too cowardly to fix something as basic as the care we give to each other.” If this time is to be different, and if – as Andy Burnham has pledged – this reform will offer “a new social contract for the 21st century,” that will be a massive political achievement and offer dignity and freedom from catastrophic personal costs in place of a lottery of what care is covered by the NHS and what is deemed to be the responsibility of individuals and their families. The following challenges are likely to be the most significant:

Andy Burnham has stated that the pensions triple lock will remain in place for this parliament, but thereafter adjustments will be made that will generate “significant savings” to fund the National Care Service. This doesn’t leave pensioners unprotected, and the state pension will continue to rise each year “at least by prices or 2.5 per cent,” and over the long term will keep pace with average earnings. The scale of savings that will be generated is unclear (although an annual figure of £15 billion over ten years has been suggested) but this is highly unlikely – of itself – to be sufficient. Previous attempts to reform social care have foundered on the rocks of affordability, and those models were less ambitious than this.

Burnham was careful to speak of care being “free at the point of use,” which leaves room for a hybrid co-payment model where people still contribute to the “hotel” elements of their care costs (similar to earlier proposals), which is closer to the approach adopted in Scotland.

The lack of detail about the structure and funding of the National Care Service that has been provided at this stage is frustrating but also leaves some loose ends. Burnham was careful to speak of care being “free at the point of use,” which leaves room for a hybrid co-payment model where people still contribute to the “hotel” elements of their care costs (similar to earlier proposals), which is closer to the approach adopted in Scotland. Even so, “free care” would be a major departure from the existing approach or from a capped cost, and much closer to the recommendations from the Sutherland Commission. The details have yet to be worked through and this will be a major task for Baroness Casey’s Big Conversation with the public.

Free care would enable people to be supported at home for longer rather than entering residential care, but to provide the level of care needed by many people would require longer and more frequent visits by home care staff. The implications for recruiting, retaining and adequately supporting the social care workforce are immense, while questions about eligibility and access to care must also be unravelled without creating a cumbersome bureaucratic process.

There are significant risks of social care being framed as an issue that is only about the care and support of older people; it isn’t. At least one third of social care support is concerned with younger disabled adults, but most of this support is community rather than residential-based, and far more of it is funded by local councils than by the disabled adults themselves. The people who face the greatest residential costs and are currently likely to have to fund it themselves are in the main older people who must use their assets and savings and stand to benefit most from the prospect of free care. It is too simplistic to see the interests of one part of the population as antithetical to those of other cohorts. Indeed, Andy Burnham’s speech carefully followed the announcement on the National Care Service by turning his focus to young people and the importance of investing in opportunity and a genuine philosophy of social security rather than “paying for failure” through the benefits system.

The risks of demonising the older population as an unaffordable cost on public finances are real. But equity between generations happens over time: we can all aspire to grow older and live a meaningful and heathy later life, but we may need support to do so. Young people who might view social care as remote from them and all about subsidising generations other than theirs will one day also be the cohort that may need care and support. All of us are touched in some way by the reality of the currently broken social care system – if not directly, then through the experience of parents, grandparents, other family and friends.

The changes in demography and life expectancy over the decades since Beveridge are both significant and a huge positive achievement. However, longer life is often accompanied by a longer proportion of life spent with needs for care and support, just as the survival of people with life-long or acquired disabilities also brings different needs for support than were anticipated by the model of social security and the NHS developed in the post-war years. Finally, the sustainability of the new approach is fundamental, and this might be the biggest challenge of all, and certainly underlines the importance of building the Big Conversation and establishing cross-Party consensus and commitment over the next three years. The worst of all worlds would be to embark on an ambitious model for a National Care Service only for it to be undermined and cancelled by a future administration. Hope alone will not be enough.

Melanie Henwood is an independent health and social care research consultant and a Visiting Research Fellow with the Institute of Public Care, at Oxford Brookes University. She has been a Specialist Adviser to the House of Commons Health Select Committee. She has also been a visiting fellow with the Personal Social Services Research Unit of the London School of Economics, and also previously held visiting fellowships with the Nuffield Institute of the University of Leeds, and with the Social Policy Research Centre, University of New South Wales, Australia.

articles.title: Inflation Costs New Jerseyans More than a Rebate Check
articles.standfirst: Missing out on a tax rebate check is certainly disheartening, but New Jersey wallets are getting actively drained by an even bigger problem in the tax code: the state’s graduated-rate income tax thresholds don’t change with inflation, either.
paragraphs: In a little over a week, New Jerseyans will be checking their mailboxes for a property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. rebate courtesy of the ANCHOR property tax relief program. But many of those boxes will turn up empty: after all, the ANCHOR gross incomeFor individuals, gross income is the total of all income received from any source before taxes or deductions. It includes wages, salaries, tips, interest, dividends, capital gains, rental income, alimony, pensions, and other forms of income. For businesses, gross income (or gross profit) is the sum of total receipts or sales minus the cost of goods sold (COGS)—the direct costs of producing goods cutoff of $250,000 has not risen with inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin since the first rebate checks were sent in 2023 based on residents’ 2019 income.

If someone surpassed that income threshold by even a few dollars in 2025, they get no check at all this year. With prices rising by about 26 percent between 2019 and 2025, many New Jerseyans who got a rebate before and saw their incomes keep pace with inflation will be check-less.

Missing out on a rebate is certainly disheartening, but New Jersey wallets are getting actively drained by an even bigger problem in the taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. code: the state’s graduated-rate income tax thresholds don’t change with inflation, either.
This is a preview of our full op-ed originally published in NJ Spotlight News.
